pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.advisor
children.doc:
Diagnostics and suggestions: what in a benchmark's setup is likely to hurt its result, with the evidence and a fix.

Every item is measured from the run (the training histories, the error-versus-budget levels, the checks, the data);
nothing is a generic tip. Each has a severity (error / warning / info), the evidence, the suggested change and, where
possible, the exact configuration edit (``apply`` writes a new configuration with them for review).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.api
children.doc:
``pp.benchmark``: prepare -> validate -> run -> report, with correctness gates and an advisor.

import pinneapple as pp
res = pp.benchmark.run(problems=["burgers", "darcy"], methods=["pinn", "fno", "deeponet"],
                       budget=pp.ComputeBudget(wall_s=300), budget_levels=[1/9, 1/3, 1], seeds=3, n_trials=4,
                       equal_flops=True, n_workers=4, out_dir="results/my_benchmark")
res.table(); res.report(); res.diagnostics

``airfoil``: the aero app's 2-D airfoil (issue #299). OpenFOAM v1912 simpleFoam, k-omega SST, Re 4e6, the app's
O-grid (pinneapple_design.aero). Data: Latin-hypercube CST shapes x angles plus the NACA polars (the app's campaign,
apps/aero_optimizer/tools/generate_dataset.py), and an OOD set (sections outside the CST box, angles below the range).
Methods: MLP (integrals), POD + MLP (fields), MeshGraphNet (both), PINNs per geometry (potential flow, RANS).
Needs OpenFOAM for ``prepare`` (``/usr/share/openfoam/etc/bashrc``, or ``FOAM_BASHRC``).

nodes. Cached in ``panel_reference.json``.

against the panel method's), and where its collocation points are.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.builtin.fields
children.doc:
Field-operator problems (input field -> output field on a grid) and the generic methods that learn them.

``FieldOperatorProblem`` reads ``prepared/<id>/data.npz`` with ``{train,val,test,ood}_{x,y}`` arrays; subclasses
generate it (``generate``) and may add a PINN formulation (``pinn_setup``). ``ArrayProblem`` wraps a user's own arrays.
Methods: FNO (``pinneapple_neural ... fno``), DeepONet (``... deeponet``), PINN (``PINNFactory``), all trained under a
``ComputeBudget`` with ``train_within_budget``.

classes.doc: The prepared arrays with pointwise Gaussian normalisers computed on the training split only.

classes.name: FieldOperatorProblem

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.builtin.standard
children.doc:
The standard operator-learning problems (Li et al. 2021, "Fourier Neural Operator for Parametric PDEs"), data from
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks``:

* ``burgers``: u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx, periodic [0, 1), u(., 0) -> u(., T).
* ``darcy``: -div(a grad u) = 1 on the unit square, u = 0 on the boundary, a -> u.
* ``navier_stokes``: 2-D vorticity, periodic, Li et al. forcing, w(., 0) -> w(., T).

Each has its PINN formulation (hard initial/boundary conditions, PINNFactory residual) and an exact solution of its
PDE that the residual gate runs through the same compiled residual.

methods.name: checks_pinn
methods.doc: The residual gate needs an exact solution: run it on a constant coefficient (a = 3) of the same PDE.

classes.name: Bilinear
classes.sig: (a: np.ndarray)
classes.doc:

outermost centres are held constant. No autograd: the coefficient does not depend on the network.

functions.name: HardNet
functions.sig: (problem: str, cfg: dict, init = None, t_end: float = 10.0)
functions.doc:
A library NeuralNetwork with input features and hard initial/boundary conditions:

burgers: (x, t) -> u = u0(x) + t N(sin 2pi kx, cos 2pi kx, 2t - 1), k = 1, 2
darcy: (x, y) -> u = 16 x(1-x) y(1-y) 0.1 N(2x - 1, 2y - 1)
navier_stokes: (x, y, t) -> w = w0(x, y) + (t/T) N_w, psi = N_psi / (4 pi^2)

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.checks
children.doc:
Correctness gates of a benchmark run.

* Architecture gates (before any training): each method's ``architecture_checks`` on its first search configuration:
  forward shapes and dtype, parameter count, FNO modes <= Nyquist and resolution invariance, DeepONet branch/trunk
  shapes, MeshGraphNet permutation equivariance, PINN autograd vs finite differences and the residual of an exact
  solution, and that the model can overfit a tiny batch.
* Training gates (after the runs, from every run file): loss finite and decreasing, divergence, "did not learn"
  (final loss not below half the initial one, or an error no better than the trivial prediction), the budget enforced,
  identical accounting across methods, evaluation off the clock, no test data in the search, train/validation gap,
  seed spread (veriphysics tolerance), and a determinism spot-check (same seed, same steps, same result).

Every check is recorded (pass / FAIL / warn / n/a with its value); none is skipped silently.

classes.name: BenchmarkConfig
classes.doc:
Everything a benchmark run depends on.

``problems`` / ``methods``: registered ids (``pp.benchmark.problems()``, ``methods()``) or objects.
``budget``: the full training budget of one run (``ComputeBudget`` or a dict ``{wall_s|flops|steps: ...}``);
``problem_budgets`` overrides it per problem. ``budget_levels``: fractions of it trained for the error-versus-budget
curves (the largest must be 1). ``seeds``: number of seeds (0..seeds-1). ``n_trials`` configurations per method in
the search, each trained for ``search_fraction`` of the budget on validation data only. ``equal_flops``: True for
every problem, False, or a list of problem ids. ``threads_per_run`` threads per training process, ``n_workers``
processes at a time. ``smoke``: tiny data and budgets, a pipeline check in minutes. ``skip_checks`` /
``allow_failed_validation``: run anyway; the report then says so on every page.
``budget_study``: ``{problem: {method: [wall-clock seconds, ...]}}``, extra runs of the best configuration (seed 0,
the problem's study instances) at budgets beyond the full one: is a method budget-limited? ``ablations``:
``{problem: {method: {name: {hyper-parameter: value}}}}``, the best configuration with these changes at the full
budget on the problem's audit instance, compared with the unchanged run (a setup audit).

methods.doc:

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.benchmark.registry
children.doc:
Problems and methods: base classes, the registry and the decorators that extend it.

A **Problem** owns its data (``prepare`` writes it, with its generation cost, into ``out_dir/prepared/<id>/``), the
verification of its reference solver, the data checks, the metrics (``columns``) and how a method's raw result maps to
them (``extract``). A **Method** declares its hyper-parameter grid (``space``) and trains under a ``ComputeBudget``
(``train``). A problem may carry its own implementation of a method as ``train_<method id>`` (the airfoil's
MeshGraphNet, the inverse-heat PINN); generic methods (FNO, DeepONet, PINN) work on any field-operator problem,
including a user's own arrays (``ArrayProblem``).

Register your own with the decorators::

    @pp.benchmark.register_problem("my_flow")
    class MyFlow(pp.benchmark.ArrayProblem): ...

    @pp.benchmark.register_method("my_net")
    class MyNet(pp.benchmark.Method): ...

children.doc:
Equal-budget benchmarks of physics-AI methods: prepare -> validate -> run -> report.

``run`` (or the CLI ``pinneapple benchmark run``) trains every method on every problem under the same
``ComputeBudget``, with an equal hyper-parameter search, several seeds and budget levels, an equal-FLOPs arm, and writes
everything to ``out_dir`` (re-running resumes from its cache). Correctness gates run by default (problem, data,
architecture, training) and are recorded; the report has a Validation section (PINNeAPPle's validation stack on the
prepared artifacts), a trust card and an advisor's "Diagnostics and suggestions".

Extend it with ``@register_problem`` / ``@register_method``, or wrap your arrays with ``ArrayProblem``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.cost
pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget
children.doc:
Equal-budget comparison of methods: a compute budget, a training loop that stops at it, FLOPs, search, amortised cost.

Comparing a PINN with a neural operator or a graph network is only fair when every method gets the same compute.
This module provides the pieces a benchmark needs to enforce and report that, independent of the model family:

``ComputeBudget``
    a wall-clock, FLOP and/or step limit; training stops at whichever is reached first.
``count_flops``
    FLOPs of one call, counted with PyTorch's own per-operator formulas (``torch.utils.flop_counter``) plus FFTs.
    Unlike ``FlopCounterMode`` it works around ``torch.autograd.grad`` (PINN residuals), because it does not install
    module hooks.
``train_within_budget``
    runs ``step(progress)`` until the budget is spent; ``progress`` in [0, 1] drives budget-aware schedules
    (``cosine_lr``); optional evaluations pause the clock so they are not charged to the method.
``equal_budget_search``
    random search with the same number of trials (and, by the caller, the same budget per trial) for every method.
``AmortizedCost``
    data-generation, training and inference cost, per new query and for ``n`` queries; break-even against another.
``relative_l2``, ``time_per_query``, ``hardware_record``
    the metrics and the hardware line every equal-budget table needs.

What is counted as a FLOP: matrix products, convolutions and attention (PyTorch's formula registry, one
multiply-add = 2 FLOPs) and FFTs (``5 N log2 N`` for a complex transform of length ``N``, half that for a real
one). Elementwise operations (activations, residual arithmetic) are not counted, as in PyTorch's own counter;
they matter for small MLPs, which is why the wall-clock budget is the primary one and FLOPs are reported with it.

classes.name: ComputeBudget
classes.doc: A training budget: any combination of wall-clock seconds, FLOPs and optimiser steps (``None`` = no limit).

methods.name: fraction
methods.sig: (wall_s: float, flops: float, steps: int) -> float
methods.doc: Fraction of the budget used: the largest over the limits that are set (1.0 = spent).

methods.name: scaled
methods.doc: The same budget times ``factor`` (for error-versus-budget curves).

classes.name: BudgetRun
classes.doc: What a budgeted training run used and how it went.

classes.name: AmortizedCost
classes.doc:
Cost of answering new queries, in seconds (or any one unit used throughout).

``data_s``: generating the training data (simulations), paid once. ``train_s``: training, paid once.
``infer_s``: one new query. ``per_query_train_s``: training that every new query needs again (a PINN trained
per instance has ``train_s = 0`` and ``per_query_train_s`` = its training time).

methods.name: break_even
methods.doc: Number of queries above which ``self`` is cheaper in total than ``other`` (None: never, 0: always).

functions.name: count_flops
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[], Any]) -> tuple[int, dict[str, int], Any]
functions.doc:
Run ``fn()`` once and count its FLOPs, forward and backward (including ``torch.autograd.grad``).

Returns ``(total, per_operator, fn_result)``. See the module docstring for what counts as a FLOP.

functions.name: cosine_lr
functions.sig: (progress: float, lr0: float, final_fraction: float = 0.03) -> float
functions.doc: Cosine decay from ``lr0`` to ``final_fraction * lr0`` over the budget (``progress`` in [0, 1]).

functions.name: set_lr
functions.sig: (optimizer, lr: float) -> None

functions.name: train_within_budget
functions.sig: (step: Callable[[float], float | None], budget: ComputeBudget, *, flops_per_step: float | None = None, count_first_step: bool = True, evaluate: Callable[[], Any] | None = None, eval_at: Sequence[float] = (), log_every_s: float = 5.0, checkpoint: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], None] | None = None, checkpoint_every_s: float = 300.0, resume: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> BudgetRun
functions.doc:
Call ``step(progress)`` (one optimiser step; may return the loss) until ``budget`` is spent.

``progress`` is the fraction of the budget used before the step, so a schedule such as ``cosine_lr`` reaches its
end exactly when the budget does, whatever the budget is.

FLOPs: with ``flops_per_step`` given it is used; otherwise, with ``count_first_step``, the first step is run
under ``count_flops`` (that step's FLOPs count towards the budget; its time does not, because counting slows it
down). Steps must then cost the same FLOPs each (fixed batch shapes), which is the usual case.

``evaluate`` is called when progress first reaches each fraction in ``eval_at`` and at the end; the clock is
paused while it runs, so evaluation is never charged to the method. Its results go into ``history``.

Long runs: every ``checkpoint_every_s`` seconds of training, ``checkpoint(state)`` is called with the loop's
accounting (steps, wall clock, FLOPs, history); save it with the model and optimiser. Passing that ``state`` back
as ``resume`` continues the same budget where it stopped (the time spent saving is not charged).

functions.name: equal_budget_search
functions.sig: (space: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]], objective: Callable[[dict[str, Any]], Any], *, n_trials: int, seed: int = 0, minimize: bool = True) -> SearchResult
functions.doc:
Random search over the grid ``space`` with exactly ``n_trials`` distinct configurations.

Give every method the same ``n_trials`` and the same budget per trial (inside ``objective``) and the search
effort is equal. ``objective(config)`` returns a score, or ``(score, info)``; non-finite scores lose.
If the grid has fewer than ``n_trials`` points, every point is tried (and ``n_trials`` reports that number).

functions.name: relative_l2
functions.sig: (pred, true, *, sample_axis: int = 0, eps: float = 1e-12) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Per-sample relative L2 error ``||pred - true|| / ||true||`` over every axis except ``sample_axis``.

functions.name: time_per_query
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[], Any], *, repeats: int = 20, warmup: int = 3, n_per_call: int = 1, no_grad: bool = True) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Median wall time of ``fn()`` divided by ``n_per_call`` (instances answered per call), under ``no_grad``
unless ``no_grad=False`` (a query that needs derivatives, e.g. a PINN's velocity from its stream function).

functions.name: hardware_record
functions.sig: () -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: CPU model, cores, memory, GPU, library versions and thread count: the line every budget table needs.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.cost.profiler
children.doc:
Computational-cost validation per operation: measure, fit scaling, check budgets, catch regressions.

Three questions this answers about any operation (a solver step, a model forward pass, a residual
evaluation, an export):

1. **How much does it cost?** ``measure`` returns wall time (median of repeats, with spread), peak
   memory and, for PyTorch work, the exact FLOP count.
2. **How does the cost grow?** ``scaling_study`` runs the operation over problem sizes, fits the
   exponent ``k`` in ``cost ~ n^k`` with a bootstrap confidence interval, and compares it with the
   complexity the author *declared* (``"n log n"``, ``"n^2"``, ...).
3. **Did it get worse?** ``Budget`` turns limits into pass/fail, and ``CostLedger`` saves a baseline and
   flags regressions. FLOP counts are deterministic, so they gate strictly; wall time is noisy, so it gates
   loosely.

What is and is not measured (read before trusting a number):

- FLOPs come from ``torch.utils.flop_counter`` and only count PyTorch operators (matmul, conv,
  attention, ...). NumPy / SciPy / pure-Python work reports ``flops=None``, never a guess. Around
  ``torch.autograd.grad`` the flop counter cannot run, so the profiler's matmul/conv count is used and
  ``flops_source="profiler"`` marks it as a lower bound.
- Peak memory: CUDA via ``torch.cuda.max_memory_allocated``; CPU via sampled process RSS when ``psutil`` is
  installed (``mem_source="rss"``), otherwise ``tracemalloc`` (Python + NumPy only, ``mem_source=
  "tracemalloc"``, which does not see PyTorch CPU tensors). RSS sampling can miss allocations that are
  reused or shorter than the sampling interval, so treat CPU memory as a lower bound.
- Time is wall clock on the machine that runs it; compare numbers only across runs on the same machine.

methods.name: max_size_within
methods.doc: Largest ``n`` whose predicted cost stays within ``budget`` (extrapolation: use with care).

classes.name: Budget
classes.doc: Limits for one operation. Any limit left as ``None`` is not checked.

methods.name: check
methods.doc: Violations as readable strings; an empty list means the budget holds.

classes.name: CostLedger
classes.doc: Named operations with their costs; save a baseline, compare later runs against it.

methods.name: track
methods.doc:
Decorator: each call measures the function (it runs ``warmup + repeats`` times plus one run each for
FLOPs and memory, so use it on side-effect-free operations), stores the record and returns the result.

methods.name: compare
methods.sig: (baseline: 'CostLedger', *, time_factor: float = 1.5, flops_factor: float = 1.05, mem_factor: float = 1.5) -> List[Regression]
methods.doc:
Operations that got worse than ``baseline``. FLOPs gate tightly (deterministic), time and memory
loosely (noisy). Operations missing from either side are ignored.

functions.name: measure
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[..., Any], *args, repeats: int = 5, warmup: int = 1, name: Optional[str] = None, flops: bool = True, memory: bool = True, size: Optional[float] = None, **kwargs) -> CostRecord
functions.doc:
Cost of one operation ``fn(*args, **kwargs)``.

Time is the median of ``repeats`` timed runs after ``warmup`` untimed ones; FLOPs and peak memory are
measured in separate runs so they do not perturb the timing.

functions.name: expected_exponent
functions.sig: (declared: Union[str, float], sizes: Sequence[float]) -> float
functions.doc: Log-log slope of the declared complexity over the sizes actually used (``n log n`` is not 1.0).

functions.name: scaling_study
functions.sig: (make_call: Callable[[int], Callable[[], Any]], sizes: Sequence[int], *, name: str = 'operation', repeats: int = 5, warmup: int = 1, declared: Optional[Union[str, float]] = None, declared_flops: Optional[Union[str, float]] = None, tolerance: float = 0.15, n_boot: int = 300, seed: int = 0, memory: bool = False) -> ScalingStudy
functions.doc:
Measure an operation over problem sizes and fit ``cost ~ n^k`` for time (and FLOPs when countable).

``make_call(n)`` builds the inputs for size ``n`` and returns a zero-argument callable; the setup is not
timed. Use at least 4 sizes spanning a factor of 10 or more, and sizes large enough that the run takes well
over a millisecond, otherwise fixed overheads flatten the fit (the R2 and the CI width say so).
``tolerance`` is the slack in the exponent when comparing with ``declared``.

children.summary: Computational-cost validation per operation: measure, fit scaling, check budgets, catch regressions.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.cost.torch_ops
children.doc:
Cost per operation for PyTorch models: the PINN training step broken into its parts, and a per-operator table.

``pinn_operation_costs`` answers "where does one PINN training step spend its time and FLOPs": forward
pass, first derivatives, second derivatives (the PDE residual's Laplacian), loss backward, optimizer step.
Derivative cost is why a PINN step costs several times a plain network step; this makes the ratio visible.

functions.name: pinn_operation_costs
functions.sig: (model, x, *, repeats: int = 5, warmup: int = 1, optimizer = None) -> Dict[str, CostRecord]
functions.doc:
Cost of each stage of a PINN step on collocation points ``x`` of shape ``(N, d)``.

Stages (each measured on its own, so ``backward`` includes the graph it needs):

- ``forward``: ``u = model(x)``
- ``grad1``: ``du/dx`` by autograd (``create_graph=True``, as in a residual)
- ``grad2``: the Laplacian ``sum_i d2u/dx_i^2`` (second derivatives, the usual PDE-residual cost)
- ``backward``: ``loss.backward()`` through the residual (a real PINN loss)
- ``step``: one optimizer step (default Adam), if ``optimizer`` is not passed

functions.name: profile_ops
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[], Any], *, top: int = 15, sort_by: str = 'self_cpu_time_total') -> List[Dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: Per-PyTorch-operator table for one call: calls, self CPU time (ms) and FLOPs (matmul/conv/attention).

children.summary: Cost per operation for PyTorch models: the PINN training step broken into its parts, and a per-operator table.

children.doc:
Computational-cost validation per operation (time, memory, FLOPs, scaling, budgets, regressions).

>>> from pinneapple_analysis.cost import measure, scaling_study, Budget
>>> rec = measure(lambda: sum(range(10**6)), repeats=5)
>>> study = scaling_study(lambda n: (lambda a=list(range(n)): sorted(a)), [10**4, 10**5, 10**6],
...                       declared="n log n")
>>> print(study.summary())
>>> Budget(max_time_s=2.0, max_time_exponent=1.3).validate(study)

``ComputeBudget``, ``train_within_budget``, ``count_flops``, ``equal_budget_search``, ``AmortizedCost``.

See ``profiler`` for exactly what is and is not measured.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation
pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation.models
children.doc:
Small chaotic models used to test data-assimilation methods, written in PyTorch so they are differentiable.

* Lorenz-96 (Lorenz 1996, "Predictability: a problem partly solved", ECMWF Seminar):
  dx_i/dt = (x_{i+1} - x_{i-2}) x_{i-1} - x_i + F, cyclic; F = 8 gives chaos with a doubling time of ~0.4 time
  units for 40 variables, the standard data-assimilation test bed.
* Lorenz-63 (Lorenz 1963, J. Atmos. Sci. 20:130).

Each model step is one RK4 step of size ``dt`` and accepts batched states (..., n).

functions.sig: (f, x: torch.Tensor, dt: float) -> torch.Tensor

functions.name: lorenz96_tendency
functions.sig: (x: torch.Tensor, F: float = 8.0) -> torch.Tensor

functions.name: lorenz96_step
functions.sig: (x: torch.Tensor, dt: float = 0.05, F: float = 8.0) -> torch.Tensor

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation.sensor_placement
children.doc:
Field reconstruction from sparse sensors with a Gaussian process, and greedy placement of the next sensors.

:class:`GaussianProcessField` is a small NumPy Gaussian process with an anisotropic Matern kernel (Rasmussen &
Williams 2006, eq. 4.14-4.17; nu in {1/2, 3/2, 5/2, inf}), a fixed or data-mean prior, Cholesky-based posterior
mean and variance (algorithm 2.1), closed-form leave-one-out residuals (eq. 5.12) and an optional fit of the
hyper-parameters by maximising the log marginal likelihood (eq. 5.8) with ``scipy.optimize.minimize``.

:func:`greedy_sensor_placement` chooses sensor locations one at a time among candidate points, each time taking the
candidate that most reduces the integrated posterior variance ``sum_x w(x) var(f(x) | sensors)`` over a set of
domain points. The posterior variance of a Gaussian process does not depend on the measured values, so the design
needs only the kernel. Greedy selection of GP sensor locations and its near-optimality for submodular criteria are
studied by Krause, Singh & Guestrin (2008); for the variance-reduction criterion see also Das & Kempe (2008). Adding
a sensor at ``c`` lowers the posterior covariance by the rank-one term
``Sigma(:, c) Sigma(c, :) / (Sigma(c, c) + noise)``, so each greedy step costs one pass over the candidates.

References
----------
Rasmussen, C. E. & Williams, C. K. I. (2006). *Gaussian Processes for Machine Learning*. MIT Press.

Krause, A., Singh, A. & Guestrin, C. (2008). Near-optimal sensor placements in Gaussian processes: theory, efficient
algorithms and empirical studies. *J. Mach. Learn. Res.* 9, 235-284.

Das, A. & Kempe, D. (2008). Algorithms for subset selection in linear regression. *Proc. 40th ACM STOC*, 45-54.

classes.name: GaussianProcessField
classes.sig: (lengthscales = 1.0, variance: float = 1.0, nu: float = 2.5, noise: float = 1e-10, mean: float | str = 0.0) -> None
classes.doc:
Gaussian-process regression of a scalar field from point sensors (Rasmussen & Williams 2006, ch. 2).

Parameters
----------
lengthscales : Matern length scale per input dimension (scalar for isotropic), in the units of ``X``.
variance : prior variance ``s2`` of the field, in (field units)^2.
nu : Matern smoothness, 0.5, 1.5, 2.5 or ``np.inf`` (squared exponential).
noise : variance of the sensor noise added to the diagonal of the training covariance.
mean : prior mean, a float, or ``"data"`` for the sample mean of ``y`` at :meth:`fit` (held fixed afterwards,
    including in :meth:`loo`).

methods.name: kernel
methods.doc: Prior covariance between the rows of ``A`` and ``B``.

methods.name: fit
methods.doc: Condition on sensor positions ``X`` (n, d) and readings ``y`` (n,).

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (Xs, return_std: bool = False, return_cov: bool = False)
methods.doc:
Posterior mean at ``Xs`` (Rasmussen & Williams 2006, alg. 2.1); with ``return_std`` / ``return_cov`` also
the standard deviation / covariance of the latent field (sensor noise not included).

methods.name: loo
methods.doc:
Leave-one-out residuals ``y_i - mu_{-i}(x_i)`` and predictive variances, in closed form
(Rasmussen & Williams 2006, eq. 5.12): ``[K^-1 y]_i / [K^-1]_ii`` and ``1 / [K^-1]_ii``, where ``K`` includes
the noise. Hyper-parameters and the prior mean are held fixed.

methods.name: log_marginal_likelihood
methods.doc: ``log p(y | X) = -1/2 y^T K^-1 y - sum log L_ii - n/2 log 2 pi`` (Rasmussen & Williams 2006, eq. 5.8).

methods.name: fit_hyperparameters
methods.sig: (X, y, fit_noise: bool = False, log_bounds = (-7.0, 7.0)) -> GaussianProcessField
methods.doc:
Maximise the log marginal likelihood over log length scales, log variance (and log noise when
``fit_noise``) with L-BFGS-B, starting from the current values, then :meth:`fit` with the optimum.
``log_bounds`` bounds every natural-log parameter.

classes.name: SensorPlacement
classes.doc:
Result of :func:`greedy_sensor_placement`.

indices : chosen rows of ``candidates``, in order of selection.
points : the chosen candidate coordinates (k, d).
integrated_variance : weighted posterior variance over the domain before the first pick and after each pick
    (k + 1,), non-increasing.

functions.name: matern_kernel
functions.sig: (A, B, lengthscales = 1.0, variance: float = 1.0, nu: float = 2.5) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Anisotropic Matern covariance ``k(a, b)`` between the rows of ``A`` (n, d) and ``B`` (m, d).

With the scaled distance ``r = sqrt(sum_i ((a_i - b_i) / l_i)^2)`` (Rasmussen & Williams 2006, eq. 4.17):
``nu = 0.5``: ``s2 exp(-r)``; ``nu = 1.5``: ``s2 (1 + sqrt3 r) exp(-sqrt3 r)``;
``nu = 2.5``: ``s2 (1 + sqrt5 r + 5 r^2 / 3) exp(-sqrt5 r)``; ``nu = inf``: ``s2 exp(-r^2 / 2)``.

functions.name: greedy_sensor_placement
functions.sig: (gp: GaussianProcessField, candidates, n_sensors: int, domain = None, weights = None, existing = None) -> SensorPlacement
functions.doc:
Choose ``n_sensors`` locations among ``candidates`` that greedily minimise the integrated posterior variance.

At each step the candidate ``c`` maximising ``sum_x w(x) Sigma(x, c)^2 / (Sigma(c, c) + noise)`` is added and
the posterior covariance is downdated by that rank-one term (Krause, Singh & Guestrin 2008; Das & Kempe 2008).
Only the kernel and noise of ``gp`` are used; it need not be fitted.

Parameters
----------
gp : :class:`GaussianProcessField` giving the kernel and the sensor noise.
candidates : admissible sensor locations (n_c, d).
n_sensors : number of sensors to add (at most ``n_c``).
domain : points (n_x, d) over which the variance is integrated (default: the candidates).
weights : quadrature weights (n_x,) (default: ``1 / n_x``, i.e. the mean variance).
existing : sensors already installed (n_e, d); the design is conditioned on them.

children.summary: Field reconstruction from sparse sensors with a Gaussian process, and greedy placement of the next sensors.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.data_assimilation.var4d
children.doc:
Strong-constraint 4D-Var through any differentiable PyTorch model: the adjoint comes from autograd.

Cost function for the initial state x0 of an assimilation window with observations y_k at steps k:

    J(x0) = 1/2 (x0 - xb)^T B^-1 (x0 - xb) + 1/2 sum_k (H_k(x_k) - y_k)^T R_k^-1 (H_k(x_k) - y_k),
    x_{k+1} = M(x_k)

(Le Dimet & Talagrand 1986, Tellus 38A:97; Courtier, Thepaut & Hollingsworth 1994, QJRMS 120:1367). The model ``M`` is
any torch function (a numerical solver written in torch, a neural surrogate, or a hybrid), so the gradient of J needs
no hand-written tangent-linear or adjoint code. The minimisation runs in the control variable v = B^{-1/2}(x0 - xb)
(the usual preconditioning, which makes the background term the identity) with L-BFGS.

:func:`gradient_check` compares the autograd gradient with finite differences (the adjoint test of operational
systems); :func:`twin_experiment` runs the classical identical-twin set-up on Lorenz-96.

classes.name: Observation
classes.doc:
Observations ``y`` at model step ``step``; ``H`` maps the state to observation space (default identity) and
``R`` is the error covariance (scalar variance, vector of variances, or full matrix).

classes.doc:
``model(x) -> x_next``; ``B_sqrt``: square root of the background covariance (scalar std, vector of stds, or

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.dimensional
children.doc:
Dimensional analysis, Buckingham pi, scaling laws and curve collapse.

**Dimensional analysis** is exact algebra on the dimensions of the quantities that describe a problem. With ``n``
quantities over ``k`` base dimensions, the dimensional matrix :math:`D` (``k x n``) holds the exponent of each base
dimension in each quantity. A product :math:`\Pi = \prod_i q_i^{\alpha_i}` is dimensionless exactly when
:math:`D\alpha = 0`, so the dimensionless groups are the null space of :math:`D`: ``n - rank(D)`` independent ones
(Buckingham 1914, Phys. Rev. 4:345). Everything here is computed in exact rational arithmetic (``fractions.Fraction``),
so a group's exponents are exact, and the basis is made of small integers.

Buckingham's theorem says that a physically complete relation among the quantities can be rewritten as a relation
among the groups. It does **not** say which quantities are relevant: that is the modelling hypothesis, always listed
as unchecked. The analyzer reports when the list is visibly insufficient: a base dimension carried by a single
quantity (that quantity cannot enter any group: it is irrelevant or a quantity is missing), or a target whose
dimension cannot be built from the others.

**Empirical normalisation** (dividing a curve by its maximum, z-scoring, min-max scaling) is something else: it uses
the data, not dimensions, and its result is not a pi group even when it is dimensionless. :class:`TrajectoryNormalizer`
keeps the two apart and labels every normalised trajectory with which one produced it.

**Curve collapse** (:class:`CurveCollapseAnalyzer`) measures how well a family of curves falls onto one after a
rescaling, against two controls: the raw curves, and the same rescaling with its scale factors permuted among the
members (a collapse no better than permuted scales is not evidence for the scaling). A collapse that flattens every
curve towards a constant is flagged as degenerate rather than reported as success.

Objects:

* :class:`Dimension`: exponents over named base dimensions (any system: SI ``L, M, T, Theta, I, N, J``, or e.g. a
  force-length-time system), from a unit string through :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`.
* :class:`PhysicalQuantity`: name, dimension, optional value (SI) and symbol.
* :class:`DimensionalMatrix`: ``D``, its exact rank and null space.
* :class:`BuckinghamPiAnalyzer` -> :class:`DimensionlessGroup` s (with recognition of named groups: Re, Pe, Fo, Ra,
  Pr, Nu, Ma, Fr, We, St, Bi, Gr, Sc), characteristic scales of a target dimension, the implied :class:`ScalingLaw`.
* :class:`ScalingLaw`: a power law, fitted in log space with confidence intervals, or implied exactly by a single group.
* :class:`TrajectoryNormalizer`, :class:`CurveCollapseAnalyzer`, :class:`SimilarityMetrics`.

classes.name: DimensionError
classes.doc: Dimensions that do not match where they must.

classes.name: Dimension
classes.doc:
Exponents over named base dimensions; zero exponents are dropped. ``Dimension()`` is dimensionless.

Arithmetic: ``a * b``, ``a / b``, ``a ** p`` (``p`` rational). Any base names may be used, so non-SI systems
(``Dimension({"F": 1, "L": -2})``) and extra bases (information, currency) work; mixing systems is the caller's
choice and is not converted.

methods.doc: ``Dimension.of(L=1, T=-1)``.

methods.doc:
Dimension of a unit string (``"kg/(m·s)"``, ``"W/m2/K"``), parsed by
:func:`pinneapple_data.physical_units.parse_unit` (SI bases ``L, M, T, Theta, I, N``).

classes.name: PhysicalQuantity
classes.doc:
A named quantity with a dimension, and optionally a value in SI (scalar or array) and a symbol.

``PhysicalQuantity.from_unit("mu", 1.8e-5, "Pa s")`` converts the value to SI and takes the dimension from the
unit. Values are optional: Buckingham analysis needs dimensions only.

methods.sig: (name: str, value: Any, unit: str, **kw) -> PhysicalQuantity

methods.name: of
methods.doc: ``PhysicalQuantity.of("U", 2.0, L=1, T=-1)``: value already in consistent units.

methods.name: sympy
methods.doc: The quantity as a positive SymPy symbol (requires sympy).

classes.name: DimensionalMatrix
classes.sig: (quantities: Sequence[PhysicalQuantity], bases: Sequence[str] | None = None)
classes.doc: The dimensional matrix ``D`` (base dimensions x quantities) with exact rank and null space.

methods.name: nullspace
methods.doc: An integer basis of ``{alpha : D alpha = 0}`` (one vector per independent dimensionless group).

classes.name: DimensionlessGroup
classes.doc: ``Pi = prod q_i ** exponents[q_i]``, exponents exact (``Fraction``).

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
``Pi`` from values in consistent units (arrays broadcast). ``values`` may map names to numbers or to
:class:`PhysicalQuantity` with a value.

methods.name: recognize
methods.sig: (aliases: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> str | None
methods.doc:
The conventional name of this group (or of its inverse / a power of it) when the quantity names follow
:data:`KNOWN_GROUPS` (``aliases`` maps your names to those). ``None`` if it is not a known group.

classes.name: ScalingLaw
classes.doc:
``y = C * prod x_i ** b_i``.

``exact=True`` when the exponents follow from dimensional analysis alone (a single group: only ``C`` is
unknown); otherwise they are fitted. ``ci`` holds confidence intervals (``level``) of ``log C`` and each
exponent from ordinary least squares in log space, which assumes multiplicative log-normal errors.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (y, x: Mapping[str, Any], target: str = 'y', level: float = 0.95) -> ScalingLaw
methods.doc: Least squares of ``log y`` on ``log x_i`` with a t-based confidence interval per coefficient.

methods.name: fit_constant
methods.doc:
The constant ``C`` of an exact law from data, by the geometric mean of ``y / prod x^b``, with a t interval
on ``log C``.

classes.name: BuckinghamPiAnalyzer
classes.sig: (quantities: Sequence[PhysicalQuantity], target: str | None = None, repeating: Sequence[str] | None = None, bases: Sequence[str] | None = None)
classes.doc:
Dimensionless groups of a set of quantities; see the module docstring.

``target``: the dependent quantity. The groups are built with repeating variables (Rayleigh's method): ``r``
dimensionally independent quantities other than the target, and one group per remaining quantity, so the target
appears in exactly one group. ``repeating`` chooses them; by default the first independent set in the given order
is used (any choice gives an equivalent basis: the groups are unique only up to products and powers).

methods.name: characteristic_scales
methods.sig: (dimension: Dimension, using: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Products of the quantities (``using``, default all but the target) with the given dimension: one
particular solution and the groups that make it ambiguous. With no ambiguity the scale is unique (e.g. the
only time scale from ``L`` and ``alpha`` is ``L^2/alpha``); otherwise every scale times any power of the
groups is another valid scale (``L/U`` and ``L^2/alpha`` differ by Pe).

methods.name: express
methods.sig: (group: DimensionlessGroup, basis: Sequence[DimensionlessGroup] | None = None) -> dict[str, Fraction] | None
methods.doc:
Exponents ``c`` with ``group = prod basis_j ** c_j`` (exact), or ``None`` when ``group`` is not a product of
the basis (it is then not dimensionless in these quantities, or uses a quantity not in the list). Shows,
e.g., that the Rayleigh number is a product of the groups found for ``g, beta, dT, L, nu, alpha``.

methods.name: scaling_law
methods.doc:
The power law implied when the target's group is the only group (``Pi_target = const``): exact exponents,
unknown constant. Raises when other groups exist (the law is then ``Pi_target = f(other groups)``, whose form
dimensional analysis does not give).

classes.name: TrajectoryNormalizer
classes.sig: (*, time_scale: float | None = None, state_scales: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, time_offset: float = 0.0, state_offsets: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, kind: str = 'dimensional', provenance: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None)
classes.doc:
Rescales trajectories, either **dimensionally** (by a time scale and state scales built from physical
quantities, whose dimensions are checked) or **empirically** (from the data: min-max, z-score, peak, initial
value). The two are labelled differently in ``source["normalization"]``; an empirical normalisation is never
called a pi representation.

methods.name: dimensional
methods.sig: (quantities: Mapping[str, PhysicalQuantity], *, time: DimensionlessGroup | None = None, states: Mapping[str, DimensionlessGroup] | None = None, state_dimensions: Mapping[str, Dimension] | None = None, state_offsets: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> TrajectoryNormalizer
methods.doc:
Scales built from quantity products. ``time`` must have the dimension of time (``T``) and each state scale
the dimension in ``state_dimensions`` (when given): otherwise :class:`DimensionError`. Values come from the
quantities' ``value`` (SI).

methods.name: empirical
methods.sig: (trajectory: Trajectory, method: str = 'minmax', time: str | None = None) -> TrajectoryNormalizer
methods.doc:
Scales from the data of ``trajectory``: ``"minmax"`` (to [0, 1]), ``"zscore"``, ``"peak"`` (divide by the
largest absolute value), ``"initial"`` (divide by the first value). ``time``: ``"span"`` divides time by the
observed span, ``None`` leaves it. These are data-dependent and **not** dimensional analysis.

classes.name: CurveCollapseAnalyzer
classes.sig: (ensemble: TrajectoryEnsemble | Sequence[Trajectory], component: str | int = 0, *, n_grid: int = 200, log_x: bool = False)
classes.doc:
Does a family of curves collapse onto one after rescaling? See the module docstring.

Each member ``k`` is a curve ``y_k(x)`` (a :class:`Trajectory` component against its time). A rescaling divides
``x`` by ``a_k`` and ``y`` by ``b_k``. The collapse measure is ``mean_x Var_k[y] / Var_x[mean_k y]`` on the
common support (0: all curves identical; about 1 or more: no collapse).

methods.name: measure
methods.sig: (x_scales: Sequence[float] | None = None, y_scales: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> float
methods.doc: The collapse measure for these scale factors (``inf`` without common support).

methods.name: analyze
methods.sig: (x_scales: Sequence[float] | None = None, y_scales: Sequence[float] | None = None, *, label: str = '', origin: str = 'dimensional', n_permutations: int = 999, seed: int | None = 0, degenerate_tol: float = 1e-08) -> DynamicsResult
methods.doc:
Collapse under the given scales, against the raw curves and a permutation control (the same scale
factors assigned to the wrong members).

methods.name: fit_exponents
methods.sig: (parameter: Sequence[float], *, x0: tuple[float, float] = (0.0, 0.0), fit_y: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Exponents ``(p, q)`` of the rescaling ``x / P^p``, ``y / P^q`` that best collapse the curves, with ``P`` a
per-member parameter (Nelder-Mead on the collapse measure). Also returns the curvature of the measure at the
optimum (a flat minimum means the exponents are poorly determined: an unstable collapse).

methods.name: sensitivity
methods.sig: (parameter: Sequence[float], x_exponent: float, y_exponent: float = 0.0, deltas: Sequence[float] = (-0.2, -0.1, -0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.1, 0.2)) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
The collapse measure when the exponents are perturbed: a sharp minimum at the nominal exponents is a
stable collapse, a flat one is not (the data cannot pin the scaling).

classes.name: SimilarityMetrics
classes.doc:
Are two systems (or datasets) similar? Dynamic similarity holds when every dimensionless group has the same
value; :meth:`groups` compares them by log-ratio. :meth:`curves` compares two normalised curves on their common
support (relative L2 and max distance).

methods.name: curves
methods.sig: (a: Trajectory, b: Trajectory, component: str | int = 0, n_grid: int = 200) -> dict[str, float]

functions.sig: (terms: Mapping[str, Dimension | PhysicalQuantity]) -> DynamicsResult
functions.doc:
Do all ``terms`` of a sum (or both sides of an equation) have the same dimension?

Example: Bernoulli ``{"p": Pa, "rho U^2/2": ..., "rho g h": ...}``. The result's ``estimate`` maps each term to
its dimension; ``applicable`` is ``False`` and ``failures`` names the terms that differ from the first.

functions.doc: ``{name: quantity}`` from quantities or iterables of them (a convenience for ``evaluate``).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.early_warning
children.doc:
Critical slowing down and early-warning indicators.

Near a local bifurcation (saddle-node, transcritical, pitchfork, Hopf) the dominant eigenvalue :math:`\lambda` of the
linearised dynamics approaches zero, so perturbations decay more slowly. For a noisy system linearised around its
equilibrium, :math:`dx = \lambda x\,dt + \sigma\,dW` with :math:`\lambda < 0`, the stationary variance is
:math:`\sigma^2 / (2|\lambda|)` and the lag-:math:`\Delta t` autocorrelation is :math:`e^{\lambda \Delta t}`: both rise
as :math:`\lambda \to 0^-` (Scheffer et al. 2009, Nature 461:53; Dakos et al. 2012, PLoS ONE 7:e41010). This module
estimates those signatures on a time series.

**An indicator is not a prediction.** A rising variance or autocorrelation is *consistent with* critical slowing down;
it does not show that a transition will happen, nor when. The same rise follows from a trend left in the data, from
noise whose amplitude grows, from a change of sampling, or from a slow forcing far from any bifurcation; and many
transitions (noise-induced, global bifurcations, rate-induced tipping) give no warning at all. Every result says this
in its assumptions and in :class:`TransitionDiagnostics`.

Pipeline (:class:`EarlyWarningAnalyzer`):

1. **Detrending** (:func:`detrend`): local linear (LOESS-type, default), Gaussian kernel smoothing or a linear fit,
   with the bandwidth as a fraction of the record; indicators are computed on the residuals. Without detrending, a trend in
   the mean inflates both indicators (the classic false positive; benchmarked).
2. **Rolling statistics** (:class:`RollingStatistics`): variance, standard deviation, coefficient of variation,
   skewness, kurtosis in windows (a fraction of the record or a time length; irregular sampling and missing values
   allowed, with a minimum count per window).
3. **Autocorrelation** (:class:`AutocorrelationAnalyzer`): lag-:math:`\Delta t` autocorrelation per window; on an
   irregular grid either by resampling to a regular grid (marked as interpolated) or from pairs of samples whose
   spacing is within a tolerance of the lag.
4. **Recovery rate** (:class:`RecoveryRateEstimator`): :math:`\hat\lambda = \ln\hat\phi / \Delta t` from the AR(1)
   coefficient per window, or from an exponential fit to a recovery after a pulse.
5. **Spectral indicators**: the fraction of power below a frequency and the low-frequency spectral exponent per
   window (Welch periodogram; spectral reddening, Kleinen et al. 2003).
6. **Trend and significance**: Kendall's :math:`\tau` of each indicator against time; its p-value against
   surrogates of the residuals that keep their autocorrelation but are stationary: an AR(1) fitted to the residuals
   (default, Dakos et al. 2012), or phase-randomised / IAAFT surrogates from
   :mod:`pinneapple_systems.time_series.predictability`.
7. **Sensitivity** (:meth:`EarlyWarningAnalyzer.sensitivity`): :math:`\tau` over a grid of windows and bandwidths, and
   over sampling intervals; a signal that holds only for one choice is fragile.
8. **Non-stationarity checks**: a Kendall trend test on the residual mean (detrending incomplete), and the ADF / KPSS
   tests of :mod:`pinneapple_systems.time_series.audit.tests` when statsmodels is installed.

Benchmarks (:func:`ramp_series`): stochastic normal forms of the saddle-node, transcritical and pitchfork bifurcations
and an Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with a decreasing restoring rate, each driven slowly towards (but not past) the
bifurcation; and negative controls with constant stability: plain, with a trend in the mean, and with growing noise.

classes.name: StabilityIndicator
classes.doc:
One indicator through time: values at the end time of each window, the Kendall trend and its significance.

``p_value`` is from surrogates (``p_kind``) when computed, else ``None``; ``kendall_p`` is the textbook p-value of
Kendall's tau assuming independent points, which windowed (overlapping) indicators violate: report the surrogate
p-value, not this one.

classes.name: RollingStatistics
classes.sig: (window: float = 0.5, *, by: Literal['fraction', 'time'] = 'fraction', min_count: int = 10)
classes.doc:
Variance, std, coefficient of variation, skewness and kurtosis in trailing windows; NaN where a window has
fewer than ``min_count`` values.

methods.name: compute
methods.sig: (t, x, which: Sequence[str] = ('variance',), raw: np.ndarray | None = None) -> dict[str, StabilityIndicator]

classes.name: AutocorrelationAnalyzer
classes.sig: (window: float = 0.5, *, by: Literal['fraction', 'time'] = 'fraction', lag: int = 1, lag_time: float | None = None, tol: float | None = None, min_count: int = 10)
classes.doc:
Lag autocorrelation per window. ``lag`` in samples on a regular grid; on an irregular grid set ``lag_time``
and ``irregular="pairs"`` (pairs whose spacing is within ``tol`` of the lag) or ``"resample"`` (the caller resamples
the trajectory first: interpolation smooths and biases the autocorrelation upwards).

classes.name: RecoveryRateEstimator
classes.doc:
Recovery rate: from the AR(1) coefficient per window, ``lambda = ln(phi) / dt`` (negative for a stable state;
approaching 0 near a bifurcation), or from a perturbation experiment, an exponential fit of ``x - x_eq``.

methods.name: from_pulse
methods.sig: (t, x, x_eq: float | None = None) -> dict[str, float]
methods.doc:
Fit ``x(t) = x_eq + A exp(-r t)`` to a relaxation after a perturbation (``x_eq`` estimated when not
given). Returns ``rate`` (r > 0), its standard error, and the fitted ``x_eq`` and ``A``.

classes.name: EarlyWarningAnalyzer
classes.sig: (*, detrend: str = 'loess', bandwidth: float = 0.1, window: float = 0.5, by: Literal['fraction', 'time'] = 'fraction', indicators: Sequence[str] = DEFAULT, surrogate: str = 'ar1', n_surrogates: int = 199, lag_time: float | None = None, min_count: int = 10, f_low: float | None = None, alpha: float = 0.05)
classes.doc:
Early-warning indicators of one series; see the module docstring.

``indicators`` chooses among ``variance``, ``std``, ``cv``, ``skewness``, ``kurtosis``, ``ac1`` (lag-1
autocorrelation, or lag-``lag_time`` on an irregular grid), ``recovery_rate``, ``low_frequency_power``,
``spectral_exponent``.

methods.name: analyze
methods.sig: (trajectory: Trajectory | tuple, component: str | int = 0, *, seed: int | None = 0) -> DynamicsResult
methods.doc: Indicators, their trends and surrogate significance, with the non-stationarity and sampling checks.

methods.name: sensitivity
methods.sig: (trajectory: Trajectory | tuple, *, windows: Sequence[float] = (0.25, 0.375, 0.5, 0.625, 0.75), bandwidths: Sequence[float] = (0.05, 0.1, 0.15, 0.2), component: str | int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Kendall tau of each indicator over a grid of windows x bandwidths (Dakos et al. 2012, Fig. 4). Returns the
tau grids and the fraction of settings with tau > 0. No surrogates (the grid is a robustness check).

methods.name: sampling_sensitivity
methods.sig: (trajectory: Trajectory | tuple, factors: Sequence[int] = (1, 2, 4, 8), *, component: str | int = 0, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Indicators after keeping every ``k``-th sample: does the signal survive coarser sampling?

classes.name: CriticalSlowingDown
classes.sig: (**kwargs)
classes.doc:
The critical-slowing-down signature: variance, lag-1 autocorrelation and the AR(1) recovery rate, which should
rise, rise and approach zero from below together.

classes.name: TransitionDiagnostics
classes.sig: (result: DynamicsResult, sensitivity: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, alpha: float = 0.05)
classes.doc:
Summary of an early-warning analysis that keeps indicator and prediction apart.

``verdict`` is one of ``"no signal"``, ``"indicator signal (not a prediction)"`` or ``"inconclusive"``; it states
which indicators rise significantly, which checks raise doubts (trend in the residuals, raw data, missing values,
sensitivity to the window), and the fixed interpretation text.

functions.name: detrend
functions.sig: (t, x, method: Literal['gaussian', 'loess', 'linear', 'none'] = 'loess', bandwidth: float = 0.1) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``(residuals, trend)``. ``bandwidth`` is a fraction of the record length (Gaussian: kernel std; loess:
tricube half-width). Missing values (NaN) stay NaN in the residuals and are ignored by the fit.

``loess`` (local linear, the default) is unbiased for a locally linear trend up to the ends of the record. The
Gaussian kernel smoother (Dakos et al. 2012) is biased near the ends by about ``slope x bandwidth``: with a
strong trend this edge bias enters the residuals and can dominate the windows that touch the ends.

functions.name: ramp_series
functions.sig: (kind: str, *, n: int = 1000, t_end: float = 500.0, sigma: float = 0.05, substeps: int = 20, seed: int | None = 0, start: float = 1.0, end: float = 0.05, trend: float = 5.0, noise_growth: float = 3.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A series sampled at ``n`` points on ``[0, t_end]`` from a stochastic normal form whose stability decreases
(``kind`` in ``saddle_node``, ``transcritical``, ``pitchfork``, ``ou_decreasing``) or stays constant (controls:
``stable``, ``stable_trend`` with an accelerating (quadratic) drift of the mean by ``trend`` stationary standard deviations, ``stable_growing_noise`` with the noise
amplitude multiplied by ``noise_growth``). The decay rate of perturbations goes linearly from ``start`` to ``end``
(> 0: the system never crosses the bifurcation). Euler-Maruyama with ``substeps`` steps per sample.

Normal forms and their equilibria (decay rate ``r`` = |eigenvalue|):

* saddle-node: ``dx = (mu - x^2) dt``, equilibrium ``sqrt(mu)``, ``r = 2 sqrt(mu)``;
* transcritical: ``dx = (-r x - x^2) dt``, equilibrium 0 (``mu = -r``);
* pitchfork: ``dx = (-r x - x^3) dt``, equilibrium 0;
* ou_decreasing: ``dx = -r x dt``.

Returns ``t``, ``x``, the true rate ``r(t)``, the theoretical lag-1 autocorrelation ``exp(-r dt)`` and variance
``sigma^2 / (2 r)`` of the linearisation. The saddle-node and transcritical basins shrink with ``r`` (width of
order ``r``): keep ``sigma / sqrt(2 r_end)`` well below it, or the path leaves the basin (``tipped_at`` is set and
the rest of ``x`` is NaN).

children.summary: Critical slowing down and early-warning indicators.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.first_passage
children.doc:
First-passage and hitting times: :math:`\tau = \inf\{t \ge 0 : X(t) \in \partial\Omega\}`.

Three ways to get the distribution of :math:`\tau`, one analyzer (:class:`FirstPassageAnalyzer`):

* **Deterministic crossing** of one trajectory (:meth:`FirstPassageAnalyzer.crossing`): the first sample at or
  past the boundary, with the crossing time interpolated linearly inside the sampling interval that brackets it.
  Works on irregular grids and skips missing samples (the bracket then spans the gap and is reported).
* **Empirical distribution** of an ensemble of observed trajectories (:meth:`FirstPassageAnalyzer.from_trajectories`):
  one crossing per member; a member that has not crossed by the end of its window is right-censored there, and the
  survival function is the Kaplan-Meier estimate with Greenwood (log-log) bands.
* **Monte Carlo** of a stochastic differential equation :math:`dX = a(t, X)\,dt + b(t, X)\,dW` with diagonal noise
  (:meth:`FirstPassageAnalyzer.monte_carlo`): Euler-Maruyama paths, with a Brownian-bridge correction for scalar
  thresholds and intervals (the probability that the path crossed and came back between two steps,
  :math:`\exp(-2 d_i d_{i+1} / (b^2 \Delta t))`), optional reflecting boundaries, and paths that never reach the
  boundary censored at the simulation horizon.

A fourth route needs no paths: the **Fokker-Planck survival** (:func:`survival_from_density`,
:func:`survival_from_solution`). The density :math:`p(x, t)` of the process killed at an absorbing boundary solves the
forward equation with :math:`p = 0` there, and :math:`S(t) = \int_\Omega p(x, t)\,dx`. Any solver of that PDE
(``pp.solve`` with a PINN, a classical solver, a closed form) therefore gives the hitting-time distribution, which can
be set against Monte Carlo or observed trajectories.

Each of the first three returns a :class:`FirstPassageResult` (a :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.DynamicsResult`) whose
:class:`HittingTimeDistribution` gives the survival function :math:`S(t) = P(\tau > t)`
(:class:`SurvivalFunction`), hitting probabilities :math:`P(\tau \le T)` with confidence intervals
(:class:`CrossingProbability`), quantiles, prediction intervals for a new realisation, and the mean (or, when paths
are censored, the restricted mean :math:`\int_0^T S(t)\,dt`, which is labelled as such: the full mean is not
identifiable from censored data).

Boundaries (:class:`BoundaryCondition`): an upper, lower or two-sided scalar threshold on one component, an interval
:math:`(l, u)` to exit, or a level set :math:`\phi(x) \ge 0` in any dimension. Several boundaries can be analysed on
the same trajectories (one :math:`\tau` per boundary). Reflecting thresholds change the dynamics of a simulation; they
are not targets.

Closed forms, used as references in the tests and available to callers:

* Brownian motion with drift to one barrier: the inverse-Gaussian density and its CDF
  (:func:`brownian_first_passage_pdf`, :func:`brownian_first_passage_cdf`, :func:`brownian_first_passage_mean`);
  Karatzas & Shreve, *Brownian Motion and Stochastic Calculus* (1991), sec. 3.5.C.
* Brownian motion with drift in an interval: exit probabilities, mean exit time and the survival series
  (:func:`brownian_exit_probability`, :func:`brownian_exit_mean`, :func:`brownian_exit_survival`); Cox & Miller,
  *The Theory of Stochastic Processes* (1965), sec. 5.7; Redner, *A Guide to First-Passage Processes* (2001), ch. 2.
* Ornstein-Uhlenbeck mean first-passage time to a level (:func:`ou_mean_first_passage`) from the backward equation
  :math:`D T'' + a T' = -1` (Gardiner, *Stochastic Methods*, 4th ed., sec. 6.2), evaluated by quadrature.

Limits: Euler-Maruyama has weak order 1 in :math:`\Delta t`; with discrete monitoring alone the first-passage time is
biased late by :math:`O(\sqrt{\Delta t})` (Asmussen, Glynn & Pitman 1995), which the bridge correction reduces but does
not remove (it uses the diffusion at the start of the step and places a bridge crossing in the middle of the step;
for an interval it adds the two one-sided probabilities). :meth:`FirstPassageAnalyzer.dt_convergence` measures the
remaining step-size dependence instead of assuming it. A deterministic crossing assumes the trajectory does not leave
and re-enter between two samples; that cannot be checked from the samples.

classes.name: BoundaryCondition
classes.doc:
The boundary :math:`\partial\Omega` (or a reflecting wall). Build one with the class methods.

``threshold(level, direction)``: ``"up"`` is hit when ``x >= level``, ``"down"`` when ``x <= level``,
``"either"`` when the component reaches ``level`` from the side it started on. ``interval(lower, upper)``: hit
on leaving ``(lower, upper)``. ``level_set(phi)``: hit when ``phi(x) >= 0``, with ``phi`` mapping ``(m, d)``
states to ``(m,)`` (e.g. ``|x| - R`` for leaving a ball). ``behaviour="reflecting"`` (thresholds only) makes it
a wall for :meth:`FirstPassageAnalyzer.monte_carlo` instead of a target.

methods.name: threshold
methods.sig: (level: float, direction: Direction = 'up', component: int | str = 0, *, name: str | None = None, behaviour: str = 'absorbing') -> BoundaryCondition

methods.name: interval
methods.sig: (lower: float, upper: float, component: int | str = 0, *, name: str | None = None) -> BoundaryCondition

methods.name: gauge
methods.sig: (X: np.ndarray, start: np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Signed distance-like value per state: ``>= 0`` on or past the boundary. ``start`` (the initial states)
fixes the side of a two-sided threshold.

methods.name: bridge_probability
methods.sig: (x_old: np.ndarray, x_new: np.ndarray, sigma: np.ndarray, dt: float, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Probability that a Brownian bridge between two inside states touched the boundary (scalar boundaries).

methods.name: reflect
methods.sig: (X: np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Mirror states that crossed a reflecting threshold back into the domain (in place).

classes.name: SDE
classes.doc:
:math:`dX = a(t, X)\,dt + b(t, X)\,dW` with diagonal noise (independent Wiener processes per component).

``drift(t, X)`` and ``diffusion(t, X)`` take ``X`` of shape ``(m, dim)`` and return arrays broadcastable to it.
``noise`` documents the hypothesis (``"additive"``: ``b`` does not depend on ``X``; ``"multiplicative"``
otherwise); the Euler-Maruyama step reads ``b`` at the start of the step (Ito).

methods.name: brownian
methods.doc: :math:`dX = \mu\,dt + \sigma\,dW`.

methods.name: ornstein_uhlenbeck
methods.sig: (theta: float, mean: float = 0.0, sigma: float = 1.0) -> SDE
methods.doc: :math:`dX = -\theta (X - m)\,dt + \sigma\,dW`.

methods.name: geometric_brownian
methods.doc: :math:`dX = \mu X\,dt + \sigma X\,dW` (multiplicative noise).

classes.name: SurvivalFunction
classes.doc:
A right-continuous step function :math:`S(t) = P(\tau > t)` with pointwise confidence bands.

``t``: event times (increasing); ``S[k]`` holds on ``[t[k], t[k+1])`` and ``S = 1`` before ``t[0]``.
``horizon``: beyond it nothing was observed and :meth:`__call__` returns ``NaN``.

classes.name: CrossingProbability
classes.doc:
:math:`P(\tau \le T)` with a confidence interval; :attr:`no_crossing` is the complement
:math:`P(\tau > T)` (probability of not reaching the boundary within the horizon).

classes.name: HittingTimeDistribution
classes.sig: (times, observed, *, horizon: float | None = None, source: str = 'samples', level: float = 0.95)
classes.doc:
The distribution of one first-passage time, from event and right-censoring times.

``times[i]`` is the hitting time of sample ``i`` when ``observed[i]``, else the time its observation stopped
(``tau > times[i]``). ``source`` says where the samples come from (``"monte carlo"``, ``"observed trajectories"``).

methods.name: uniformly_censored
methods.doc: True when every censored sample was censored at the horizon (e.g. Monte Carlo with one end time).

methods.name: hitting_probability
methods.sig: (T: float | None = None, level: float | None = None) -> CrossingProbability
methods.doc:
:math:`P(\tau \le T)` (default: the horizon). Without censoring before ``T`` the estimate is the binomial
proportion with a Wilson interval; otherwise it is the Kaplan-Meier estimate with its band.

methods.name: quantile
methods.doc:
Smallest ``t`` with :math:`P(\tau \le t) \ge q`; ``inf`` when the estimate never reaches ``q`` within
the horizon (the quantile lies beyond what was observed).

methods.name: quantile_ci
methods.doc: Confidence interval of the ``q`` quantile from the survival band (Brookmeyer & Crowley 1982).

methods.name: prediction_interval
methods.doc:
Interval that contains the first-passage time of a new realisation with probability ``level`` (central,
from the estimated quantiles; the upper end is ``inf`` when it lies beyond the horizon).

methods.name: mean
methods.doc:
The mean first-passage time when every sample hit; otherwise the restricted mean
:math:`\int_0^{T} S(t)\,dt` up to the horizon, labelled ``restricted`` (a lower bound of the true mean).

methods.name: density
methods.doc:
Histogram density of the event times normalised by *all* samples (a defective density when some never
hit): ``(bin_edges, density)``. Only meaningful without early censoring.

classes.name: FirstPassageResult
classes.doc: A :class:`DynamicsResult` with the hitting-time distribution of each boundary (``distributions``).

classes.name: FirstPassageAnalyzer
classes.sig: (boundaries: BoundaryCondition | Sequence[BoundaryCondition], *, horizon: float | None = None, level: float = 0.95)
classes.doc:
First-passage analysis of one or more target boundaries; see the module docstring.

``horizon``: the ``T`` of :math:`P(\tau \le T)` (default: the end of the data or of the simulation).

methods.name: crossing
methods.doc: First crossing of each boundary by one trajectory (deterministic: no distribution is inferred).

methods.name: from_trajectories
methods.doc: Hitting-time distributions from observed trajectories, each censored at the end of its own window.

methods.name: simulate
methods.sig: (sde: SDE, x0, *, t_max: float, dt: float, n_paths: int, seed: int | None = 0, bridge: bool = True, reflecting: Sequence[BoundaryCondition] = (), keep_paths: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Raw Monte Carlo: hitting times ``(n_boundaries, n_paths)`` (``inf`` when not hit by ``t_max``) and
diagnostics. :meth:`monte_carlo` wraps it into a result.

methods.name: monte_carlo
methods.sig: (sde: SDE, x0, *, t_max: float, dt: float, n_paths: int = 10000, seed: int | None = 0, bridge: bool = True, reflecting: Sequence[BoundaryCondition] = (), keep_paths: int = 0) -> FirstPassageResult
methods.doc: Monte Carlo hitting-time distributions of ``sde`` from ``x0``; see the module docstring.

methods.name: dt_convergence
methods.sig: (sde: SDE, x0, *, t_max: float, dts: Sequence[float], n_paths: int = 20000, seed: int = 0, statistic: str = 'mean', boundary: str | None = None, bridge: bool = True, reflecting: Sequence[BoundaryCondition] = ()) -> DynamicsResult
methods.doc:
The statistic for each step in ``dts`` (largest first), its Monte Carlo error, the successive changes,
the observed order when three steps with a constant ratio are given, and a Richardson extrapolation.

methods.name: sensitivity
methods.sig: (models: Mapping[Any, SDE] | Callable[[float], SDE], values: Sequence[float] | None = None, *, x0, t_max: float, dt: float, n_paths: int = 20000, seed: int = 0, statistic: str = 'p_hit', boundary: str | None = None, bridge: bool = True) -> DynamicsResult
methods.doc: The statistic across models with common random numbers (same seed for every model).

functions.name: wilson_interval
functions.sig: (k: int, n: int, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion ``k / n`` (Wilson 1927, JASA 22:209).

functions.name: kaplan_meier
functions.sig: (times, observed, *, level: float = 0.95, horizon: float | None = None) -> SurvivalFunction
functions.doc:
Kaplan-Meier estimate of the survival function from right-censored times (Kaplan & Meier 1958, JASA 53:457).

``observed[i]`` is ``True`` when ``times[i]`` is an event and ``False`` when it is a censoring time. Bands:
Greenwood variance on the log-log scale (Kalbfleisch & Prentice 2002, sec. 1.4), which stays inside [0, 1].
Censored times tied with an event time are counted at risk at that event (the usual convention).

functions.name: brownian_first_passage_pdf
functions.sig: (t, x0: float, b: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Density of the first time :math:`X = x_0 + \mu t + \sigma W` reaches ``b``:
:math:`f(t) = a / (\sigma \sqrt{2\pi t^3})\, \exp(-(a - \nu t)^2 / (2\sigma^2 t))`, ``a = |b - x0|``,
``nu`` the drift towards ``b``. Defective (integrates to :math:`e^{2\nu a/\sigma^2} < 1`) when ``nu < 0``.

functions.name: brownian_first_passage_cdf
functions.sig: (t, x0: float, b: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
:math:`P(	au \le t) = \Phi((
u t - a)/(\sigma\sqrt t)) + e^{2
u a/\sigma^2}\,\Phi((-a - 
u t)/(\sigma\sqrt t))`.

functions.name: brownian_first_passage_mean
functions.sig: (x0: float, b: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> float
functions.doc:
:math:`E[\tau] = a / \nu` for drift towards the barrier; ``inf`` otherwise (``nu = 0``: finite almost surely
but infinite mean; ``nu < 0``: the barrier may never be reached).

functions.name: brownian_exit_probability
functions.sig: (x0: float, lower: float, upper: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> float
functions.doc: Probability of leaving ``(lower, upper)`` through ``upper`` (scale function of drifted Brownian motion).

functions.name: brownian_exit_mean
functions.sig: (x0: float, lower: float, upper: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Mean exit time from ``(lower, upper)``: :math:`y(L-y)/\sigma^2` without drift,
:math:`(L\,P_{up} - y)/\mu` with drift (``y = x0 - lower``, ``L = upper - lower``).

functions.name: brownian_exit_survival
functions.sig: (t, x0: float, lower: float, upper: float, mu: float, sigma: float, n_terms: int | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
:math:`P(\tau > t)` of exit from ``(lower, upper)`` by eigenfunction expansion of the backward equation.

With ``k = mu/sigma^2``, ``S = e^{-k y - \mu^2 t/(2\sigma^2)} \sum_n c_n \sin(n\pi y/L) e^{-\lambda_n t}``,
``\lambda_n = n^2\pi^2\sigma^2/(2L^2)``, ``c_n = (2/L)\,a_n (1 - (-1)^n e^{kL})/(k^2 + a_n^2)``,
``a_n = n\pi/L``. The series converges fast for ``t`` away from 0; ``n_terms`` defaults to enough terms for
``exp(-lambda_n t) < 1e-16`` at the smallest positive ``t`` (at most 20 000).

functions.name: ou_mean_first_passage
functions.sig: (x0: float, level: float, theta: float, mean: float = 0.0, sigma: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Mean first-passage time of :math:`dX = -\theta (X - m)dt + \sigma dW` from ``x0`` to ``level``.

From the backward equation :math:`(\sigma^2/2) T'' - \theta (x - m) T' = -1` with :math:`T(\text{level}) = 0`
and a natural boundary on the far side:
:math:`T(x_0) = \frac{\sqrt{\pi}}{\sigma\sqrt{\theta}} \int_{x_0}^{\text{level}}
\operatorname{erfcx}(-(y - m)\sqrt{\theta}/\sigma)\,dy` for an upper level (mirrored for a lower one),
evaluated by adaptive quadrature (``scipy.integrate.quad``).

functions.name: survival_from_density
functions.sig: (t, x, density, *, normalise: bool = False, level_tol: float = 0.001) -> DynamicsResult
functions.doc:
Hitting-time distribution from a Fokker-Planck density with an absorbing boundary (see the module docstring).

``density[k, i]`` is :math:`p(x_i, t_k)`. The result's ``estimate`` holds ``t``, ``S``, ``pdf``, ``hazard``,
``p_hit``, ``median`` and ``restricted_mean`` (the full mean is not identifiable past ``t[-1]`` unless
``S(t[-1]) = 0``). Diagnostics: the initial mass (should be 1), the largest increase of ``S`` (should be 0) and
the most negative density, each against ``level_tol``.

functions.name: survival_from_solution
functions.sig: (solution: Any, x, t, *, space_coord: str = 'x', time_coord: str = 't', component: str | int = 0, normalise: bool = False, level_tol: float = 0.001) -> DynamicsResult
functions.doc:
:func:`survival_from_density` on a ``pp.solve`` result: ``solution.predict`` on the grid ``x`` by ``t``.

``solution`` needs ``problem.coords`` (exactly ``space_coord`` and ``time_coord``), ``problem.fields`` and
``predict(points)``. The solution's provenance (method, wall time) is copied into ``details["solution"]``.

children.summary: First-passage and hitting times: :math:\tau = \inf\{t \ge 0 : X(t) \in \partial\Omega\}.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.fisher
children.doc:
Fisher information, Cramér-Rao bounds and experimental design.

The Fisher information of a parameter vector :math:`\theta` is :math:`I(\theta) = E[\nabla\log p\,\nabla\log p^T]`.
Under the regularity conditions (a likelihood differentiable in :math:`\theta`, whose support does not depend on
:math:`\theta`, and a nonsingular :math:`I`), every **unbiased** estimator satisfies the Cramér-Rao bound
:math:`\operatorname{Cov}(\hat\theta) \succeq I(\theta)^{-1}`, and for a function :math:`g(\theta)` (a prediction,
a first-passage time) :math:`\operatorname{Var}(\hat g) \ge \nabla g^T I^{-1} \nabla g`. This module keeps three
quantities apart and labels each:

* the **theoretical bound** (:class:`CramerRaoBound`): a property of the model and the design, not of any estimator;
* the **empirical performance** of an estimator (:func:`estimator_performance`): least-squares fits of simulated
  data, whose spread may exceed the bound (finite samples, non-linearity) or fall below it (bias, bounds);
* the **Bayesian** (Laplace) posterior covariance :math:`(I + P)^{-1}` with a prior precision :math:`P`, which is
  not a Cramér-Rao bound (a prior makes the estimator biased).

How the information is computed (:class:`FisherInformation`):

* ``gaussian``: :math:`I = J^T \Sigma^{-1} J` for independent Gaussian noise, with :math:`J = \partial y/\partial\theta`
  from :func:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.forward.jacobian` (the model's own sensitivities, e.g. the forward
  sensitivity equations of :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ode_model.ODEForwardModel`, else PyTorch
  autograd through ``predict_torch``, else central differences); with a parameter-dependent noise level
  :math:`\sigma_i(\theta)` the term :math:`2\,\partial\sigma_i\,\partial\sigma_i^T / \sigma_i^2` is added;
* ``poisson``: :math:`I = J^T \operatorname{diag}(1/\lambda) J` for counts with mean :math:`\lambda(\theta)`;
* ``from_loglik``: the expectation of the score outer product, by Monte Carlo over simulated data, for any
  likelihood; the score from central differences, PyTorch or JAX (optional backends, detected at call time);
* ``linear_gaussian``: :math:`X^T X / \sigma^2`, exact.

Design (:class:`ExperimentalDesign`, :class:`ObservationScheduler`): choose measurements from candidates to optimise a
criterion of the total information (with the information already in hand and an optional prior): D (maximise
:math:`\log\det I`), A (minimise :math:`\operatorname{tr} I^{-1}`), E (maximise :math:`\lambda_{\min}`), c (minimise
the bound on a target :math:`g`), Bayesian D (D with the prior precision). Greedy selection followed by exchange
passes (Fedorov 1972); replicates allowed. :class:`InformationGain` scores one more measurement;
:class:`SamplingStrategy` compares whole schedules; :class:`ParameterIdentifiability` gives the local verdict from the
information matrix and delegates the full analysis (profile likelihood, posterior) to the existing
:func:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.identifiability.analyze_identifiability`.

Limits: everything is local, at one parameter point (the design is optimal for the nominal parameters: a locally
optimal design); the bound is attained only asymptotically or for linear-Gaussian models; a rank-deficient
information matrix means non-identifiable directions at that point, not a proof of global non-identifiability.

classes.name: FisherInformationMatrix
classes.doc:
``F`` (``p x p``) in the physical parameters ``names`` at ``theta``. ``how`` says how the derivatives were
obtained, ``kind`` which likelihood (``gaussian``, ``poisson``, ``score-mc``, ``linear``), ``n_obs`` how many
measurements it contains. ``mc_se`` holds the Monte Carlo standard error of each entry when ``F`` was
estimated by sampling.

methods.name: total
methods.doc: ``F`` plus the prior precision when one is attached.

methods.name: null_directions
methods.doc: Parameter combinations (unit eigenvectors) that the data do not inform at this point.

methods.name: criteria
methods.doc:
D (``log det F``), A (``tr F^-1``), E (smallest eigenvalue), condition number and, with a target
gradient, c (``g^T F^-1 g``). Singular matrices give ``-inf`` / ``inf``.

methods.name: with_prior
methods.doc: The same information with a Gaussian prior precision (``p x p`` or one value per parameter).

methods.name: crlb
methods.sig: (target: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], float] | Mapping[str, Callable] | None = None, rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> CramerRaoBound

classes.name: CramerRaoBound
classes.doc:
Lower bound on the covariance of unbiased estimators: ``cov = F^-1``, ``std`` per parameter, ``correlation``
and, for targets ``g``, ``target_std`` from ``grad g^T F^-1 grad g``. With a prior attached this is the Laplace
posterior covariance instead (``bayesian = True``), which is not a Cramér-Rao bound.

methods.name: from_fim
methods.sig: (fim: FisherInformationMatrix, target = None, rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> CramerRaoBound

classes.name: FisherInformation
classes.doc: Constructors of :class:`FisherInformationMatrix`; see the module docstring.

methods.name: gaussian
methods.sig: (model: ForwardModel, obs: Observations, parameters: Sequence[Parameter] | None = None, *, theta: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, method: str = 'auto', sigma_model: Callable[[Mapping[str, float], Observations], np.ndarray] | None = None, rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> FisherInformationMatrix
methods.doc:
``J^T diag(1/sigma^2) J`` at ``theta`` (default: the parameters' values). ``sigma_model(theta, obs)``
makes the noise level depend on the parameters (e.g. a relative error) and adds its information.

methods.sig: (model: ForwardModel, obs: Observations, parameters: Sequence[Parameter] | None = None, *, theta: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, method: str = 'auto') -> FisherInformationMatrix
methods.doc:
Counts ``y_i ~ Poisson(lambda_i(theta))`` with ``lambda`` the model's prediction: ``J^T diag(1/lambda) J``.
``obs.sigma`` is ignored.

methods.name: linear_gaussian
methods.sig: (X, sigma: float | np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, theta: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> FisherInformationMatrix

methods.sig: (loglik: Callable, theta: Mapping[str, float], simulate: Callable[[Mapping[str, float], np.random.Generator], Any], *, n_mc: int = 2000, seed: int | None = 0, backend: str = 'fd', rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> FisherInformationMatrix
methods.doc:
``E[s s^T]`` by Monte Carlo: ``simulate(theta, rng)`` draws a data set, ``loglik(theta_vector, y)`` is its
log-likelihood. The score ``s`` is computed by ``backend``: ``"fd"`` (central differences, NumPy),
``"torch"`` (``loglik`` written with PyTorch operations on a tensor) or ``"jax"`` (with ``jax.numpy``).
The Monte Carlo standard error of each entry is returned in ``mc_se``.

Local identifiability verdict from the information matrix (:meth:`local`), or the full analysis with profile

Local sensitivities of the predictions: raw ``dy/dtheta``, relative ``(theta/y) dy/dtheta`` and noise-scaled

(Sobol, Morris) analysis lives in :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity`.

methods.sig: (g: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], float], rel_step: float = 1e-05) -> dict[str, float]

methods.sig: (n: int, criterion: str = 'D', *, target: Callable[[Mapping[str, float]], float] | None = None, replicates: bool = True, exchange: bool = True, max_passes: int = 20) -> DynamicsResult

classes.doc:
When to measure: candidate times on a grid over ``t_range`` for one observable, then
:class:`ExperimentalDesign`. ``inputs`` holds the other input columns (constant), ``sigma`` the noise level

Value of more measurements over a current information matrix ``fim``: the gain in ``log det`` (D), the
expected information gain (mutual information) of a linear-Gaussian posterior
``0.5 log det((F + F_new + P) / (F + P))`` (requires a prior or a nonsingular ``F``), and the reduction of the
bound on a target.

Named schedules and their comparison. Builders return :class:`Observations` with ``n`` rows over

criteria and bounds of each schedule (same model, same noise).

functions.sig: (model: ForwardModel, obs: Observations, parameters: Sequence[Parameter] | None = None, *, n_rep: int = 200, seed: int | None = 0, method: str = 'auto') -> DynamicsResult
functions.doc:
Empirical performance of the least-squares (Gaussian maximum-likelihood) estimator against the Cramér-Rao
bound: ``n_rep`` data sets simulated at the nominal parameters with the noise of ``obs``, each fitted by
:func:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.estimation.least_squares_fit`. Reports the bias, the empirical
standard deviation and the efficiency ``crlb_var / empirical_var`` per parameter (1: the bound is attained).
