children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.koopman
children.doc:
Koopman operator and spectral analysis: DMD, EDMD, dictionaries of observables, eigenfunctions, residuals.

The Koopman operator of a map :math:`F` acts on observables: :math:`(\mathcal K g)(x) = g(F(x))`. It is linear even
when :math:`F` is not, so a nonlinear system has a spectral decomposition in the space of observables. Data-driven
methods approximate :math:`\mathcal K` on a finite dictionary :math:`\psi = (\psi_1, \dots, \psi_m)` from snapshot
pairs :math:`(x_n, y_n = F(x_n))`:

* **EDMD** (Williams, Kevrekidis & Rowley 2015, J. Nonlinear Sci. 25:1307): with :math:`\Psi_X, \Psi_Y` the
  dictionary evaluated on the pairs, :math:`G = \Psi_X^* \Psi_X / N`, :math:`A = \Psi_X^* \Psi_Y / N`,
  :math:`K = G^{+} A`, so :math:`\psi(F(x)) \approx \psi(x) K`. An eigenpair :math:`K\xi = \lambda\xi` gives the
  approximate eigenfunction :math:`\varphi(x) = \psi(x)\xi`, exact when the dictionary spans an invariant subspace.
* **DMD** (Schmid 2010; exact DMD, Tu et al. 2014, J. Comput. Dyn. 1:391): EDMD with the identity dictionary,
  computed through a rank-:math:`r` SVD of the snapshot matrix so that high-dimensional states (PDE snapshots) cost
  :math:`O(D N r)`. The rank is chosen by the optimal hard threshold of Gavish & Donoho (2014, IEEE TIT 60:5040), by
  an energy fraction, or given. **TLS-DMD** (Hemati et al. 2017, Theor. Comput. Fluid Dyn. 31:349) removes the bias
  that noise in the data puts on the eigenvalues (towards damping).
* **Residuals** (ResDMD, Colbrook & Townsend 2024, Comm. Pure Appl. Math. 77:221): for each candidate eigenpair,
  :math:`\mathrm{res}(\lambda,\xi)^2 = \xi^*(L - \lambda A^* - \bar\lambda A + |\lambda|^2 G)\xi / \xi^* G \xi`
  with :math:`L = \Psi_Y^*\Psi_Y/N`: zero for an exact eigenfunction, large for a spurious eigenvalue produced by the
  truncation. A spectrum is not reported as trustworthy without them.
* **Continuous time**: :math:`\omega = \log\lambda / \Delta t` (the principal branch: frequencies above the Nyquist
  frequency :math:`\pi/\Delta t` alias), or the generator fitted from derivative data (gEDMD, Klus et al. 2020,
  Physica D 406:132416) with the dictionary differentiated along the velocity by central differences.

Objects: :class:`ObservableDictionary` (identity, monomials, RBF, Fourier, custom, neural observables from a PyTorch
module), :class:`DMD` and :class:`EDMD` (estimators) returning a :class:`KoopmanOperator` (the fitted operator, with
:class:`KoopmanEigenvalues`, :class:`KoopmanEigenfunctions`, :class:`DynamicMode` s, residuals, stability),
:class:`KoopmanReconstruction` (reconstruction and multi-step prediction errors), :class:`SpectralAnalyzer`
(frequencies, growth rates, mode ranking, noise sensitivity, order selection, comparison with a nonlinear
state-space regression).

Name: this :class:`KoopmanOperator` is a fitted finite-dimensional approximation (NumPy, no training). It is not
:class:`pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.koopman.KoopmanOperator`, the learnable linear layer inside the deep
Koopman autoencoder; that class is unchanged and a trained autoencoder's encoder can be used here as a dictionary
(:meth:`ObservableDictionary.neural`).

classes.name: ObservableDictionary
classes.doc:
A list of observables ``psi_k(X) -> (n,)`` with names; ``__call__(X)`` gives ``Psi`` of shape ``(n, m)``.

``state_index``: positions of the dictionary entries equal to the state components (set by the builders that
include them); reconstruction then reads the state off those entries, otherwise it fits a linear map.

methods.name: identity
methods.sig: (d: int, names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> ObservableDictionary

methods.name: monomials
methods.sig: (d: int, degree: int, *, constant: bool = True, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, only: Sequence[tuple[int, ...]] | None = None) -> ObservableDictionary
methods.doc:
All monomials of total degree ``<= degree`` (or the exponent tuples in ``only``); the linear ones come
first after the constant.

methods.name: rbf
methods.sig: (centers, epsilon: float, *, kind: str = 'gaussian', with_state: bool = True) -> ObservableDictionary
methods.doc:
Radial basis functions at ``centers`` (``(k, d)``): ``exp(-(eps r)^2)`` (gaussian) or
``sqrt(1 + (eps r)^2)`` (multiquadric); the state coordinates are prepended when ``with_state``.

methods.name: fourier
methods.sig: (d: int, n_freq: int, period: float | Sequence[float] = 2 * np.pi, *, with_state: bool = False) -> ObservableDictionary
methods.doc: ``1, cos(2 pi k x_i / P), sin(2 pi k x_i / P)`` for ``k = 1..n_freq`` per component (periodic states).

methods.name: custom
methods.sig: (funcs: Sequence[Callable], names: Sequence[str] | None = None, state_index: Sequence[int] | None = None) -> ObservableDictionary

methods.name: neural
methods.sig: (model: Callable, n_out: int, *, with_state: bool = True, d: int | None = None, name: str = 'nn') -> ObservableDictionary
methods.doc:
Observables given by a trained network (e.g. the encoder of a Koopman autoencoder): ``model`` maps a
PyTorch tensor ``(n, d)`` to ``(n, n_out)``. Evaluated without gradients; the dictionary is then fixed (the
network is not trained here).

classes.name: DynamicMode
classes.doc:
One eigen-triple: discrete eigenvalue ``lam``, continuous ``omega = log(lam)/dt`` (when ``dt`` is known),
frequency (cycles per unit time), growth rate, the mode in state space, its amplitude in the data, and the
ResDMD residual of the eigenpair.

classes.name: KoopmanEigenvalues
classes.doc: Discrete eigenvalues (sorted by decreasing modulus) and, with ``dt``, the continuous ones.

methods.name: match
methods.doc:
For each reference eigenvalue, the distance to the nearest computed one (optimal one-to-one matching
when the counts allow).

classes.name: KoopmanEigenfunctions
classes.doc: ``phi_k(x) = psi(x) xi_k``: coefficients ``xi`` (``m x r``) on the dictionary.

classes.name: KoopmanOperator
classes.sig: (K: np.ndarray, dictionary: ObservableDictionary | None, B: np.ndarray, *, dt: float | None, method: str, gram: tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray] | None = None, basis: np.ndarray | None = None, mean: np.ndarray | None = None, info: dict | None = None)
classes.doc:
A fitted finite-dimensional Koopman approximation; see the module docstring. Built by :class:`DMD` and
:class:`EDMD`, not directly.

``K`` acts on row vectors of dictionary values, ``psi(F(x)) ~ psi(x) K``; ``B`` maps dictionary values to the
state, ``x ~ psi(x) B``.

methods.name: lift
methods.doc: Dictionary values (EDMD) or reduced coordinates (DMD) of the states ``X``.

methods.name: residuals
methods.doc: ResDMD residual of every eigenpair (``None`` without the Gram matrices).

methods.name: modes
methods.doc:
Dynamic modes: ``x ~ sum_k phi_k(x) v_k`` with ``V = xi^+ B``; amplitudes from ``X0`` (the training
states when stored).

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: States ``x_0 .. x_steps`` from ``x0`` by propagating the lifted state linearly (``(steps + 1, d)``).

methods.name: generator
methods.doc: Continuous-time generator on the dictionary, ``logm(K) / dt`` (principal branch).

classes.name: DMD
classes.sig: (rank: int | float | str = 'gavish-donoho', *, tls: bool = False, center: bool = False, lag: int = 1, dt: float | None = None)
classes.doc: Exact DMD (optionally TLS-debiased) on states; see the module docstring.

classes.name: EDMD
classes.sig: (dictionary: ObservableDictionary, *, ridge: float = 0.0, lag: int = 1, dt: float | None = None)
classes.doc: Extended DMD on a dictionary of observables; see the module docstring.

methods.name: fit_generator
methods.sig: (X, dXdt, *, h: float = 1e-05, dt: float = 1.0) -> DynamicsResult
methods.doc:
Generator EDMD from states and their time derivatives: ``dpsi/dt = grad psi . f`` by central differences
along ``f``; the returned operator is ``expm(L dt)`` for a step ``dt`` so it predicts like the discrete one,
and ``generator()`` gives ``L``. Residuals are not defined for this fit (``None``).

classes.name: KoopmanReconstruction
classes.doc:
Errors of a fitted operator on trajectories: one-step (data-driven pairs) and multi-step (open-loop from the
first state of each trajectory), relative to the RMS of the data.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (operator: KoopmanOperator, trajectories: Sequence[np.ndarray] | np.ndarray, horizon: int | None = None) -> KoopmanReconstruction

classes.name: SpectralAnalyzer
classes.doc:
Analyses around a Koopman estimator: frequencies and growth rates, ranking modes, sensitivity of the
eigenvalues to noise, order selection by held-out prediction, and comparison with a nonlinear state-space
regression on the same dictionary.

methods.name: spectrum
methods.sig: (result: DynamicsResult, *, residual_tol: float | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

methods.name: noise_sensitivity
methods.sig: (estimator, clean: np.ndarray, levels: Sequence[float], reference: Sequence[complex], *, reps: int = 10, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
Eigenvalue error (nearest-match, mean over ``reps``) when white noise of relative std ``level`` is added to
the states.

methods.name: select_order
methods.sig: (make_estimator: Callable[[Any], Any], candidates: Sequence[Any], train, test, *, horizon: int = 10) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Held-out multi-step error for each candidate order (rank or dictionary); the smallest wins.

methods.name: compare_with_state_regression
methods.sig: (dictionary: ObservableDictionary, train, test, *, horizon: int = 20, ridge: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc:
EDMD (linear propagation in the lifted space) against a nonlinear state-space model on the same dictionary,
``x_{n+1} = psi(x_n) W`` iterated in the state (NARX-type regression).

functions.name: snapshot_pairs
functions.sig: (data, *, lag: int = 1) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, float | None]
functions.doc:
``(X0, X1, dt)`` with rows ``x_n`` and ``x_{n+lag}`` from a :class:`Trajectory` (regular grid), a
:class:`TrajectoryEnsemble` (pairs within each member, never across members), an ``(n, d)`` array, or an explicit
``(X0, X1)`` tuple. Pairs with a missing value are dropped.

functions.name: gavish_donoho_rank
functions.sig: (s: np.ndarray, shape: tuple[int, int]) -> int
functions.doc:
Optimal hard threshold for singular values with unknown noise level (Gavish & Donoho 2014):
``tau = omega(beta) * median(s)``, ``omega(beta) ~ 0.56 beta^3 - 0.95 beta^2 + 1.82 beta + 1.43``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.dynamics.trajectories
children.doc:
Trajectories: the common input of the dynamics toolkit, and the adapters that make one from any source.

A :class:`Trajectory` is a state ``x(t_i)`` in ``R^d`` sampled at increasing times ``t_i``, which may be irregular.
Missing values are ``NaN`` (per component, so a sensor that drops out does not remove the others). The
observation window ends at ``observed_until`` (by default the last sample): an event that has not happened by then
is *right-censored*, which methods such as first-passage estimation must treat differently from "never happens".
``source`` records where the numbers came from, so a result can say whether it was computed on measurements, a
simulation, a closed form or a learned model's prediction.

A :class:`TrajectoryEnsemble` is several trajectories of the same variables (Monte Carlo paths, repeated
experiments, runs at different parameters); they may have different time grids and different windows.

Adapters (each returns a :class:`Trajectory`):

* :func:`from_array` -- arrays already in memory.
* :func:`from_table` / :func:`from_csv` -- a table of columns (dict, pandas DataFrame, CSV file) with units read
  from the headers (``"T [K]"``, ``"p (bar)"``) by :func:`pinneapple_data.physical_units.split_header`.
* :func:`from_solution` -- a ``pp.solve`` result (``Solution``: PINN, classical solver, closed form) sampled at a
  point of space over time.
* :func:`from_model` -- any callable of time (a trained PINN, a surrogate); PyTorch / JAX outputs are converted.
* :func:`from_snapshots` -- PDE snapshots ``u(t, x...)`` (a solver's output, or an FNO / DeepONet rollout on its
  grid) flattened into a state vector, with the spatial shape kept for :meth:`Trajectory.snapshots`.

What a trajectory does not do: it never fills a gap silently. :meth:`Trajectory.resample` interpolates only inside
the data, leaves ``NaN`` outside, and marks the result as interpolated.

classes.name: Trajectory
classes.doc:
``x(t_i)`` in ``R^d`` at strictly increasing times; see the module docstring.

``t``: ``(n,)`` finite, strictly increasing. ``x``: ``(n, d)`` (a 1-D ``x`` is one component), ``NaN`` where a
value is missing. ``names``: one per component. ``units``: unit text per component name and ``"t"`` for time
(optional; ``None`` means not stated, not dimensionless). ``observed_until``: end of the observation window,
``>= t[-1]``. ``source``: ``{"kind": one of SOURCE_KINDS, ...details}``.

methods.name: is_regular
methods.doc: True when every step equals the median step within ``rtol`` (relative).

methods.name: dt
methods.doc: The step of a regular grid, ``None`` for an irregular one (see :meth:`sampling`).

methods.name: sampling
methods.doc: Step statistics: min, median, max and the ratio max/min (1 for a regular grid).

methods.name: missing
methods.doc: Boolean ``(n, d)`` mask of missing values.

methods.name: censored
methods.doc: True when the window extends past the last sample (observation stopped without a final sample).

methods.name: component
methods.doc: Values of one component, ``(n,)``.

methods.name: window
methods.sig: (t0: float | None = None, t1: float | None = None) -> Trajectory
methods.doc: Samples with ``t0 <= t <= t1``. The window of the result ends at ``min(t1, observed_until)``.

methods.name: dropna
methods.doc: Drop samples with a missing component (``how="any"``) or with all components missing (``"all"``).

methods.name: resample
methods.doc:
Values at ``t_new`` by ``"linear"`` interpolation or ``"previous"`` (zero-order hold), per component,
from that component's non-missing samples only. Outside a component's data range the value is ``NaN``
(no extrapolation). The result is marked ``source["resampled"]``: interpolated values are not
measurements, and any statistic computed on them inherits the interpolation.

Several trajectories of the same variables (Monte Carlo paths, repeated experiments, a parameter sweep).

Members may have different time grids, windows and missing values; :meth:`stack` needs a common grid.

functions.sig: (t, x, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, observed_until: float | None = None, kind: str = 'array', **source) -> Trajectory

functions.name: from_table
functions.sig: (table: Mapping[str, Sequence[Any]] | Any, time: str, columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, kind: str = 'experimental', sort: bool = False, **source) -> Trajectory
functions.doc:
A trajectory from a table of columns: a mapping ``{header: values}`` or a pandas ``DataFrame``.

Units are read from the headers (``"T [K]"`` -> component ``"T"`` in ``"K"``); ``time`` and ``columns`` may
name a header either in full or by its name without the unit. Empty cells and ``nan``/``NA`` text are
missing values. Rows whose time is missing are dropped (counted in ``source["dropped_rows"]``).
``sort=True`` sorts unsorted rows by time; duplicate time stamps are always refused.

functions.sig: (path: str, time: str, columns: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, delimiter: str = ',', kind: str = 'experimental', sort: bool = False, **source) -> Trajectory

functions.name: from_solution
functions.sig: (solution: Any, t, at: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, time_coord: str = 't', **source) -> Trajectory
functions.doc:
Fields of a ``pp.solve`` result at one point of space, over the times ``t``.

``solution`` is a ``Solution`` (anything with ``problem.coords``, ``problem.fields`` and ``predict(points)``).
``at`` gives every coordinate other than ``time_coord``; ``fields`` defaults to all. The source kind is
``"pinn"`` for ``method="pinn"``, ``"analytic"`` for closed forms, ``"simulation"`` for classical and
external solvers, ``"model"`` otherwise. The values are the solution's predictions, not measurements: they
carry its error, which this adapter does not estimate (check it with ``pp.trust_card``).

functions.name: from_model
functions.sig: (fn: Callable[[Any], Any], t, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, *, kind: str = 'model', column: bool = False, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, **source) -> Trajectory
functions.doc:
Evaluate a callable of time (a trained PINN, a surrogate, a closed form) on ``t``.

``fn`` receives ``t`` as ``(n,)`` (or ``(n, 1)`` with ``column=True``) and returns ``(n,)`` or ``(n, d)``;
a PyTorch tensor or JAX array is converted. To evaluate a PyTorch module, wrap it so it receives a tensor
(``lambda t: net(torch.as_tensor(t, dtype=torch.float32))``); this adapter does not guess devices or dtypes.

functions.name: from_snapshots
functions.sig: (t, snapshots, *, name: str = 'u', kind: str = 'simulation', coords: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, unit: str | None = None, **source) -> Trajectory
functions.doc:
PDE snapshots ``u(t_i, grid)`` of shape ``(n_t, *spatial)`` as a trajectory of dimension ``prod(spatial)``.

Components are named ``"u[0]"``, ``"u[1]"``, ... in C order; ``coords`` (e.g. ``{"x": x_axis}``) and the
spatial shape are kept in ``source`` and :meth:`Trajectory.snapshots` restores the grid. Use ``kind="fno"`` or
``"deeponet"`` for an operator network's rollout on its grid.

children.summary: Trajectories: the common input of the dynamics toolkit, and the adapters that make one from any source.

children.doc:
Mathematical toolkit for dynamical systems.

Five frameworks that operate on trajectories from any source (measurements, simulations, closed forms, PINN / FNO /
DeepONet predictions), each with its benchmarks:

* :mod:`.first_passage`: first-passage and hitting times (deterministic crossing, Kaplan-Meier from observed
  trajectories, Monte Carlo of SDEs with Brownian-bridge correction, closed forms). Guide:
  ``docs/guides/dynamics_first_passage.md``.

* :mod:`.dimensional`: dimensional analysis and Buckingham pi in exact rational arithmetic, scaling laws,
  dimensional vs empirical normalisation, curve collapse with a permutation control, similarity. Guide:
  ``docs/guides/dynamics_dimensional.md``.

* :mod:`.fisher`: Fisher information (Gaussian, Poisson, any likelihood by score Monte Carlo with finite
  differences, PyTorch or JAX), Cramér-Rao bounds on parameters and on targets, identifiability, and experimental
  design (D, A, E, c, Bayesian D) built on :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems`. Guide:
  ``docs/guides/dynamics_fisher.md``.

* :mod:`.early_warning`: critical slowing down and early-warning indicators (rolling variance and autocorrelation,
  recovery rate, spectral indicators, detrending, surrogate significance, window / bandwidth / sampling
  sensitivity), with the indicator kept apart from any prediction. Guide: ``docs/guides/dynamics_early_warning.md``.

* :mod:`.koopman`: Koopman operator and spectral analysis (exact and TLS DMD with Gavish-Donoho rank selection,
  EDMD on dictionaries of observables including neural ones, eigenvalues, eigenfunctions, ResDMD residuals,
  generator EDMD, prediction and reconstruction). Its :class:`KoopmanOperator` is a fitted NumPy operator, distinct
  from the trainable layer ``pinneapple_neural.architectures.rom.koopman.KoopmanOperator``. Guide:
  ``docs/guides/dynamics_koopman.md``.

The frameworks share:

* the method contract (:mod:`._contract`): :class:`MethodCard` (inputs, assumptions, configuration, outputs,
  role, failure and applicability conditions, written before a run) and :class:`DynamicsResult` (estimate,
  uncertainty, checked and unchecked assumptions, diagnostics, convergence, applicability, reproducibility);
* backend detection (:mod:`._backends`): NumPy and SciPy are the core; PyTorch and JAX are detected without being
  imported and used only where a method offers automatic differentiation;
* trajectories (:mod:`.trajectories`): :class:`Trajectory` and :class:`TrajectoryEnsemble` with irregular
  sampling, missing values and right-censored observation windows, and the adapters from arrays, tables and CSV
  files, ``pp.solve`` solutions, callables (trained networks) and PDE snapshots.

Guide to the shared parts: ``docs/guides/dynamics_toolkit.md``.
children.summary: Mathematical toolkit for dynamical systems.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.acoustic
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.acoustic -- acoustic/vibration
condition-spectrum synthetic generation (resonance/impact-echo style
NDE) and physics-informed training.

Physical picture
-----------------
A slender rod/bar of length L, longitudinal wave speed c0, is struck
once (a simulated hammer tap near one end) and its free-free vibration
u(x, t) is propagated forward with an explicit finite-difference
time-domain (FDTD) scheme for the 1D wave equation

    u_tt = c(x)^2 * u_xx

A defect (e.g. a local wall-thinning or a partial crack) is modeled as
a LOCAL REDUCTION in wave speed, ``c(x) = c0 * sqrt(1 - severity)``
inside a small region -- since the longitudinal wave speed of a rod is
``c = sqrt(E/rho)``, reducing the effective local stiffness (as a crack
or thinning would) lowers c there. A sensor at a fixed location records
u(t); its FFT is the "condition spectrum". Because the defect locally
slows the wave, the resonant (modal) frequencies of the whole bar shift
DOWN relative to the defect-free baseline -- this is the classic
resonance/impact-echo defect signature (see e.g. Cawley & Adams, "The
location of defects in structures from measurements of natural
frequencies", J. Strain Analysis, 1979, for the general principle that
a local stiffness loss produces a mode-shape-dependent natural-frequency
shift; the FDTD wave-equation approach used here reproduces this
directly from first principles rather than via their closed-form
sensitivity formula).

Free-free boundary conditions are approximated with reflecting
(Neumann, du/dx=0) ends via simple ghost-node mirroring -- the standard
free-free elastic-bar boundary condition.

Simplification note: 1D scalar wave equation only (no cross-sectional/
shear/bending coupling, no material damping beyond none -- the bar
rings undamped for the simulated duration); a real impact-echo signal
also decays from radiation and internal friction, deliberately omitted
here to keep the ground-truth PDE this module's PINN needs to learn a
single, clean equation.

Generate a synthetic impact-echo / resonance condition-spectrum
dataset via 1D FDTD. Returns baseline (no-defect) and defect-case
time traces and spectra, plus InspectionPINN training data for the
defect-case displacement field u(x, t).

Returns a dict with:
  x_grid, t_grid       -- 1D spatial/time grids
  c_field              -- (nx,) wave-speed map used for the defect case
  u_field              -- (nt, nx) defect-case displacement history
  freqs, spectrum_defect, spectrum_baseline -- FFTs of the sensor trace
  x, y                 -- InspectionPINN (x,t) -> u supervised pairs
  x_col                -- physics collocation points
  c_scale, u_scale     -- normalization constants

functions.name: make_acoustic_physics_loss
functions.sig: (x_grid: np.ndarray, c_field: np.ndarray) -> PhysicsLossFn
functions.doc:
Build a `(model, batch) -> (loss, comps)` physics loss enforcing
the 1D wave equation ``u_tt - c(x)^2 * u_xx = 0`` via autograd, with
``c(x)`` looked up from the (fixed, precomputed) FDTD wave-speed map
-- the same "known material map" pattern as the eddy-current and MFL
modules' physics losses.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.base
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.base -- shared PINN backbone and generic
training wrapper for the inspection/NDE modalities in this package.

``InspectionPINN`` is intentionally a thin MLP, following the exact
constructor/forward pattern of
``pinneapple_neural.architectures.pinns.vanilla.VanillaPINN`` (this
package does not need inverse-parameter support or anything else
VanillaPINN doesn't already offer, so it is not subclassed directly --
duplicating its small, stable contract keeps this package's only
dependency on the neural stack at the ``PINNBase`` level, per
``pinneapple_neural/architectures/pinns/base.py``'s own "single source of
truth" contract: ``forward(*inputs, **kwargs) -> PINNOutput``,
``predict(*inputs) -> Tensor``, autograd helpers, checkpoint I/O, and
ONNX/TorchScript export are all inherited for free).

``train_generic_inspection_pinn`` is a thin wrapper around
``pinneapple_neural.trainer.trainer.Trainer`` (the same Trainer used
throughout the rest of the codebase, see
``examples/trainer/03_physics_aware_pinn_ode.py`` and
``examples/end_to_end/03_pinn_physics_loss_training.py`` for the pattern
being followed here): it turns a plain dict of numpy/torch arrays into
the ``{"x", "y", "x_col"}``-keyed ``DataLoader`` batches Trainer expects,
wires an optional physics residual through
``pinneapple_neural.trainer.losses.CombinedLoss`` +
``PhysicsLossHook``, and calls ``Trainer.fit``. None of the six modality
modules in this package hand-roll a training loop -- they all end up
here.

classes.name: InspectionPINN
classes.sig: (in_dim: int, out_dim: int, hidden: List[int] = (64, 64, 64), activation: str = 'tanh', *, modality: str = 'generic', dtype: torch.dtype = torch.float32)
classes.doc:
Generic coordinate -> inspection-signal MLP, physics-informed via an
externally supplied residual (see each modality module's
``make_*_physics_loss`` factory).

Constructor mirrors ``VanillaPINN`` exactly (``in_dim``, ``out_dim``,
``hidden``, ``activation``) plus a ``modality`` label carried purely
for bookkeeping (checkpoint metadata / repr) -- it has no effect on
the network itself. Every modality module in this package builds one
of these with a modality-appropriate ``(in_dim, out_dim)`` (e.g.
``(2, 2)`` for a complex field over an (r, z) plane, ``(2, 1)`` for a
real scalar field over (x, t), etc.) and trains it via
``train_generic_inspection_pinn`` with a modality-specific physics
residual.

methods.name: forward
methods.sig: (*inputs, physics_fn: Optional[Callable[..., Any]] = None, physics_data: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None) -> PINNOutput

functions.name: train_generic_inspection_pinn
functions.sig: (model: InspectionPINN, synthetic_data: Dict[str, Any], physics_loss_fn: Optional[PhysicsLossFn] = None, *, epochs: int = 200, lr: float = 0.001, batch_size: int = 32, val_fraction: float = 0.2, w_supervised: float = 1.0, w_physics: float = 1.0, device: str = 'cpu', log_dir: str = 'runs/inspection', run_name: str = 'inspection_pinn', seed: Optional[int] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Train an ``InspectionPINN`` on a synthetic-data dict via
``pinneapple_neural.trainer.trainer.Trainer`` -- the same Trainer, the
same ``CombinedLoss(SupervisedLoss + PhysicsLossHook)`` pattern, used
by every other physics-aware training example in this repo (see
``examples/trainer/03_physics_aware_pinn_ode.py``).

Parameters
----------
model : an ``InspectionPINN`` (or any ``PINNBase`` with a matching
    ``forward(x) -> PINNOutput`` contract).
synthetic_data : dict with keys
    ``"x"``    -- (N, in_dim) supervised input coordinates
    ``"y"``    -- (N, out_dim) supervised targets
    ``"x_col"`` -- (M, in_dim) physics collocation points (optional;
                    falls back to reusing ``"x"`` when omitted).
physics_loss_fn : callable ``(model, batch) -> (loss, comps)`` as
    expected by ``PhysicsLossHook``. Pass ``None`` for pure
    supervised training (no modality module in this package does,
    but the option exists e.g. for ablations).

Returns
-------
The dict returned by ``Trainer.fit`` (``best_val``, ``best_path``,
``history``, ...).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.eddy_current
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.eddy_current -- probe-scan synthetic
signal generation and physics-informed training for eddy-current NDE, on
top of the *existing* axisymmetric complex-Helmholtz FDM solver in
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.eddy_current_fdm``.

This module does NOT reimplement the Helmholtz solve -- it calls
``solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current`` / ``annular_current_source`` /
``eddy_current_density`` directly, exactly per that module's own
documented functional API, and adds two things that module doesn't
have: (1) a synthetic probe-SCAN signal (a coil response as a function
of lateral scan position, not just a single field solve) and (2) a PINN
training path whose physics loss reuses the same governing equation.

Probe-scan approximation (read before using for anything beyond a demo)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
``eddy_current_fdm`` solves the AXISYMMETRIC (2D, rotationally
symmetric about the z-axis) magnetostatic/eddy-current equation. A real
eddy-current probe scan moving laterally across a small localized flaw
(e.g. a crack) is NOT axisymmetric -- it is a fully 3D problem. Rather
than build a 3D solver (out of scope here), this module keeps the
existing axisymmetric solver and reinterprets the scan as follows: a
small disk-shaped conductivity anomaly ("defect") is placed inside the
conductor at a radius ``coil_r_center + scan_position`` for each
requested lateral scan offset, and the coil-region eddy-current-density
response is recorded relative to a defect-free baseline solve. This is
an axisymmetric SURROGATE for a lateral B-scan over a radially
symmetric flaw (e.g. a corrosion pit or annular groove directly under
the probe's sweep line) -- it is NOT a literal 3D moving-probe-over-a-
crack simulation, and is documented here as an explicit, honest
simplification, not a validated instrument model.

Governing equation (reused from eddy_current_fdm.py's own docstring)
------------------------------------------------------------------------
    d2A/dr2 + (1/r) dA/dr - A/r2 + d2A/dz2 - i*omega*mu*sigma*A = -mu*J

The PINN physics loss below enforces this equation (with J=0, evaluated
in the homogeneous conductor bulk away from the coil and the defect,
where the FDM ground truth already satisfies it exactly) on a PINN with
2 real output channels (Re(A), Im(A)) via autograd -- the complex
Helmholtz operator split into its real/imaginary parts:

    L[A_r] + omega*mu*sigma*A_i = 0
    L[A_i] - omega*mu*sigma*A_r = 0

where L[.] = d2(.)/dr2 + (1/r)d(.)/dr - (.)/r2 + d2(.)/dz2. Because this
homogeneous-bulk equation is linear and source-free, it is invariant
under any constant rescaling of A -- so training against a numerically
rescaled target (done below purely for gradient conditioning) does not
change what the residual being driven to zero means physically.

functions.name: generate_eddy_current_synthetic
functions.sig: (scan_positions: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, *, nr: int = 24, nz: int = 40, r_bounds: tuple = (0.001, 0.05), z_bounds: tuple = (-0.03, 0.03), omega: float = 2.0 * np.pi * 100000.0, sigma_bulk: float = 5000000.0, mu_r: float = 1.0, coil_r_center: float = 0.02, coil_z_center: float = 0.012, coil_width_r: float = 0.004, coil_width_z: float = 0.004, coil_turns: float = 100.0, coil_current: float =...
functions.doc:
Generate a synthetic eddy-current probe-scan dataset.

Physically: a lumped coil (via `annular_current_source`, the same
lumped-coil source term eddy_current_fdm.py's own docstring
describes) sits above a conductive half-space (z < 0 is the
conductor, z > 0 is air, sigma=0). The coil is driven at angular
frequency `omega`. `solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current` gives the
baseline vector-potential field A(r, z). For each requested lateral
`scan_position`, a small disk-shaped conductivity defect
(`sigma *= defect_sigma_frac` inside a disk of `defect_radius`) is
placed at radius ``coil_r_center + scan_position`` (see module
docstring for why this is an axisymmetric surrogate for a lateral
scan, not a literal 3D one) and the field is re-solved; the
DIFFERENTIAL coil-region eddy-current density (defect minus
baseline) is the synthetic probe-scan "signal" -- exactly the
differential impedance-plane signal a real eddy-current instrument
displays for a flaw indication.

Returns a dict with:
  r, z            -- SAME 1D grids passed to solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current
  A_baseline      -- (len(r), len(z)) complex, SAME shape/dtype convention
                      as solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current's own return value
  scan_positions  -- (n_scan,) lateral offsets (m)
  scan_signal     -- (n_scan,) complex differential probe signal
  x, y            -- InspectionPINN supervised training pairs: (r, z)
                      coordinates and the (rescaled) [Re(A), Im(A)] target,
                      subsampled from the baseline field
  x_col           -- (n_collocation, 2) points in the homogeneous
                      conductor bulk (away from coil and defect), used
                      for the physics residual
  a_scale, omega, mu, sigma_bulk -- parameters needed to rebuild/interpret
                      the physics residual and undo the target rescaling

functions.name: make_eddy_current_physics_loss
functions.sig: (omega: float, mu: float, sigma: float) -> PhysicsLossFn
functions.doc:
Build a `(model, batch) -> (loss, comps)` physics-loss callable
(the ``PhysicsLossHook`` contract) enforcing the real/imaginary split
of the axisymmetric complex-Helmholtz operator from
``eddy_current_fdm.build_axisymmetric_helmholtz_system``, with J=0
(valid in the homogeneous conductor bulk collocation region -- see
`generate_eddy_current_synthetic`).

functions.name: train_eddy_current
functions.sig: (synthetic_data: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, *, hidden = (64, 64, 64), epochs: int = 200, lr: float = 0.001, batch_size: int = 32, device: str = 'cpu', seed: Optional[int] = 0, log_dir: str = 'runs/inspection_eddy_current', run_name: str = 'eddy_current_pinn', w_supervised: float = 1.0, w_physics: float = 1.0, **synthetic_kwargs) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Generate (if not supplied) eddy-current synthetic data, build an
`InspectionPINN` and train it via `train_generic_inspection_pinn`
with the Helmholtz-residual physics loss above.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.emat
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.emat -- a deliberately simplified
Electromagnetic Acoustic Transducer (EMAT) synthetic signal generator
and physics-informed training path.

What a real EMAT does (for context, not what this module solves)
-------------------------------------------------------------------
An EMAT couples an RF coil's induced eddy currents with a static bias
magnetic field: the resulting Lorentz body force ``F = J x B0`` launches
an elastic wave directly in a conductive test-piece, with no couplant
(unlike a piezoelectric transducer). A first-principles EMAT model is a
COUPLED electromagnetic + elastodynamic problem (see Hirao & Ogi,
"EMATs for Science and Industry: Noncontacting Ultrasonic
Measurements", Springer, 2003, and Ogi, J. Appl. Phys. 82, 1997, for the
Lorentz-force EMAT generation mechanism) -- a full 2D/3D solve of that
kind is well beyond this module's scope (it would essentially require
coupling ``eddy_current_fdm.py``'s Helmholtz solve to a 2D elastic-wave
solver, a substantial undertaking of its own).

What this module actually does (explicit simplification)
-----------------------------------------------------------
The electromagnetic generation step is reduced to a SCALAR forcing
term ``F(x, t) = J0 * envelope(t) * footprint(x)`` (a burst-modulated,
spatially-localized force under the coil footprint -- footprint(x) is
a Gaussian standing in for the coil's real current-density profile,
and envelope(t) is a tone-burst standing in for the Lorentz-force
time-history), which drives a 1D scalar elastic wave equation

    rho * u_tt = G(x) * u_xx + F(x, t)

with a local shear-modulus reduction ``G(x)`` modeling a defect
(thinning/void), the same "local property change reflects/attenuates a
wave packet" NDE signature used throughout this package. Solved via the
same explicit FDTD scheme as ``pinneapple_analysis.inspection.acoustic``.
This is honestly a 1D scalar surrogate, not a validated EMAT model --
its purpose is to demonstrate the "EM source term + elastic-wave
response" PINN training pattern the plan calls for, not to predict a
real instrument's output.

functions.name: generate_emat_synthetic
functions.sig: (*, L: float = 0.3, rho: float = 7800.0, G0: float = 80000000000.0, n_points: int = 60, duration: float = 6e-05, coil_position: float = 0.05, coil_footprint: float = 0.02, burst_freq: float = 1000000.0, n_cycles: float = 3.0, J0: float = 5000000000.0, receiver_position: float = 0.85, defect_position: float = 0.5, defect_width: float = 0.02, defect_severity: float = 0.4, n_supervised: int = 400,...
functions.doc:
Generate a synthetic EMAT pitch-catch signal: a Lorentz-force-like
tone burst launches an elastic wave from the coil footprint; a defect
(local stiffness drop) partially reflects/attenuates it before it
reaches the receiver.

Returns a dict with:
  x_grid, t_grid    -- 1D grids
  c_field           -- (nx,) wave-speed map (sqrt(G(x)/rho))
  F_field           -- (nt, nx) EM forcing term used to drive the wave
  u_field           -- (nt, nx) displacement history
  receiver_trace    -- u(t) at the receiver
  x, y, x_col       -- InspectionPINN training data (see other modules)
  c_scale, u_scale  -- normalization info

functions.name: make_emat_physics_loss
functions.sig: (x_grid: np.ndarray, c_field: np.ndarray, coil_x0: float, footprint_sigma: float, burst_freq: float, n_cycles: float, t0_burst: float, J0_over_rho: float) -> PhysicsLossFn
functions.doc:
Build a `(model, batch) -> (loss, comps)` physics loss enforcing
the FORCED wave equation ``u_tt - c(x)^2 u_xx - F(x,t) = 0``, with
``c(x)`` looked up from a fixed material map (as in the `acoustic`
module) and ``F(x,t)`` evaluated in CLOSED FORM (it is an explicit
function of x,t used to generate the ground truth, so no
interpolation table is needed for it).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.guided_wave_ultrasonic
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.guided_wave_ultrasonic -- 1D guided-wave
(Lamb/torsional-wave style) dispersion + defect-reflection synthetic
signal generation, plus physics-informed training.

Physical picture (simplified -- see caveat)
---------------------------------------------
A real guided wave in a plate or pipe (Lamb waves, SH waves, torsional
waves in a pipe, ...) is DISPERSIVE: its phase/group velocity depends on
frequency, governed by the Rayleigh-Lamb frequency equation, a
transcendental system requiring root-finding across branches (see Rose,
"Ultrasonic Guided Waves in Solid Media", Cambridge University Press,
2014). Solving that exactly is out of scope here.

CAVEAT / simplification: this module instead uses the classic
Klein-Gordon-type dispersive wave equation

    u_tt = c0^2 * u_xx - beta(x) * u

whose plane-wave dispersion relation is ``omega^2 = c0^2 k^2 + beta``,
i.e. a wave that only propagates above the cutoff frequency
``sqrt(beta)/(2*pi)`` and is increasingly dispersive near it -- the same
QUALITATIVE signature (a cutoff frequency, group velocity below phase
velocity) as the lowest-order guided-wave mode of a real waveguide, but
NOT a fit to any specific mode's exact Rayleigh-Lamb dispersion curve.

A defect (e.g. a wall-loss region) is modeled as a local change in
``beta(x)`` (an effective local impedance/cutoff change), producing a
partial reflection and transmission of an incident tone-burst wave
packet -- the classic guided-wave NDE defect signature: time-of-flight
to the reflected echo locates the defect, and the reflection/attenuation
amplitude relates to its severity. Solved via the same explicit FDTD
scheme used elsewhere in this package.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.magnetic_flux_leakage
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.magnetic_flux_leakage -- a lightweight
2D nonlinear-permeability magnetostatic FDM ground truth for Magnetic
Flux Leakage (MFL) inspection, plus a physics-informed (PIML) training
path.

Physical picture (simplified, illustrative -- see caveats below)
------------------------------------------------------------------
A steel plate is magnetized by a yoke: this module models that as a
Dirichlet boundary condition on a magnetic SCALAR potential phi(x, y)
(``phi = +phi0`` at the left edge, ``phi = -phi0`` at the right edge,
representing the yoke's two poles), with the plate occupying the
remaining domain. Away from any free current, magnetostatics reduces to

    div(mu(x, y) * grad(phi)) = 0,          B = -mu * grad(phi)

which is solved by a standard variable-coefficient 5-point finite
DIFFERENCE / finite-VOLUME stencil (harmonic-mean face permeability,
the standard treatment for a discontinuous coefficient elliptic PDE --
see e.g. LeVeque, "Finite Difference Methods for ODEs and PDEs", 2007,
Sec. 3.7), with a subsurface DEFECT modeled as a small region of very
low permeability (mu ~ mu0, i.e. as if it were air/void -- a corrosion
pit or crack) embedded in the steel.

Steel is NONLINEAR: this module uses a simple Frohlich-Kennelly-type
saturation law

    mu(H) = mu0 + mu0*(mu_r_max - 1) / (1 + (|H| / H_sat)**2)

(a standard simple single-valued -- i.e. non-hysteretic -- saturation
curve shape used for illustrative nonlinear-magnetics demonstrations;
NOT a fit to any specific certified steel grade's measured B-H curve)
solved self-consistently via PICARD ITERATION: solve the linear problem
with the current mu-field guess, recompute H = |grad(phi)| and hence a
new mu(H), and repeat.

Leakage signal: the vertical flux density Bz just beneath the top
surface (a finite-difference derivative of phi at the last interior
row) is used as the synthetic "probe scan" signal -- a defect locally
diverts flux around/through its low-permeability region, producing a
local Bz anomaly directly above it, exactly the MFL detection mechanism
(see e.g. ASNT NDT Handbook, "Magnetic Flux Leakage Testing").

Caveats (explicit, not to be treated as a validated instrument model):
this is a 2D cross-section, not 3D; hysteresis is ignored; the leakage
readout uses the last interior grid row as a stand-in for a lifted
sensor rather than solving the field in the air gap above the plate.

Solve the nonlinear MFL magnetostatic scalar-potential problem via
Picard iteration. `defect_mask` (nx, ny) bool marks the low-permeability
flaw region (held fixed at mu0, never updated by the saturation law).
Returns (x, y, phi, mu) -- actually (x, y, phi) plus mu is returned
separately by the caller; see `generate_magnetic_flux_leakage_synthetic`.

  phi, mu         -- (nx, ny) solved scalar potential and converged
                      permeability field

  x_train, y_train (as InspectionPINN "x"/"y") -- supervised (x,y)->phi pairs

functions.name: make_mfl_physics_loss
functions.sig: (x_grid: np.ndarray, y_grid: np.ndarray, mu_field: np.ndarray) -> PhysicsLossFn
functions.doc:
Build a `(model, batch) -> (loss, comps)` physics loss enforcing a
SIMPLIFIED version of div(mu*grad(phi))=0: `mu(x,y) * laplacian(phi)`,
i.e. dropping the `grad(mu).grad(phi)` cross term. This is an honest
simplification -- exact only where mu varies slowly, which is most of
the domain except right at the sharp defect boundary -- adopted so the
residual needs only a fixed, precomputed mu(x,y) lookup rather than a
differentiable representation of mu's own spatial gradient.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inspection.phased_array_ultrasonic
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection.phased_array_ultrasonic -- synthetic
B-scan generation from an array of point-source/receiver elements via
delay-and-sum (Total Focusing Method, TFM) beamforming, plus
physics-informed training.

Physical picture
-----------------
An N-element linear phased-array probe sits on the surface (z=0) of a
test-piece; a point-like defect (scatterer) sits at depth (x_d, z_d). In
PULSE-ECHO mode, element i transmits and receives its own echo: the
round-trip time-of-flight is ``2 * dist(element_i, defect) / c`` and the
received amplitude decays geometrically (``1/dist``) -- each element's
time trace is modeled as a RICKER WAVELET (the standard synthetic
ultrasonic pulse shape used throughout seismic/NDE simulation; it is the
second derivative of a Gaussian and closely resembles a real
piezoelectric transducer's broadband pulse response) centered at that
arrival time.

The B-scan IMAGE is then reconstructed via delay-and-sum / Total
Focusing Method (TFM) beamforming (Holmes, Drinkwater & Wilcox,
"Post-processing of the full matrix of ultrasonic transmit-receive array
data for non-destructive evaluation", NDT&E International, 2005): for
every hypothesis pixel (x, z), sum each element's recorded trace at the
travel time implied by that hypothesis location -- constructive
interference focuses the image at the true scatterer location.

Physics-loss caveat (read before treating this as more than a PIML
regularizer): the reconstructed image intensity is a nonlinear function
of the underlying acoustic pressure field, not itself a solution of the
wave equation. This module nonetheless trains the PINN's image-intensity
surrogate against a 2D HELMHOLTZ consistency constraint
(``laplacian(p) + k0^2 * p = 0`` at the array's carrier wavenumber
``k0 = 2*pi*f0/c``) as a smooth, wave-consistent regularizer -- the same
spirit as a matched-field-processing image inheriting spatial-frequency
content from the governing wave equation -- NOT an exact physical law
for image intensity. This is stated explicitly so it is not mistaken for
a first-principles derivation.

children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inspection -- Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) /
inspection PINN suite: synthetic signal generation + physics-informed
training for six inspection modalities.

Relationship to neighboring packages
-------------------------------------
``pinneapple_perception`` (audio_modal, video_piv, image_geometry) goes
SENSOR-MEDIA -> PHYSICS-OBSERVABLE: it extracts a physical quantity
(a frequency, a velocity field, a boundary) FROM a generic media
artifact (audio, video, an image) that was presumably captured of a
real system, for use as a downstream training/validation signal.

This package goes the other, complementary direction: SENSOR-SIGNAL ->
INTERNAL-MATERIAL-STATE. Each modality module here generates a
physically-plausible SYNTHETIC inspection signal (an eddy-current probe
scan, an MFL leakage trace, an ultrasonic B-scan, ...) from a physics
model of the test-piece, and trains a physics-informed neural network
(``InspectionPINN``) to map (probe/scan coordinates) -> (an internal
material/defect state), constrained by the same governing PDE that
generated the data. Where ``pinneapple_perception`` interprets media
that already exists, this package is training a physics-constrained
model to relate an inspection signal to what's underneath the surface
that produced it -- the inverse-flavored problem NDE inspection
actually poses.

Relationship to ``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.eddy_current_fdm``
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------
That module ALREADY implements a full axisymmetric complex-Helmholtz FDM
solver for eddy-current physics (5-point stencil sparse assembly, a
lumped-coil source term, derived eddy-current density/flux) -- this
package's ``eddy_current`` module does not reimplement any of that. It
calls the existing solver directly and adds exactly what was missing: a
synthetic PROBE-SCAN signal (the solver only produces one field solve at
a time, not a scan) and a PINN training path whose physics loss reuses
the same governing Helmholtz equation.

What's here
-----------
``base``
    ``InspectionPINN`` -- a thin MLP subclassing `PINNBase` (mirrors
    `VanillaPINN`'s constructor exactly) -- and
    ``train_generic_inspection_pinn`` -- a thin wrapper around
    ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.trainer.Trainer`` shared by all six
    modalities below.

Six modality modules, each exposing ``generate_<modality>_synthetic(...)``
(coordinates + a physically-plausible, EXPLICITLY SYNTHETIC/ILLUSTRATIVE
signal -- never measured data) and ``train_<modality>(...)``:

``eddy_current``
    Probe-scan signal built on top of ``eddy_current_fdm``'s existing
    axisymmetric Helmholtz solve; PINN physics loss reuses that same
    equation (split into real/imaginary parts).
``magnetic_flux_leakage``
    A new lightweight 2D nonlinear-permeability (Frohlich-Kennelly
    saturation, Picard-iterated) magnetostatic FDM ground truth, with a
    simple two-pole magnet Dirichlet boundary condition; PIML loss
    enforces a locally-linearized ``div(mu*grad(phi))=0``.
``acoustic``
    1D FDTD wave-equation impact-echo / resonance-spectrum synthetic
    generator (a defect locally slows the wave, shifting modal
    frequencies down); PIML loss enforces the wave equation.
``emat``
    A deliberately simplified scalar Lorentz-force-like EM source term
    driving a 1D elastic wave equation (full coupled EM+elastodynamic
    EMAT physics is out of scope -- see the module docstring for the
    explicit simplification).
``guided_wave_ultrasonic``
    1D dispersive (Klein-Gordon-type) guided-wave pulse-echo synthetic
    generator -- a simplified stand-in for the true Rayleigh-Lamb
    dispersion relation (see module docstring).
``phased_array_ultrasonic``
    Synthetic pulse-echo B-scan from an array of point elements,
    reconstructed via delay-and-sum / Total Focusing Method beamforming;
    PIML loss applies a 2D Helmholtz consistency regularizer to the
    image-intensity surrogate (an honestly-labeled approximation, not an
    exact physical law for image intensity -- see module docstring).

Deliberately NOT included: a 7th "chemical" inspection modality -- that
overlaps ``pinneapple_systems.process_components.reaction_kinetics`` and
is out of this package's scope.
children.summary: Non-Destructive Evaluation (NDE) / inspection PINN suite: synthetic signal generation + physics-informed training for six inspection modalities.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems
pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.activation_mapping
children.doc:
Cardiac activation mapping from sparse measurements with a physics-informed network (eikonal model).

The approach of Sahli Costabal, Yang, Perdikaris, Hurtado and Kuhl ("Physics-informed neural networks for cardiac
activation mapping", Front Phys 8:42, 2020), reimplemented from its general description (the paper itself was not
accessible from the session that wrote this, so no setting or number of it is used here):

* two networks on the tissue domain: the activation time ``T(x, y)`` and the conduction velocity ``V(x, y) > 0``;
* loss = mean squared misfit of ``T`` at the measurement sites + the eikonal residual ``(V |grad T| - 1)^2`` at
  random collocation points + a total-variation penalty on ``V`` (piecewise-smooth tissue, scar borders);
* ``V`` is bounded to ``[v_min, v_max]`` by a sigmoid output.

:func:`interpolate_baseline` is the comparison every activation-mapping method should beat: linear interpolation of
the measured times (Delaunay), which is what clinical mapping systems display between electrodes. The conduction
velocity of any map comes from :func:`pinneapple_physics.biology.excitable.conduction_velocity`.

classes.sig: (bounds, config: EikonalPINNConfig | None = None)

methods.doc: Activation time and conduction velocity at ``points`` (n, 2).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.amortized
children.doc:
Amortised inference: a mixture density network trained on simulated (parameters, observations) pairs that returns
the posterior of the parameters for any observation in one forward pass (Bishop 1994; the neural posterior
estimation of Papamakarios & Murray 2016).

    sim = lambda Z: surrogate(Z)                         # (n, d) unit-cube parameters -> (n, m) observations
    mdn = fit_mdn(sim, d=1, noise=lambda Y, rng: Y + 0.01 * rng.standard_normal(Y.shape), n_sims=20000)
    S = mdn.sample(y_obs, 4000)                          # posterior samples of the unit-cube parameters
    cal = posterior_coverage(mdn, Z_test, Y_test)        # are the credible intervals honest on known cases?

The prior is uniform on the unit cube (draws come from ``prior`` if given); ``noise(Y, rng)`` adds what separates
a measurement from the simulator (measurement noise, model discrepancy, surrogate uncertainty), so the posterior
is wide where the data cannot tell the parameters apart and multimodal where several designs give the same
measurement. Parameters are modelled in logit space (the posterior never leaves the cube). Training runs under a
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget.ComputeBudget` with :func:`train_within_budget`.

methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, n: int, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: ``n`` posterior samples (n, d) in the unit cube for one observation ``y`` (m,).

methods.name: log_prob
methods.doc: log p(z | y) (unit-cube density) of each row of ``z`` (n, d) for one observation ``y``.

methods.name: summary
methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, level: float = 0.9, n: int = 4000, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]

functions.name: hdi
functions.sig: (samples: np.ndarray, level: float = 0.9, bins: int = 60) -> list[list[float]]
functions.doc:
Highest-density set of 1-D samples as a list of intervals (several when the posterior is multimodal), from a
histogram: the smallest set of bins holding ``level`` of the mass. Bins are ranked by a [1, 2, 1]/4-smoothed
count (so sampling noise does not punch one-bin holes into a mode) while the mass is counted from the raw
histogram; intervals separated by a single bin are merged.

central credible interval (per parameter), and the rank of the truth among the posterior samples (uniform for a
calibrated posterior; Talts et al. 2018). Also the posterior-mean error.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.binn
children.doc:
Biologically-informed neural networks (BINNs) for reaction-diffusion: learn the diffusivity, growth and delay
terms of ``u_t = T(t) (D(u) u_x)_x + G(u) u`` as networks, from sparse data.

Lagergren, Nardini, Baker, Simpson and Flores, PLoS Comput Biol 16(12):e1008462 (2020), arXiv:2005.13073,
reimplemented from the paper's Methods (no code copied). A :class:`ReactionDiffusionBINN` is a
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.missing_term.NeuralTermDiscovery` whose missing terms are functions of
the state (``D(u)``, ``G(u)``) and of time (``T(t)``) instead of the coordinates:

* ``u_MLP(x, t)``: 3 hidden layers of 128 sigmoid units, softplus output times the carrying capacity K;
* ``D_MLP(u / K)``, ``G_MLP(u / K)``, ``T_MLP(t)``: 3 x 32 sigmoid units; outputs softplus x D_max, linear x G_max and
  sigmoid;
* loss = GLS misfit (Eq 6, gamma = 0.2, the t = 0 rows weighted 10) on mini-batches of the training split + PDE
  residual at 10,000 uniformly random (x, t) per step + the constraints of Eq 16 (ranges, monotonicity of D, G, T)
  with the paper's weights alpha_i;
* Adam (default settings), 80 / 20 train / validation split, the network with the best validation GLS kept, early
  stopping after ``patience`` steps without improvement.

After training, :meth:`ReactionDiffusionBINN.forward_gls` solves the PDE with the learned terms
(:func:`pinneapple_physics.biology.cell_migration.solve_reaction_diffusion`) and scores it against the data, which is
how the paper selects among retrainings; :meth:`ReactionDiffusionBINN.mechanistic_guess` fits the closed forms of
Eq 12 to the learned curves (the paper's starting point for the BINN-guided model).

classes.sig: (config: BINNConfig | None = None)

methods.sig: (x, t, U, verbose: bool = False) -> ReactionDiffusionBINN

methods.doc: ``D`` or ``G`` at densities (cells/mm^2), ``T`` at times (days).

methods.name: forward_gls
methods.doc: GLS error of the PDE solved with the learned terms (the paper's model-selection score).

methods.name: mechanistic_guess
methods.doc:
Least-squares fit of Eq 12 to the learned curves: ``D0 + D (u/K)^m`` on the observed density range,
``r (1 - u/K)`` and the logistic ``1 / (1 + exp(-(beta1 t + beta0)))`` (units mm^2/day, 1/day).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.calibration
children.doc:
Model calibration: fit model parameters to measurements, with honest uncertainty and a held-out check.

:func:`calibrate` does, on one model and one set of measurements:

1. splits the measurements into a fit set and a held-out set (given, a random fraction, or the last rows by an input
   such as time: an extrapolation test);
2. weighted least squares in the scaled parameters (trust-region reflective inside the bounds; robust losses on
   request);
3. **identifiability** (:func:`~.identifiability.analyze_identifiability` of the fit design at the calibrated
   values): a parameter the data cannot determine gets *no* confidence interval: it is reported "not estimable"
   with the reason and the combination the data do fix;
4. **confidence intervals** for the estimable parameters, two ways: from the Jacobian at the optimum
   (``cov = s^2 (J^T W J)^-1`` with ``s^2 = chi2/dof``, Student t quantile; symmetric in ln for log parameters) and
   by a residual bootstrap (refit on ``y_hat + resampled standardised residuals * sigma``, percentile interval);
5. residuals, metrics before (starting values) and after on the fit set and on the held-out measurements, and the
   prediction of every measurement before and after.

Every number comes from these runs; ``warnings`` lists what makes them doubtful (a parameter on its bound, a reduced
chi-square far from 1, held-out error much larger than the fit error, too few points for the bootstrap).

use it, widened by ``sqrt(chi2/dof)`` when the residuals are larger, never narrowed. ``False`` when sigma is only
a relative weight: the noise level is then estimated from the residuals (``s^2 = chi2/dof``).

The inverse-problems core in the shared data contracts (``pinneapple_data.contracts``).

``"identifiability"``, ``"calibration"``, ``"inverse"``), parameters travel as a ``ParameterSpace``, and a

whose calibrated values and held-out errors go on to uncertainty or optimisation studies.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.counterfactual_attribution
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.counterfactual_attribution --
exact Shapley-value attribution of a measured change in a scalar outcome
across a small set of candidate causes, evaluated through counterfactual
runs of ANY caller-supplied model (a physics simulator, a trained
surrogate, or any other value function) -- plus an ambiguity classifier
for when two causes cannot be told apart from the available evidence.

SELECTED FORMULATION: exact Shapley-value attribution (Shapley, "A Value
for n-Person Games", in Contributions to the Theory of Games II, Annals
of Mathematics Studies 28, Princeton University Press, 1953; the same
cooperative-game-theory construction underlying SHAP -- Lundberg & Lee,
"A Unified Approach to Interpreting Model Predictions", NeurIPS 2017).
Given n candidate causes, each togglable between a BASELINE and a
CURRENT value, and a value function v(S) = the model's scalar output
with every cause in subset S set to its current value and every other
cause at baseline:

    phi_i = sum over subsets S of (N minus {i}):
                [|S|! (n-|S|-1)! / n!] * (v(S union {i}) - v(S))

Shapley's own axioms (efficiency, symmetry, additivity, null player)
make this the UNIQUE allocation with the EFFICIENCY property: the
attributed contributions sum EXACTLY to v(full set) - v(empty set),
including every pairwise/higher-order interaction between causes. A
naive one-factor-at-a-time sensitivity sweep does not have this exact-
closure property whenever causes interact.

COST: exact computation requires 2^n evaluations of v() for n candidate
causes (e.g. 32 for n=5) -- each evaluation is whatever the caller's
value function costs (a full physics solve, a forward pass, ...). This
is appropriate for an on-demand diagnostic, not a real-time control loop;
`ExactShapleyAttributor` caches by subset so repeated calls (e.g. after
changing which causes are "current") don't re-evaluate v() needlessly.

AMBIGUITY / IDENTIFIABILITY: `classify_ambiguity` addresses a common
follow-on question -- can the data actually tell two overlapping causes
apart? Two causes are treated as INSEPARABLE if (a) their attributed
contributions overlap within their stated uncertainty bands, AND (b) the
available measurement set includes no channel unique to either cause's
own signature. When both hold, the result is explicitly marked
indeterminate together with the specific measurement that would resolve
it, rather than silently picking a winner.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.discovery
children.doc:
The standard equation-discovery workflow (#1192): sparse regression over a library of candidate terms, the model
chosen on data never fitted, its terms with bootstrap intervals and inclusion probabilities, and the equations as
text the library parses (and as LaTeX).

* **ODEs** (:func:`discover_ode`, SINDy: Brunton, Proctor & Kutz, *PNAS* 113 (2016) 3932): states sampled in time;
  derivatives by a Savitzky-Golay smoothing derivative (noise is estimated and stated); a polynomial library of the
  states up to ``degree`` plus the caller's terms.
* **PDEs** (:func:`discover_pde`, PDE-FIND: Rudy, Brunton, Proctor & Kutz, *Sci. Adv.* 3 (2017) e1602614): a field
  on a grid; ``u_t`` regressed on products of ``u`` powers and its spatial derivatives.

Selection: sequentially thresholded least squares (STLSQ) over a path of thresholds; each model is scored by AICc
on the held-out part (the last ``holdout`` of the time window), so a term survives only when it predicts data it
never saw. The selected model is refitted ``n_bootstrap`` times on resampled rows (ensemble SINDy, Fasel et al.
*Proc. R. Soc. A* 478 (2022)): a term's inclusion probability and its coefficient interval. For ODEs the chosen
model is integrated from the held-out window's first state and compared with the data (a model that fits
derivatives but diverges is rejected).

functions.name: discover_ode
functions.sig: (t: np.ndarray, Y: np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str], *, degree: int = 2, holdout: float = 0.2, thresholds: Sequence[float] | None = None, window: int | None = None, n_bootstrap: int = 100, rollout_fraction: float = 0.25, rollout_tol: float = 0.1, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Discover ``dY/dt = f(Y)`` from states ``Y`` (n, d) sampled at uniform times ``t``.

``window``: the Savitzky-Golay window; by default each of 7, 11, 15, 21, 31, 41 points is tried and the one
whose model best reproduces the held-out window wins. The rollout runs over the first ``rollout_fraction`` of
the held-out window (chaotic systems diverge beyond their predictability time whatever the coefficients) and
its error is relative to the whole signal's RMS.

functions.name: discover_pde
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, t: np.ndarray, *, max_power: int = 2, max_deriv: int = 3, holdout: float = 0.2, thresholds: Sequence[float] | None = None, n_bootstrap: int = 50, trim: int = 5, smooth: int | None = None, form: str = 'strong', weak_support: tuple[float, float] = (0.24, 0.3), seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Discover ``u_t = f(u, u_x, u_xx, ...)`` from a field ``u`` (nx, nt) on a uniform grid (PDE-FIND).

``smooth``: a Savitzky-Golay window (cubic) applied along x and t before differentiating; by default it is used
when the field's high-frequency content says it is noisy (finite differences of noise grow as 1/dx^k).

``form``: ``"strong"`` regresses ``u_t`` on the library evaluated pointwise (PDE-FIND); ``"weak"`` regresses
the equation integrated against test functions (:func:`_weak_system`, of ``weak_support`` fractions of the x
and t extents), which removes the bias that noisy derivatives put in the strong form. A strong-form result is
also checked against the weak form (``discover.weak_form``): a term that only the strong form selects, or that
it drops, is named, because noise in the derivatives (errors in the variables of the regression) can make one
term stand in for part of another, e.g. ``-u`` for part of ``u_xx`` on a smooth field.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman
children.doc:
Ensemble Kalman Inversion (EKI) for derivative-free inverse problems.

EKI is a derivative-free iterative method for PDE-constrained parameter
identification.  It maintains an ensemble of parameter candidates and updates
them via Kalman-like cross-covariance computations, requiring only forward
model evaluations (no gradients of G).

Implemented methods
-------------------
EnsembleKalmanInversion   standard EKI (Iglesias et al. 2013)
IteratedEKI               Tikhonov-regularized EKI / TEKI (Chada et al. 2020)

Both support:
- Parallel ensemble evaluation (via vectorised forward_fn)
- Configurable ensemble size (J ≈ 2–3 × p is often sufficient)
- Early stopping via ensemble collapse detection
- Full convergence history

Mathematical formulation
------------------------
Forward model:      G : R^p → R^k        (parameter → observations)
Observations:       y ∈ R^k               (noisy measurement vector)
Noise covariance:   Γ ∈ R^{k×k} (s.p.d.)

EKI update rule (for ensemble member j):

    g^(j) = G(θ^(j))
    C_θg  = (1/J) Σ_j (θ^(j) − θ̄)(g^(j) − ḡ)^T   ∈ R^{p×k}
    C_gg  = (1/J) Σ_j (g^(j) − ḡ)(g^(j) − ḡ)^T   ∈ R^{k×k}
    K     = C_θg (C_gg + Γ)^{-1}                    (Kalman gain)
    θ^(j) ← θ^(j) + K (y + η^(j) − g^(j)),   η^(j) ~ N(0, Γ)

For IteratedEKI, artificial parameters are appended to the state vector so
Tikhonov regularisation is incorporated analytically.

References
----------
- Iglesias, Law & Stuart (2013) "Ensemble Kalman Methods for Inverse Problems"
  Inverse Problems 29, 045001.
- Chada, Stuart & Tong (2020) "Tikhonov Regularisation in Ensemble Kalman
  Inversion" arXiv:1901.11493.
- Garbuno-Inigo et al. (2020) "Interacting Langevin Diffusions" SIAM J Appl
  Dyn Syst.

classes.name: EKIConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for Ensemble Kalman Inversion.

Parameters
----------
n_ensemble : int
    Ensemble size J.  Rule of thumb: J ≈ 3 × p (number of parameters).
    Larger J → more accurate covariance estimates, higher cost.
n_iterations : int
    Maximum number of EKI update steps.
noise_cov : np.ndarray, optional
    Observation noise covariance Γ ∈ R^{k×k}.  If None, uses noise_std²·I.
noise_std : float
    Noise standard deviation σ (used when noise_cov is None).
init_spread : float
    Standard deviation used to perturb the initial ensemble around
    ``theta_init``.  Set to 0 to start all members at the same point.
lambda_reg : float
    Tikhonov regularisation strength λ ≥ 0.  Only used by IteratedEKI.
    λ = 0 recovers standard EKI.
prior_mean : np.ndarray, optional
    Prior mean θ₀ for regularisation.  Defaults to ``theta_init``.
prior_cov : np.ndarray, optional
    Prior covariance C₀ for regularisation.  If None uses the identity I
    (so the regularisation term reduces to λ ‖θ − θ₀‖²).
tol_collapse : float
    Stop early when ensemble spread < tol_collapse (collapsed ensemble).
seed : int, optional
verbose : bool
print_every : int

classes.name: EKIHistory
classes.doc:
Convergence history of an EKI run.

Attributes
----------
iterations : list[int]
data_misfit : list[float]
    ‖G(θ̄) − y‖²_{Γ⁻¹} at each iteration (ensemble mean).
ensemble_spread : list[float]
    Mean per-dimension standard deviation of the ensemble in θ-space
    (collapse diagnostic; shrinks to zero as the ensemble collapses).
theta_mean_history : list[np.ndarray]
    Ensemble mean at each stored iteration.

classes.name: EnsembleKalmanInversion
classes.sig: (forward_fn: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], config: Optional[EKIConfig] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Standard Ensemble Kalman Inversion.

Parameters
----------
forward_fn : callable
    Maps a **batch** of parameters to observations.
    Signature: ``(theta_batch: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray``
    Input shape (J, p), output shape (J, k).
    Batching is mandatory so the method can parallelise ensemble evals.
config : EKIConfig, optional

methods.name: initialize
methods.doc: Set up the ensemble.

methods.name: theta_mean
methods.doc: Current ensemble mean θ̄.

methods.name: theta_cov
methods.doc: Current ensemble covariance C ∈ R^{p×p}.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Perform one EKI update.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, theta_init: np.ndarray, *, ensemble: Optional[np.ndarray] = None) -> EKIHistory
methods.doc: Run full EKI until convergence or max iterations.

classes.name: IteratedEKI
classes.doc:
Tikhonov-regularized Ensemble Kalman Inversion (TEKI).

Adds Tikhonov regularisation by extending the state space:

    G̃(θ) = [G(θ);  √λ (θ − θ₀)]   ∈ R^{k+p}
    ỹ    = [y;     0_p]
    Γ̃    = diag(Γ, C₀)                     (C₀ = prior_cov, default I)

Running standard EKI on the augmented system minimises:

    J(θ) = ‖G(θ) − y‖²_{Γ⁻¹} + λ ‖θ − θ₀‖²

For λ → 0 recovers standard EKI; for λ → ∞ shrinks to prior mean.

Parameters
----------
forward_fn : callable
    Same as EnsembleKalmanInversion.
config : EKIConfig
    Set ``lambda_reg`` > 0 and optionally ``prior_mean``.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (y: np.ndarray, theta_init: np.ndarray, *, ensemble: Optional[np.ndarray] = None) -> EKIHistory

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.estimation
children.doc:
Estimators shared by identifiability, calibration and the inverse studio.

* :func:`least_squares_fit`: weighted nonlinear least squares in the scaled parameters ``z`` (trust-region
  reflective, bounds respected), optionally with a Gaussian prior and a smoothness penalty (MAP / Tikhonov), and
  with any subset of parameters held fixed (used by the profile likelihood);
* :func:`gradient_fit`: L-BFGS-B on the same misfit with an exact gradient (the model's adjoint solve, or autograd);
* :func:`metropolis`: adaptive random-walk Metropolis (Haario et al. 2001) on the Gaussian likelihood with flat
  priors inside the bounds (plus the optional Gaussian prior), for posterior means, intervals and correlations.

Misfit convention everywhere: ``chi2 = sum(((pred - values) / sigma) ** 2)``.

classes.name: Prior
classes.doc:
Gaussian prior on the scaled parameters (``mean``/``std`` in ``z``: for a log parameter ``std=0.5`` means a
factor of about 1.6) and an optional smoothness penalty ``weight * |L z|^2`` (e.g. first differences of the
zones of a field).

functions.name: least_squares_fit
functions.sig: (model: ForwardModel, params: ParameterSet, obs: Observations, *, z0: np.ndarray | None = None, free: Sequence[int] | None = None, prior: Prior | None = None, loss: str = 'linear', max_nfev: int = 200, derivatives: str = 'auto') -> FitResult
functions.doc:
Minimise ``chi2 (+ prior)`` over the scaled parameters. ``free``: indices of ``z`` that move (the others stay
at ``z0``). ``loss``: ``"linear"`` (Gaussian) or a robust scipy loss (``"soft_l1"``, ``"huber"``, ``"cauchy"``).

functions.name: gradient_fit
functions.sig: (model: ForwardModel, params: ParameterSet, obs: Observations, *, z0: np.ndarray | None = None, prior: Prior | None = None, gradient: str = 'adjoint', max_iter: int = 300) -> FitResult
functions.doc:
L-BFGS-B on ``0.5 * (chi2 + prior)`` with an exact gradient: ``"adjoint"`` (``model.adjoint_gradient``: one
forward and one adjoint solve per iteration, whatever the number of parameters) or ``"autograd"``
(``model.predict_torch``).

functions.name: metropolis
functions.sig: (model: ForwardModel, params: ParameterSet, obs: Observations, *, z0: np.ndarray, cov0: np.ndarray | None = None, n_steps: int = 4000, burn: int | None = None, prior: Prior | None = None, seed: int = 0, thin: int = 2, max_seconds: float = 30.0) -> PosteriorSamples
functions.doc:
Adaptive random-walk Metropolis in ``z``: flat prior inside the bounds (times ``prior`` if given), Gaussian
likelihood with the observations' sigma. The proposal covariance starts at ``cov0`` (e.g. the inverse Fisher
information, regularised) and adapts to the chain (Haario et al. 2001) after the first quarter. Stops early at
``max_seconds`` (the summary reports the number of samples actually drawn).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.forward
children.doc:
Forward models, parameters and observations: the common language of identifiability, calibration and inversion.

One inverse problem is three things:

* a :class:`ForwardModel` that predicts each observation from the parameter values (``predict(theta, inputs,
  observable)``): an analytic formula, a text expression (:class:`ExpressionModel`), any Python callable or external
  solver wrapped by :class:`CallableModel`, or a table of simulated results interpolated over the parameters
  (:class:`TabulatedModel`);
* the unknown :class:`Parameter` list, each with bounds and a scale (log for positive physical constants);
* the :class:`Observations`: one row per measurement, with its inputs (position, time, ...), the observable it
  measures (a temperature, a heat flux, ...), the value (optional before an experiment) and its noise ``sigma``.

The analysis works in scaled coordinates ``z`` (``ln theta`` for log parameters, ``theta / scale`` otherwise), so a
sensitivity ``dy/dz`` of a log parameter is the change of the prediction for a 100 % relative change of the
parameter, and the Fisher information of different units can be compared.

Everything here is NumPy; a model that also defines ``predict_torch`` gets exact autograd Jacobians and gradients,
and a model with ``sensitivities`` (e.g. a discretised PDE with forward/adjoint sensitivities) supplies its own.

classes.name: Parameter
classes.doc:
One adjustable parameter. ``value`` is the nominal value (analysis point) or the initial guess (estimation).

``log`` (default: ``lower > 0``) analyses and estimates the parameter in ``ln`` space, the natural scale of a
positive physical constant. ``fixed`` keeps it at ``value``. ``truth`` is only for synthetic studies (a known
answer to check recovery against); it is never used by the estimators.

methods.name: scale
methods.doc: Linear parameters are divided by this (|value|, or 1) so every ``z`` is of order one.

classes.sig: (parameters: Sequence[Parameter])
classes.doc: The free parameters of a problem and the map between ``theta`` (dict, physical units) and ``z`` (vector).

methods.name: theta
methods.doc: All parameters (fixed ones at their value) as a dict; the free ones from ``z`` when given.

classes.name: Observations
classes.doc:
Measurements: ``inputs`` (column name -> array of n), ``observable`` (n labels: which model output each row
measures), ``values`` (n, NaN or ``None`` before the experiment) and ``sigma`` (n, the noise standard deviation).

methods.name: split
methods.sig: (holdout_fraction: float = 0.25, seed: int = 0, by: str | None = None) -> tuple[Observations, Observations]
methods.doc:
(fit, held out). ``by="<input>"`` holds out the rows with the largest values of that input (e.g. the last
times: an extrapolation test); otherwise a random subset of rows, at least one in each part.

``pinneapple_data.data_health.load_table``). ``sigma`` is a number or a column name; rows with a missing
input or value are dropped (the count is kept in ``meta["dropped_rows"]``).

Simulated results as a model: a table with parameter columns, input columns and one output column (e.g. a

Interpolation is a thin-plate RBF on coordinates scaled to [0, 1] (exact at the table rows). Queries outside the

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.heat_diffusivity
children.doc:
Recover the diffusivity alpha of the 1-D heat equation from noisy readings at one instant, with a PINN that learns
the field and alpha together, and say how well the readings can determine alpha at all.

Problem (dimensionless, the textbook test case)::

    u_t = alpha u_xx on 0 < x < 1,   u(0, x) = sin(pi x),   u(t, 0) = u(t, 1) = 0
    exact solution u(t, x) = exp(-pi^2 alpha t) sin(pi x)

Synthetic readings: ``n_observations`` points at ``t = OBSERVATION_TIME`` drawn from the exact solution with
``alpha_true``, plus Gaussian noise ``noise_std``. The PINN (``pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.factory``:
``PINNProblemSpec`` with ``inverse_params=["alpha"]``, ``PINN(..., inverse_params_names=["alpha"])``) stores alpha as
an ``nn.Parameter`` updated by the same Adam step and the same loss (PDE residual + initial/boundary conditions +
data misfit) as the network weights; the call sequence is the one of
``examples/pinn_solver/04_factory_inverse_parameter_heat_1d.py``.

Identifiability: the Fisher information of the readings for alpha, linearised at the recovered value
(``LocalSensitivity`` + ``IdentifiabilityAnalyzer``), gives the Cramer-Rao lower bound on the standard error of any
unbiased estimator from these sensor positions and this noise. It is a bound for the exact model, not an error bar
of the PINN estimate (which also carries optimisation and network error).
