children.doc:
Global and local sensitivity analysis: which parameters really control the result.

=========================================  =====================================================================
``sobol_indices(fn, space, n)``            first-order, total (and second-order) Sobol indices, bootstrap intervals
``saltelli_design`` / ``sobol_from_runs``  the same from runs done elsewhere (OpenFOAM, CalculiX, a campaign)
``first_order_given_data(X, y)``           first-order indices from an existing dataset (no designed experiment)
``morris(fn, space, r)``                   elementary-effects screening (mu*, sigma), ``r (d + 1)`` evaluations
``effect_curves(fn, space)``               main effects (partial dependence) and ICE curves
``local_derivatives(fn, x0, torch_fn=)``   Jacobian by autodiff (torch) or central differences
``freeze_recommendation`` / ``verify_freeze``  which inputs can be fixed, and the direct check of that claim
``testfunctions``                          Ishigami and Sobol' G with their exact indices
``sensitivity_study`` / ``study_cost``     all of the above on one model, and its cost in evaluations
=========================================  =====================================================================

Inputs are described as in :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.distributions` (uniform, normal, truncated normal,
lognormal, triangular). The estimators are checked against the exact indices of the Ishigami and G functions in
``tests/test_sensitivity.py``. The older :class:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.GlobalSensitivity` (uniform
bounds, no intervals) remains for its callers.
children.summary: Global and local sensitivity analysis: which parameters really control the result.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation
pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation.kalman
children.doc:
Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for
sequential state estimation / data assimilation.

Relocated from ``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py``
(a single-file implementation tightly coupled *by location*, not by
API, to ``DigitalTwin``) so it can be used standalone -- fuse a plain
physics model with a stream of sensor observations -- without building
a full ``DigitalTwin``. The implementation already operated purely on
plain ``np.ndarray`` state/observation vectors and user-supplied
transition/observation callables ``f``/``h``; it never referenced
``DigitalTwin``, ``SystemState``, or ``Observation``, so no API
generalization was needed for the move -- this is the same code,
verbatim, at a general-purpose home.

``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py`` now contains
a thin re-export shim pointing back here (the same convention as
``pinneapple_models/registry.py``), so every existing caller
(``DigitalTwin._build_default_filter`` included) keeps working
unchanged.

This is classic sequential/recursive *state* filtering (predict ->
observe -> update, repeated over a time series) -- not to be confused
with ``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman``'s
``EnsembleKalmanInversion`` / ``IteratedEKI`` (EKI/TEKI), which are
derivative-free *parameter* estimation methods that iterate an
ensemble to a converged parameter estimate rather than filtering a
state through time.

References
----------
- Evensen (2009) "Data Assimilation: The Ensemble Kalman Filter"
- Asch, Bocquet, Nodet (2016) "Data Assimilation"

classes.name: ExtendedKalmanFilter
classes.sig: (n_state: int, n_obs: int, f: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], h: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], Q: np.ndarray | None = None, R: np.ndarray | None = None, F_jac: Callable | None = None, H_jac: Callable | None = None, *, eps_fd: float = 1e-05) -> None
classes.doc:
Extended Kalman Filter for state estimation.

State: x ∈ R^n
Observation: y ∈ R^m

Dynamics:   x_k = f(x_{k-1}) + w_k,  w ~ N(0, Q)
Observation: y_k = h(x_k)    + v_k,  v ~ N(0, R)

Parameters
----------
n_state : int        state dimension
n_obs : int          observation dimension
f : callable         state transition x_{k-1} -> x_k
h : callable         observation function x_k -> y_k
Q : np.ndarray       process noise covariance (n_state, n_state)
R : np.ndarray       observation noise covariance (n_obs, n_obs)
F_jac : callable     Jacobian of f wrt x (optional; uses finite diff if None)
H_jac : callable     Jacobian of h wrt x (optional; uses finite diff if None)

methods.name: initialize
methods.sig: (x0: np.ndarray, P0: np.ndarray | None = None) -> None
methods.doc: Set initial state estimate and covariance.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Predict step: propagate state and covariance.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Update step: fuse observation y with the prior.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Predict + update in one call.

classes.name: EnsembleKalmanFilter
classes.sig: (n_state: int, n_obs: int, f: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], h: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], Q: np.ndarray | None = None, R: np.ndarray | None = None, n_ens: int = 100, inflation: float = 1.02, seed: int = 0) -> None
classes.doc:
Stochastic Ensemble Kalman Filter.

Better for high-dimensional or non-linear systems than EKF.
Internally maintains an ensemble of N_ens state samples.

Parameters
----------
n_state : int         state dimension
n_obs : int           observation dimension
f : callable          state transition x -> x'
h : callable          observation operator x -> y
Q : np.ndarray        process noise covariance
R : np.ndarray        observation noise covariance
n_ens : int           ensemble size (default 100)
inflation : float     covariance inflation factor (>1 prevents filter divergence)

methods.name: initialize
methods.sig: (x0: np.ndarray, P0: np.ndarray | None = None) -> None
methods.doc: Initialize ensemble around x0.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Propagate each ensemble member through the dynamics.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Stochastic EnKF analysis step.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Predict + update in one call.

functions.name: gaspari_cohn
functions.sig: (d: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Gaspari & Cohn (1999, QJRMS 125:723) fifth-order compactly supported correlation of the normalised distance
``d`` = distance / half-width (zero for d >= 2).

functions.name: enkf_analysis
functions.sig: (ens: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, hx: np.ndarray, r_var: np.ndarray, *, loc_xy: np.ndarray | None = None, loc_yy: np.ndarray | None = None, inflation: float = 1.0, rng: np.random.Generator | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Stochastic EnKF analysis (perturbed observations; Burgers et al. 1998, Mon. Wea. Rev. 126:1719) of an
ensemble ``ens`` (N, n_state) given observations ``y`` (m,), their forecast equivalents ``hx`` (N, m) and
independent observation-error variances ``r_var`` (m,).

``loc_xy`` (n_state, m) and ``loc_yy`` (m, m) are Schur-product localisation weights (e.g. :func:`gaspari_cohn`
of distances); ``inflation`` multiplies the forecast anomalies first. Returns the analysis ensemble (N,
n_state). Use it with any batched model: forecast the N members, call this, repeat.

children.summary: Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) and Ensemble Kalman Filter (EnKF) for sequential state estimation / data assimilation.

children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.state_estimation -- Sequential state estimation
(data assimilation) building blocks.

Relocated from ``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py``
(implementation code coupled to ``DigitalTwin`` only by its location in
the tree, not by its API) so any use case -- ``examples/``, other
``pinneapple_*`` packages, or standalone scripts -- can fuse a plain
physics model with streaming/batch sensor observations directly,
without building a full ``DigitalTwin``.
``pinneapple_systems/digital_twin/assimilation/kalman.py`` now contains
a thin re-export shim pointing back here (the same convention as
``pinneapple_models/registry.py``), so every existing caller keeps
working unchanged.

Sub-modules
-----------
kalman
    ``ExtendedKalmanFilter`` (linearized EKF, finite-difference or
    user-supplied Jacobians) and ``EnsembleKalmanFilter`` (stochastic
    EnKF for higher-dimensional / non-linear systems). Both drive a
    user-supplied state-transition ``f`` and observation operator ``h``
    through the classic predict -> observe -> update recursion over a
    time series of plain ``np.ndarray`` states and observations.

Note
----
This is sequential/recursive *state* filtering, not to be confused
with ``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.ensemble_kalman``'s
``EnsembleKalmanInversion`` / ``IteratedEKI`` (Ensemble Kalman
**Inversion**), a derivative-free *parameter* estimation technique that
iterates an ensemble to a converged parameter estimate rather than
filtering a state through time.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.study_contracts
children.doc:
The shared data contracts (:mod:`pinneapple_data.contracts`) for uncertainty and sensitivity studies.

- :func:`space_from_contract` / :func:`space_to_contract`: a ``ParameterSpace`` is bounds per parameter; a study needs
  a distribution per parameter. A continuous or integer parameter becomes uniform on its bounds unless
  ``metadata["distributions"][name]`` gives another distribution (``{"dist": "normal", "mean": .., "std": ..}``)
  (integer parameters are sampled as continuous: the model must accept non-integer values);
  a constant parameter is held at its value; categorical and log-scaled parameters are refused (no ordering /
  no log-uniform sampling here) rather than silently treated as uniform.
- :func:`model_from_ref` / :func:`model_to_ref`: ``ModelRef`` <-> :class:`~pinneapple_analysis.study_models.StudyModel`
  (``zoo:<name>`` URIs, or ONNX bytes supplied with the reference).
- :func:`uncertainty_result` / :func:`sensitivity_result`: a ``StudyResult`` from the dicts of
  :func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.study.uncertainty_study` and
  :func:`pinneapple_analysis.sensitivity.study.sensitivity_study`, with the checks that actually ran.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate
pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.benchmark_workflow
children.doc:
The standard model-benchmarking workflow (#1191): candidates on one protocol, ranked with intervals, a winner
named only when it is separated from the others.

Candidates are library families trained here (``gp``, ``mlp_ensemble``, ``quadratic``) and/or models that already
exist (``pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model_source`` predictors: zoo, exported, TorchScript, callables), evaluated on
the same points. Protocol, recorded in the result:

* data: a Sobol design over a tool (a fresh design per seed) or a table (a fresh split per seed); every candidate of a
  seed sees the same training rows and the same test points;
* metrics per candidate and seed: relative RMSE and max error on the test points (inside the box), the same on an
  extrapolation set ``extrapolate`` beyond the box (tools only), interval coverage when the model gives one, fit and
  prediction time;
* ranking: test squared errors pooled over seeds; for the best candidate against each other one, a paired bootstrap
  of the mean difference; the best is the winner only when every 95 % interval excludes zero, otherwise the tied
  candidates are named.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.examples
children.doc:
Example surrogate datasets that need no download.

``airfoil_rans``  the zoo dataset ``airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6``: OpenFOAM RANS (k-omega SST, Re = 4e6) of CST airfoils;
                  inputs the six CST coefficients and the angle of attack, outputs Cl and Cd (Cm is not recorded);
                  group = the shape (whole airfoils can be held out). Its train and test splits are pooled (the
                  study re-splits); unsteady runs of the train split, recorded at the final iteration rather than
                  time-averaged, are left out.
``burgers_fields`` viscous Burgers ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on x in [-1, 1], u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x), u(+-1, t) = 0,
                  solved exactly (Cole-Hopf, Gauss-Hermite quadrature: ``pinneapple_physics.closed_form.burgers``)
                  for ``n`` viscosities log-uniform in ``nu_range``; output the field u(x, t) on an ``nx`` x ``nt``
                  grid, t in [0, t_max]. Small viscosities form a steep front at x = 0 (a near-discontinuity); the
                  recommended shift split holds out the smallest viscosities.
``cantilever_3d``  the 3-D solid FEM cantilever of the ROM Lab (``apps/rom_lab/examples/cantilever_designs.npz``: 100
                  Latin-hypercube designs over height H, width W and load angle) as a field dataset on its
                  31 x 4 x 7 node lattice: displacement (ux, uy, uz, mm) and von Mises stress (MPa). The FEM solve
                  time is measured here, on this machine, by solving ``n_timed`` stored designs again (and checking
                  that they reproduce the stored fields). The shift split holds out the smallest load angles.
                  The von Mises stress is declared non-negative (``meta["nonnegative"]``): the study trains on
                  its square root and predicts its square.

functions.doc:
A numerical-solver baseline for ``burgers_fields``: the library's explicit upwind/FTCS finite-difference
scheme (``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.fdm``) on ``nx`` points with a stable time step, interpolated
to the dataset grid. Returns ``solve(X, coords) -> (n, n_points)``; its error against the exact solution and its
cost per query are what a surrogate competes with.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.heldout
children.doc:
Held-out errors of a field surrogate trained on snapshots (``data.from_snapshots``), in the terms of the snapshots:
per field over all held-out samples, per region of the body, and on the scalar quantities an engineer reads off the
field (the largest displacement at a loaded face, the largest stress).

    from pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.heldout import heldout_report
    rep = heldout_report(snaps, data, model, st.splits.test)
    rep["fields"]["von_mises"]["rel_l2"], rep["fields"]["von_mises"]["regions"], rep["qois"]

Every number compares the model's prediction at a held-out sample's parameters with the stored full-order result.

functions.name: region_rel_l2
functions.sig: (pred, true, regions: dict[str, Sequence[int]]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Relative L2 error restricted to each region's points, over all samples: ``pred``/``true`` (n, m) or
(n, m, components) with the points on axis 1.

functions.name: heldout_report
functions.sig: (snaps, data: SurrogateData, model, idx, *, grow: float = 0.1) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Errors of ``model`` (a ``SurrogateModel`` or anything with ``predict_array``) on the samples ``idx``:
``fields`` (relative L2 over all of them, per region: the dataset's node sets grown by ``grow`` times the body,
see ``rom.views.zones``; ``per_sample``: the mean and median of the per-sample errors and the share of the pooled
weight, the squared field, that the ``heaviest`` samples hold), ``qois`` (per sample, true and predicted: the largest magnitude of each vector field on
each node set, the largest value of each scalar field) and ``samples`` (relative L2 per sample and field). Fields
declared non-negative (``data.meta["nonnegative"]``, e.g. a von Mises stress) also count the predicted values
below zero, which are physically invalid: ``fields[name]["negative_values"]`` and per sample
``negative_<name>``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.limits
children.doc:
Where a surrogate may be used: validity bounds, an out-of-distribution gate, and where its errors concentrate.

``OODGate`` is the batched form of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.Envelope`` (same rule, vectorised): a query is out of distribution when an input is
outside the training range, or when its nearest training sample is farther than ``knn_limit`` times the typical
training spacing (standardised inputs, log10 for positive inputs), i.e. inside the box but in a hole of the data.

``limitations`` measures, on held-out samples only: the error inside and outside the gate, the error per input
quartile (where the error concentrates), the worst samples, the extrapolation ratio (shift error / test error) and,
for fields, where on the grid the error is largest.

classes.name: OODGate
classes.sig: (X_train: np.ndarray, names: Sequence[str], knn_limit: float = 3.0)

methods.name: assess
methods.doc: Per row: ``ood``, inputs ``outside`` the range, ``knn_distance`` (x typical spacing), ``reasons``.

functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, true: np.ndarray, scale: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Per sample: RMS over outputs of (pred - true) / scale (``scale``: per-output std of the training targets; for
fields the per-sample relative L2 is used instead, see ``study``).

functions.name: limitations
functions.sig: (gate: OODGate, X_eval: np.ndarray, err: np.ndarray, sets: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], X_train: np.ndarray, *, field_err: np.ndarray | None = None, coords: np.ndarray | None = None, coord_names: Sequence[str] = (), metric: str = 'error') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``X_eval`` / ``err``: held-out samples (test and shift) and their per-sample error; ``sets``: name -> boolean
mask over them. ``field_err``: (n_eval, n_points) pointwise absolute error, for the error map.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.methods
children.doc:
Surrogate candidates: which methods apply to a dataset, and how each is trained under a ``ComputeBudget``.

==========  =====================================================  ===========================================
id           method                                                 applies to
==========  =====================================================  ===========================================
ridge        quadratic-polynomial ridge regression (scikit-learn)   scalars, fields (classical baseline)
gp           Gaussian process, Matern-5/2 ARD + noise; fields on    up to ``GP_MAX_N`` training samples
             POD coefficients (scikit-learn)
gbt          gradient-boosted trees (XGBoost if installed, else     scalars
             scikit-learn HistGradientBoosting)
mlp          multilayer perceptron (PyTorch)                        scalars, fields (all grid points as outputs)
fno          Fourier neural operator, parameters as constant        fields on a 1-D or 2-D uniform grid
             input channels (``pinneapple_neural``)
deeponet     DeepONet, branch = parameters, trunk = coordinates     fields
             (``pinneapple_neural``)
pinn         physics-informed MLP u(parameters, coordinates):       fields with a declared PDE (``pde.py``)
             data loss + PDE residual
==========  =====================================================  ===========================================

Every method sees the same training samples, normalisation (training split only) and validation samples. The
iterative methods (mlp, fno, deeponet, pinn) train until the same ``ComputeBudget`` is spent
(``train_within_budget``) and keep their best validation checkpoint out of ten evaluations, whose time is not
charged; the one-shot fits (ridge, gp, gbt) are fitted once and report the time they used, which can be below the
budget (they are never given more).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model
children.doc:
A trained surrogate packaged for use: predict with the OOD gate, save / load, export, model card.

``SurrogateModel.save(dir)`` writes ``model.pkl`` (the fitted candidate, pickled) and ``card.json`` (inputs,
outputs, validity bounds, OOD gate, held-out metrics, limitations, trust report, dataset hash, the model file's
sha256). ``load`` verifies that hash before unpickling. Unpickling runs code: load only models you produced
(the gateway stores the ones it publishes; it never unpickles an upload).

``export(path, "torchscript" | "onnx")`` writes a self-contained graph of the PyTorch candidates (mlp, fno,
deeponet, pinn) that takes raw inputs ``(n, d)`` and returns raw outputs ``(n, p)`` (normalisation included); the
scikit-learn and XGBoost candidates have no such export here.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.model_source
children.doc:
Use a model already trained instead of training one (#1190): your own (TorchScript, ONNX, a callable, or a model
exported by :mod:`.workflow`), one from the PINNeAPPle zoo, or train one. Every model passes an applicability gate
before it is used, forward or inverse, and the result is re-verified by the solver when there is one.

* :func:`zoo_candidates` ranks the zoo's models for a problem by the outputs it needs and the inputs it has (names,
  then units), with what is missing.
* :func:`open_model` gives one :class:`Predictor` (inputs, outputs, units, bounds, ``predict``) whatever the source.
* :func:`gate` before use: the query inside the model's validity box (and its extra constraints), the problem's
  units convertible to the model's, and a check against references: the zoo's stored reference (its card's
  metrics recomputed) or a few solves of the reference tool, with the error against the model's claimed accuracy.
* :func:`use_model` runs it forward at the query points or inverse (the parameters that reproduce observations,
  bounded least squares through the model), then re-verifies with the solver when one is given.

fields: extra_mask: Callable[[Mapping[str, np.ndarray]], np.ndarray] | None = None

functions.name: zoo_candidates
functions.sig: (outputs: Sequence[str], inputs: Sequence[str] = (), units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Zoo models ranked for a problem: outputs matched (by name, or by unit when ``units`` names them), inputs the
problem lacks; best first.

functions.name: open_model
functions.sig: (source: str, *, path: str | None = None, name: str | None = None, fn: Callable | None = None, inputs: Sequence[str] = (), outputs: Sequence[str] = (), bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, claimed_rel_error: float | None = None) -> Predictor
functions.doc:
One predictor from ``source``: ``"zoo"`` (``name``), ``"workflow"`` (``path`` of a model exported by
:func:`.workflow.surrogate_modeling`), ``"torchscript"`` / ``"onnx"`` (``path`` plus the declared ``inputs``,
``outputs``, ``bounds``, ``units``: a file carries no physics, so its card is the caller's), ``"callable"``
(``fn(**inputs) -> dict``).

functions.name: onnx_function
functions.sig: (path: str, inputs: Sequence[str], outputs: Sequence[str]) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
An ONNX file as ``f(X) -> Y``: ``X`` (N, len(inputs)) in the declared input order, ``Y`` (N, len(outputs))
in float64.

The file's own signature is checked against the declared card when it is opened, and a mismatch is refused with
both name lists: one input tensor needs ``len(inputs)`` columns (or one tensor per declared input, by name); one
output tensor needs ``len(outputs)`` columns (or one tensor per declared output, by name). Each input is cast to
the tensor's own element type (float64 data into a float32 model, and the reverse). A model exported with a
fixed batch dimension is run in chunks of that size (the last chunk padded and the padding dropped).

functions.name: gate
functions.sig: (p: Predictor, query: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]], *, problem_units: Mapping[str, str] | None = None, reference: Callable[..., Mapping[str, float]] | None = None, n_reference: int = 8, tolerance: float | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]

recomputed. ``tolerance``: relative error allowed (default: twice the model's claimed error, else 5 %).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.pde
children.doc:
PDE declarations for physics-informed surrogates: which residual a PINN candidate adds to its data loss.

A declaration names the equation, maps its coordinates to the field's coordinate names and its coefficients to
input columns (or constants)::

    {"type": "burgers", "coords": {"x": "x", "t": "t"}, "coefficients": {"nu": "nu"}}

Supported equations (``u`` the scalar field):

========== =============================== ==================
type        residual                        coords / coefficients
========== =============================== ==================
heat        u_t - alpha u_xx                x, t / alpha
burgers     u_t + u u_x - nu u_xx           x, t / nu
advection   u_t + c u_x                     x, t / c
poisson_1d  k u_xx + f                      x / k, f
laplace_2d  u_xx + u_yy                     x, y / -
========== =============================== ==================

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.study
children.doc:
Surrogate study: train every applicable candidate on the same data and budget, measure on unseen data, pick one.

``run_study(data, ...)``

1. splits once (``make_splits``): train / validation / held-out test, plus a distribution-shift set never seen in
   training (whole groups, the edge of the input space, or one end of an input);
2. lists every candidate with the reason it does or does not apply (fields vs scalars; PINN only with a declared
   PDE; GP sample limit);
3. trains each applicable candidate for each seed under the same ``ComputeBudget``
   (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.equal_budget``) and measures, in physical units, the held-out and shift errors,
   training time, inference time per query, parameter count and model size;
4. selects the method with the lowest **validation** error (the test and shift sets never choose), and packages it
   as a ``SurrogateModel`` with its limitations (validity bounds, OOD gate, where errors concentrate) and a trust
   report (``pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport``) whose checks all ran on held-out data.

Error metrics: scalars, ``nrmse`` = RMSE / standard deviation of the training targets, per output then averaged;
fields, ``rel_l2`` = ||pred - true|| / ||true|| per sample, averaged.

methods.doc: The study as a report: data, protocol, comparison, chosen model, trust checks, limitations.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.surrogate.workflow
children.doc:
The standard surrogate-modeling workflow (#1186): data or a design of experiments over a tool, the model family
``recommend_architecture`` picks (or none), the library's equal-budget comparison, checks on solves never trained
on, and an exported model that refuses to extrapolate.

1. **Data**: an uploaded table (``table``: rows of inputs and outputs) or a Sobol design of experiments over a tool
   (``tool``: a callable or a library tool id, ``bounds`` per input, ``outputs`` it returns). The cost of one tool
   call is measured.
2. **Which model**: :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation.recommend_architecture` with
   the measured cost and ``n_uses`` (how many predictions the model will serve). ``none`` stops here with its
   reason: call the tool (``force=True`` trains anyway, to compare).
3. **Families on one protocol**: :func:`pinneapple_autolab.study.benchmark.benchmark` (k-fold CV on train + val,
   cross-conformal 90 % intervals, the selection rule written in the record); the GP, the MLP ensemble and the
   quadratic response surface (the baseline to beat).
4. **Checks** on ``n_fresh`` new tool calls inside the box (or the table's held-out rows): relative RMSE against
   ``accuracy_target``, coverage of the 90 % interval (binomial band at that sample size), and that the selected
   family beats the quadratic baseline.
5. **Export**: the selected models with their intervals and a model card (inputs, ranges, units, errors, checks,
   provenance); :func:`load_surrogate` returns a predictor that raises on inputs outside the trained box.

The exported predictor: ``predict({"x": .., ...}) -> {output: (mean, 90 % half width)}``; raises ValueError for
an input outside the trained box (no silent extrapolation). Load only files you produced: it is a pickle.

children.doc:
Surrogate models from simulation results: select, compare at equal budget, measure on unseen data, package.

>>> from pinneapple_analysis import surrogate
>>> data = surrogate.examples.airfoil_rans()                 # OpenFOAM RANS campaign, Cl and Cd
>>> study = surrogate.run_study(data, budget=5.0, seeds=2)   # every applicable method, same splits and budget
>>> study.best, study.ranking("test"), study.trust["decision"]
>>> study.model.predict({"T0": 0.15, ..., "alpha_deg": 4.0})  # outputs + per-row OOD assessment
>>> study.model.save("model_dir")

Modules: ``data`` (tables and arrays -> ``SurrogateData``), ``splits`` (held-out and distribution-shift splits),
``methods`` (ridge, gp, gbt, mlp, fno, deeponet, pinn and when each applies), ``pde`` (declared equations for the
PINN), ``limits`` (validity bounds, OOD gate, error concentration), ``model`` (``SurrogateModel``), ``study``
(``run_study``), ``examples`` (datasets that need no download), ``contracts`` (``DatasetSpec``, ``ModelRef``,
``StudyResult`` of ``pinneapple_data.contracts``; imported on use). Needs ``pip install "pinneapple[surrogate]"``
(scikit-learn; Parquet, HDF5 and ONNX support).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.trust
pinneapple_analysis.trust.field_card
children.doc:
Trust card of a field on a grid: the physics checks a result must pass before anyone uses it.

``trust_card`` takes a field sampled on a tensor-product grid (from any source: a PINN, a solver, a file written
by another code) and checks it with NumPy only:

* sanity: finite values, values inside the physical range;
* PDE residual: ``laplace(u) = f`` (``"laplace"`` / ``"poisson"``) or ``u_t = alpha laplace(u) + f`` (``"heat"``),
  by finite differences on the interior of the grid;
* boundary conditions: Dirichlet values on named faces (``"x_min"``, ``"y_max"``, ...);
* conservation: the divergence theorem, net flux through the boundary against the integral of the source
  (steady problems);
* maximum principle (steady problems without a source): no interior value outside the boundary range;
* reference: relative L2 error against a reference field or a closed form;
* applicability (OOD): the grid, or the query points, inside the bounds the model was trained on.

The checks feed two existing views: the six questions of the lab trust card
(``pinneapple_lab.curation.trust_stages``) and the deploy decision of ``TrustReport`` (``APPROVED``, ``REVIEW``,
``REJECT``; a failing critical check rejects).

>>> import numpy as np
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.trust.field_card import trust_card
>>> x = y = np.linspace(0, 1, 41)
>>> X, Y = np.meshgrid(x, y, indexing="ij")
>>> u = np.sin(np.pi * X) * np.sinh(np.pi * Y) / np.sinh(np.pi)
>>> card = trust_card({"x": x, "y": y}, u, pde="laplace",
...                   dirichlet={"x_min": 0.0, "x_max": 0.0, "y_min": 0.0, "y_max": lambda P: np.sin(np.pi * P[:, 0])})
>>> card.decision
'APPROVED'

One check: ``kind`` is ``sanity``, ``physics``, ``reference`` or ``generalization`` (the lab vocabulary);
``passed`` is ``None`` when the check could not run, with the reason in ``detail``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_gate
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_gate — ``TrustGate``: pre-consumption
trust scoring of a trained model's own prediction, before it is allowed
to feed a live digital twin.

Distinct from two existing, adjacent mechanisms — this is neither of them:

- ``pinneapple_llm.guardrail.PhysicsGuardrail`` verifies a *problem spec*
  an LLM proposed (residual re-check, dimensional analysis, conservation)
  before training even starts.
- ``pinneapple_systems.digital_twin.monitoring.anomaly.MahalanobisDetector``
  scores a live sensor *innovation vector* against a running Kalman
  filter's state covariance, continuously, once a twin is already
  running.

``TrustGate`` scores one specific prediction from an already-trained
model, combining up to three independent [0, 1] sub-scores:

- an out-of-distribution (OOD) score: the fraction of query points whose
  Mahalanobis distance to the model's training-coordinate distribution has
  a chi-squared p-value (``scipy.stats.chi2.sf``) of at least ``ood_level``
  (default 0.01: the point lies inside the 99 % region of a Gaussian with
  the training mean and covariance). Each point is tested on its own -- the
  same Mahalanobis-distance +
  chi-squared concept ``MahalanobisDetector`` already uses, reimplemented
  here (rather than called directly) because it fits once from a static
  training sample instead of updating per Kalman step, a different call
  shape;
- a residual score: re-evaluating a PDE residual on the model's own
  prediction (any ``pinneapple_systems.component_modeling
  .physics_residuals``-shaped ``residual(model, coords, **kwargs) ->
  Tensor`` function, or a ``pinneapple_systems.component_library.Physics``
  instance);
- an optional ensemble-variance score, if a ``DeepEnsemble`` (or anything
  exposing ``.predict(x) -> (mean, std)``) is supplied.

classes.name: TrustGate
classes.sig: (*, ood_weight: float = 0.4, residual_weight: float = 0.4, ensemble_weight: float = 0.2, ood_level: float = 0.01)

methods.name: fit
methods.doc:
Fit the OOD reference from a real sample of training
coordinates (mean + covariance).

methods.name: fit_from_bounds
methods.doc:
Cheap approximation when no real training-coordinate sample is
kept around: treats the domain as a uniform box and derives a
diagonal covariance from each axis's range (``var = range**2 / 12``,
the variance of a ``Uniform(a, b)``). Coarser than :meth:`fit` —
use it only when the real sample isn't available.

methods.name: coord_bounds_from_checkpoint
methods.doc:
Reads ``checkpoint["metadata"]["domain_bounds"]`` if present —
the common place a training pipeline in this repo records domain
bounds. Raises ``KeyError`` (loudly, not a silent empty dict) if
absent, since a made-up domain would make :meth:`fit_from_bounds`
silently meaningless.

methods.name: ood_p_values
methods.doc:
Per query point: probability of a Mahalanobis distance this large or larger under the fitted
distribution (chi-squared with ``dim`` degrees of freedom). Low => far out of distribution. NaN
coordinates give a p-value of 0.

methods.name: score
methods.sig: (model: Any, x: torch.Tensor, *, residual_fn: Callable[..., torch.Tensor] | None = None, residual_kwargs: dict[str, Any] | None = None, ensemble: Any | None = None) -> TrustScore
methods.doc:
Combines whichever sub-scores are available into one [0, 1]
weighted average (renormalized over only the parts actually
computed). Raises if none of {fitted OOD, residual_fn, ensemble}
were provided — a trust score with no evidence is not a score.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report
children.doc:
pinneapple_analysis.trust.trust_report — relatório de confiança para decidir o deploy de um modelo.

Junta checagens independentes (acurácia contra referência, consistência física, OOD, calibração de
incerteza, comparação com dado experimental) numa decisão única: APPROVED, REVIEW ou REJECT. Cada
checagem usa o mesmo vocabulário das provas do E11 do PINNeAPPle-CFD:

- ``supports``: a checagem passou no critério;
- ``contradicts``: a checagem falhou no critério;
- ``not_run``: a checagem não foi executada (com o motivo). Não entra no score, mas conta na cobertura.

Regras (escolhas de projeto, documentadas e revogáveis, não normas):

1. Qualquer checagem ``critical`` com ``contradicts`` → REJECT.
2. Qualquer outra ``contradicts`` → REVIEW.
3. Cobertura (checagens executadas / total) abaixo de ``min_coverage`` → REVIEW. ``min_coverage`` e ``min_score``
   vêm da política do usuário (``pinneapple_veriphysics.policy``: a passada, a do ambiente ou a salva como padrão)
   e, sem nenhuma, dos padrões da biblioteca (0.6 e 0.8).
4. Score (média ponderada das checagens executadas) abaixo de ``min_score`` → REVIEW.
5. Caso contrário → APPROVED.

``from_trust_score`` converte o ``TrustScore`` do ``TrustGate`` (OOD, resíduo, ensemble) em checagens.

methods.name: score
methods.doc: Média ponderada das checagens executadas (supports = 1, contradicts = 0). None se nenhuma foi executada.

Um sub-score ``None`` vira ``not_run`` com o motivo. ``limite_sub_score`` é uma escolha de projeto.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty
pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.aleatoric
children.doc:
Aleatoric (data) uncertainty via heteroscedastic NLL regression.

The model predicts both a mean μ(x) and a log-variance log σ²(x).
Loss = 0.5·log σ² + 0.5·(y − μ)²·exp(−log σ²)  — Gaussian NLL, numerically stable.

This captures *irreducible* uncertainty: noise in the data that no model can remove.
For reducible (epistemic) uncertainty use MCDropout, EnsembleUQ, or decompose_uncertainty.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import AleatoricHead, aleatoric_nll_loss

    base = MyModel()
    model = AleatoricHead(base, out_dim=1, in_dim=2)
    # model(x) → (mean, log_var), both shape (N, out_dim)

    optimizer = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
    for x_batch, y_batch in loader:
        mean, log_var = model(x_batch)
        loss = aleatoric_nll_loss(mean, log_var, y_batch)
        loss.backward(); optimizer.step(); optimizer.zero_grad()

    # Inference
    model.eval()
    with torch.no_grad():
        result = model.predict_with_uncertainty(x_test)
    # result.aleatoric_std  →  predicted noise std

classes.name: AleatoricHead
classes.sig: (base: nn.Module, out_dim: int, in_dim: int, *, hidden: int = 64) -> None
classes.doc:
Wrap a deterministic model with a learned aleatoric variance head.

The base model is unchanged; a small MLP projects the ORIGINAL INPUT
``x`` (not the base model's output) to a log-variance estimate, so the
predicted noise level is a genuine function of the input features --
"heteroscedastic" means input-conditioned noise, and a head fed only the
point prediction would force every input mapping to the same predicted
mean to also get the same predicted variance, which defeats that. During
training, optimize with :func:`aleatoric_nll_loss`.

Parameters
----------
base : nn.Module
    Pre-existing model returning ``(N, out_dim)`` tensors.
out_dim : int
    Dimensionality of the model output (= number of predicted fields).
in_dim : int
    Dimensionality of the model's input ``x`` (the log-variance head's
    own input).
hidden : int
    Width of the log-variance MLP (default 64).

Outputs
-------
forward(x) → ``(mean, log_var)`` — both shape ``(N, out_dim)``.

methods.name: forward
methods.doc: Return ``(mean, log_var)`` tensors, both shape ``(N, out_dim)``.

methods.name: predict_with_uncertainty
methods.doc: Run a deterministic forward pass and return a :class:`UQResult`.

functions.name: aleatoric_nll_loss
functions.sig: (mean: Tensor, log_var: Tensor, target: Tensor, *, min_log_var: float = -10.0, max_log_var: float = 10.0) -> Tensor
functions.doc:
Heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL loss.

Parameters
----------
mean : Tensor — predicted mean, shape ``(N, D)`` or ``(N,)``.
log_var : Tensor — predicted log-variance, same shape.
target : Tensor — ground truth, same shape as *mean*.
min_log_var, max_log_var : float — clamping bounds for numerical stability.

Returns
-------
Tensor — scalar loss.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.applicability
children.doc:
Where is a model's prediction reliable? Applicability gates on the inputs and a routing rule that sends the cases
the model cannot answer to the high-fidelity solver.

:class:`ApplicabilityDomain` is fitted on the model's reference data (its training or calibration inputs) and tells,
for every query point:

- ``outside``: an input lies outside the validity range (the declared bounds, or the range of the data);
- ``sparse``: inside the range, but the nearest reference points are farther than for ``level`` of the reference
  points themselves (k-nearest-neighbour distance in standardised inputs, leave-one-out on the reference): the model
  interpolates across a hole in its data;
- ``inside``: in range and as close to the data as the data are to each other.

The Mahalanobis p-value of :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustGate` is reported as well (it flags points far from
the bulk of a roughly Gaussian cloud; the k-NN test also catches holes inside the range).

:func:`route_cases` combines the gate with the prediction interval: a case goes to the high-fidelity solver when it is
outside or sparse, when its interval is wider than the accuracy the decision needs, or when the interval straddles a
decision limit (the surrogate cannot tell on which side the case falls).

classes.name: ApplicabilityDomain
classes.doc: k-NN density gate plus range gate on standardised inputs. Build with :meth:`fit`.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (X_ref, names: Sequence[str] | None = None, bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, k: int = 5, level: float = 0.99) -> ApplicabilityDomain
methods.doc:
Fit on reference inputs ``X_ref`` (n, d). ``bounds`` (``{name: (lo, hi)}``) overrides the data range for
the variables it names (e.g. a model card's validity range).

methods.name: assess
methods.doc:
Per query row: ``status`` (inside / sparse / outside), ``in_range``, ``out_of_range`` (names),
``knn_distance`` (standardised), ``density_ratio`` (threshold / distance: >= 1 is as dense as the data),
``neighbours_within`` (reference points within the threshold radius) and ``mahalanobis_p``.

functions.name: route_cases
functions.sig: (status, pred, lower, upper, tolerance: float | None = None, limits: tuple[float | None, float | None] | None = None) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Routing rule, one entry per case: ``{"route": "surrogate" | "high_fidelity", "reasons": [...]}``.

A case goes to the high-fidelity solver when (any of) its inputs are ``outside`` the validity range, its
neighbourhood is ``sparse``, its interval half-width exceeds ``tolerance`` (the accuracy the decision needs, in
output units), or the interval contains a limit of ``limits = (lo, hi)`` (the decision is not determined).

functions.name: routing_summary
functions.sig: (routes: Sequence[dict]) -> dict
functions.doc: Counts of each route and of each reason code (a case can have several).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.calibration
children.doc:
Calibration metrics for probabilistic regression models.

A well-calibrated model should assign uncertainty estimates that match
empirical frequencies.  This module provides standard metrics for diagnosing
and reporting calibration quality.

References
----------
Kuleshov, V., Fenner, N. & Ermon, S. (2018). *Accurate Uncertainties for Deep
Learning Using Calibrated Regression*. ICML.

Levi, D. et al. (2022). *Evaluating and Calibrating Uncertainty Prediction in
Regression Tasks*. Sensors, 22(15).

classes.name: CalibrationMetrics
classes.doc:
Collection of calibration and sharpness metrics for regression UQ.

All methods are static/class methods and accept plain ``Tensor`` inputs.
No instantiation is required; use the class directly as a namespace:

.. code-block:: python

    ece = CalibrationMetrics.expected_calibration_error(
        y_pred, y_true, y_std, n_bins=15
    )
    cov = CalibrationMetrics.coverage_at_level(y_pred, y_true, y_std, alpha=0.1)

Notes
-----
Inputs are tensors or arrays of one shape, ``(N,)`` or ``(N, D)``; they are
computed in float64. For multi-output models, metrics are computed
element-wise and then averaged across output dimensions (so a calibrated
model has ``coverage_at_level`` close to ``1 - alpha`` whatever ``D``).
NaN or Inf inputs raise ``ValueError``.

methods.name: expected_calibration_error
methods.sig: (y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, y_std: Tensor, n_bins: int = 15) -> float
methods.doc: Compute the Expected Calibration Error (ECE) for regression.

methods.name: coverage_at_level
methods.sig: (y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, y_std: Tensor, alpha: float = 0.1) -> float
methods.doc: Compute empirical coverage of the (1 - alpha) Gaussian interval.

methods.name: calibration_plot_data
methods.sig: (y_pred: Tensor, y_true: Tensor, y_std: Tensor, n_bins: int = 15) -> dict[str, list[float]]
methods.doc: Compute data for a reliability / calibration diagram.

methods.doc: Compute sharpness: the mean predictive standard deviation.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal
children.doc:
Split Conformal Prediction for regression.

Split conformal prediction provides *distribution-free*, *finite-sample* valid
coverage guarantees without making any assumptions about the data-generating
process.

References
----------
Vovk, V., Gammerman, A. & Shafer, G. (2005). *Algorithmic Learning in a
Random World*. Springer.

Angelopoulos, A. N. & Bates, S. (2022). *A Gentle Introduction to Conformal
Prediction and Distribution-Free Uncertainty Quantification*.
arXiv:2107.07511.

classes.name: ConformalPredictor
classes.sig: (model: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor], alpha: float = 0.1) -> None
classes.doc:
Split conformal predictor for regression tasks.

Given a calibration set ``(x_cal, y_cal)`` and a coverage level
``1 - alpha``, :meth:`calibrate` computes the smallest prediction-interval
half-width that achieves the target marginal coverage.

:meth:`predict` then returns symmetric prediction intervals
``[y_hat - q, y_hat + q]`` for new inputs.

Parameters
----------
model:
    Any callable ``f: Tensor -> Tensor`` that returns point predictions.
    Typically a trained ``nn.Module``.
alpha:
    Miscoverage level.  The predictor targets ``(1 - alpha)`` marginal
    coverage.  Must be in ``(0, 1)``.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If *alpha* is not in ``(0, 1)``.

Examples
--------
>>> cp = ConformalPredictor(model, alpha=0.1)
>>> cp.calibrate(x_cal, y_cal)
>>> y_pred, lower, upper = cp.predict(x_test)
>>> cov = cp.coverage(x_test, y_test)
>>> print(f"Empirical coverage: {cov:.3f}")  # should be ≈ 0.90

methods.name: is_calibrated
methods.doc: ``True`` after :meth:`calibrate` has been called successfully.

methods.doc: Compute non-conformity scores on the calibration set.

methods.doc: Return point prediction and calibrated prediction intervals.

methods.doc: Compute empirical marginal coverage on a held-out test set.

functions.name: conformal_quantile
functions.sig: (scores: Any, alpha: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The split-conformal quantile of any array of non-conformity scores (NumPy, list or tensor): the
``ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha))``-th smallest score, clipped to the largest (see ``_conformal_quantile``).

A new score exchangeable with the ``n`` calibration scores exceeds it with probability at most ``alpha``
when ``ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha)) <= n``; ``conformal_quantile_valid`` says whether ``n`` is large enough.

functions.name: conformal_quantile_valid
functions.sig: (n: int, alpha: float) -> bool
functions.doc:
True when ``n`` calibration scores are enough for the finite-sample guarantee at level ``alpha``
(``n >= ceil(1 / alpha) - 1``); otherwise the quantile is clipped to the largest score and the guarantee
does not hold.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal_study
children.doc:
Split-conformal prediction intervals for any model's predictions (NumPy), with the coverage *measured* on a
held-out test split that the calibration never saw.

:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal.ConformalPredictor` wraps a torch model; this module works on
predictions alone, so it serves a zoo model, an ONNX graph, a solver-trained surrogate or a column of predictions in
a CSV file alike::

    study = conformal_study(y_cal, pred_cal, y_test, pred_test, alpha=0.1)
    study.coverage, study.coverage_ci        # fraction of held-out targets inside their interval, Wilson interval
    lo, hi = conformal_interval(pred_new, study.q)

Scores are absolute residuals ``|y - pred|`` (constant width) or, when a per-point scale is given (an ensemble
standard deviation, a predicted sigma), normalised residuals ``|y - pred| / scale`` (width proportional to the
scale: locally adaptive). The guarantee is marginal coverage of at least ``1 - alpha`` for exchangeable data
(Vovk et al. 2005; Angelopoulos & Bates 2022, arXiv:2107.07511); it says nothing about a region the calibration
data do not cover, which is why the coverage is also reported per group.

classes.name: ConformalStudy
classes.doc:
Split-conformal calibration and its held-out evaluation.

``coverage`` is the fraction of the *test* targets inside their interval; ``coverage_ci`` its Wilson interval
at ``level``; ``reliability`` the measured test coverage at other nominal levels (same calibration data), so a
reader sees whether the guarantee holds across levels, not only at the one chosen.

methods.name: meets_target
methods.doc:
The measured coverage is consistent with the guarantee: the target lies at or below the upper end of
the Wilson interval (a shortfall the test size cannot resolve is not called a failure).

functions.name: conformal_scores

functions.doc: Non-conformity scores: ``|y - pred|``, divided by ``scale`` when given.

functions.name: conformal_quantile

functions.doc:
The finite-sample conformal quantile: the ``ceil((n + 1)(1 - alpha))``-th smallest score (the largest when
that exceeds ``n``; with ``n < 1 / alpha - 1`` the guarantee needs more calibration points).

functions.name: conformal_interval
functions.sig: (pred, q: float, scale = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``(lower, upper)`` = ``pred -+ q`` (times ``scale`` for normalised scores).

functions.name: min_calibration_size
functions.sig: (alpha: float) -> int
functions.doc: Smallest calibration set for which the conformal quantile is finite at level ``1 - alpha``.

functions.name: coverage_by_group

Measured coverage per group (e.g. bins of an input or of the prediction): where the marginal guarantee

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.core
children.doc:
Shared types and unified interface for pinneapple_uq.

This module provides:
- ``UQResult``: structured container for predictions with uncertainty estimates.
- ``uq_predict``: unified dispatch function for all supported UQ methods.

classes.name: UQResult
classes.doc:
Container for predictions with associated uncertainty estimates.

Attributes
----------
mean:
    Point-estimate prediction tensor, shape ``(N, D)`` or ``(N,)``.
std:
    Total predictive standard deviation (aleatoric + epistemic), same
    shape as ``mean``.
aleatoric_std:
    Standard deviation of the *data* (irreducible) noise component.
    ``None`` when the UQ method cannot separate uncertainty sources —
    e.g. plain MCDropout without a variance head.
    Populated by :class:`~pinneapple_uq.aleatoric.AleatoricHead` and
    :func:`~pinneapple_uq.decomposition.decompose_uncertainty`.
epistemic_std:
    Standard deviation of the *model* (reducible) uncertainty.
    ``None`` when the UQ method cannot separate uncertainty sources.
    Populated by :func:`~pinneapple_uq.decomposition.decompose_uncertainty`.
samples:
    Optional raw samples used to compute statistics, shape ``(S, N, D)``
    where *S* is the number of stochastic forward passes or ensemble
    members. ``None`` when the method does not expose raw samples.
metadata:
    Arbitrary key-value store for method-specific information (e.g. method
    name, dropout probability, number of ensemble members).

methods.name: lower_bound
methods.doc: Return the lower bound of the (1 - alpha) Gaussian interval.

methods.name: upper_bound
methods.doc: Return the upper bound of the (1 - alpha) Gaussian interval.

methods.name: confidence_interval
methods.doc: Return a symmetric Gaussian confidence interval.

functions.name: uq_predict
functions.sig: (model: Any, x: Tensor, method: Literal['mc_dropout', 'ensemble', 'aleatoric', 'decompose'] = 'mc_dropout', device: Optional[torch.device] = None, **kwargs) -> UQResult
functions.doc:
Unified interface for uncertainty-aware prediction.

Dispatches to the appropriate UQ wrapper based on *method* and returns a
:class:`UQResult`.  The model is **not** modified in place; a wrapper is
created temporarily.

Parameters
----------
model:
    A trained ``nn.Module`` (or any callable returning a ``Tensor``).
x:
    Input tensor, shape ``(N, ...)``.
method:
    UQ method to use.  Supported values:

    * ``"mc_dropout"`` — Monte Carlo Dropout via
      :class:`~pinneapple_uq.mc_dropout.MCDropoutWrapper`.
    * ``"ensemble"`` — Ensemble UQ via
      :class:`~pinneapple_uq.ensemble.EnsembleUQ`.  When using this method,
      pass ``models`` as a keyword argument containing a list of
      ``nn.Module`` instances.

device:
    Device to run inference on.  Defaults to the device of ``x`` when
    ``x`` is already a tensor, otherwise ``"cpu"``.
**kwargs:
    Additional keyword arguments forwarded to the underlying UQ class or
    its ``predict_with_uncertainty`` method.

    For ``mc_dropout``:
        - ``n_samples`` (int, default 100) — stochastic forward passes.
        - ``dropout_p`` (float, default 0.1) — dropout probability.
        - ``seed`` (Optional[int]) — RNG seed for reproducibility.

    For ``ensemble``:
        - ``models`` (List[nn.Module], **required**) — ensemble members.

Returns
-------
UQResult
    Prediction mean, std, (optionally) samples, and metadata.

Raises
------
ValueError
    If an unsupported *method* is requested.

Examples
--------
>>> result = uq_predict(my_model, x, method="mc_dropout", n_samples=200)
>>> lower, upper = result.confidence_interval(alpha=0.05)

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.decomposition
children.doc:
Variance decomposition: total predictive uncertainty = aleatoric + epistemic.

Theory
------
Given *S* stochastic forward passes of a model that returns ``(μ_i, log σ²_i)``:

  Predictive mean   μ̄  = E[μ_i]
  Aleatoric var        = E[σ²_i]       (average predicted data noise)
  Epistemic var        = Var[μ_i]      (spread of the predicted means)
  Total var            = aleatoric + epistemic

For purely deterministic models (ensemble / MC-dropout *without* a variance head),
only epistemic variance can be estimated; set ``has_aleatoric=False``.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import AleatoricHead, MCDropoutWrapper, MCDropoutConfig
    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import decompose_uncertainty

    # 1) Build a model that outputs (mean, log_var)
    aleatoric_model = AleatoricHead(my_base_model, out_dim=1, in_dim=2)

    # 2) Wrap with MC Dropout to activate stochasticity
    mcd = MCDropoutWrapper(aleatoric_model, MCDropoutConfig(n_samples=50))

    # 3) Decompose
    result = decompose_uncertainty(mcd, x_test, has_aleatoric=True, device="cuda")
    print("aleatoric:", result.aleatoric_std.mean().item())
    print("epistemic:", result.epistemic_std.mean().item())

functions.name: decompose_uncertainty
functions.sig: (model: Any, x: Tensor, *, n_samples: int = 100, has_aleatoric: bool = True, device: Optional[Union[str, torch.device]] = None) -> UQResult
functions.doc:
Decompose predictive uncertainty into aleatoric and epistemic parts.

The *model* is called ``n_samples`` times with only its Dropout-family
submodules switched to stochastic mode (the rest of the model, including
any BatchNorm/LayerNorm, stays in eval mode throughout -- see
``mc_dropout._set_dropout_training``). Each call should return either:

* ``Tensor`` of shape ``(N, D)`` — point prediction (epistemic only).
* ``(Tensor, Tensor)`` — ``(mean, log_var)`` (aleatoric + epistemic).

Parameters
----------
model : Any
    A callable (e.g., ``MCDropoutWrapper`` wrapping ``AleatoricHead``).
x : Tensor — input, shape ``(N, ...)``.
n_samples : int — number of stochastic forward passes.
has_aleatoric : bool
    ``True`` when *model* returns ``(mean, log_var)`` tuples.
    ``False`` when it returns plain tensors (epistemic only).
device : optional — moves model and data to this device.

Returns
-------
UQResult
    ``mean`` : predictive mean ``μ̄``.
    ``std`` : total predictive std ``sqrt(aleatoric_var + epistemic_var)``.
    ``aleatoric_std`` : ``sqrt(E[σ²_i])``.
    ``epistemic_std`` : ``sqrt(Var[μ_i])``.
    ``samples`` : stacked mean samples ``(S, N, D)``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.drift
children.doc:
Drift monitoring of a deployed surrogate: accuracy, calibration, input shift and residual trend in one report.

A surrogate trained on one input distribution degrades silently when the operating point moves. Given a batch of new
predictions with their measured (or high-fidelity) truth, :func:`assess_drift` computes

* the normalised RMSE ``sqrt(mean(r^2)) / std(y_true)`` and the bias ``mean(r)`` of the residuals
  ``r = y_pred - y_true``, with a t-type test of ``bias = 0``;
* the empirical coverage of the central Gaussian interval ``y_pred +- z sigma`` at ``level``, compared with the
  binomial standard error ``sqrt(level (1 - level) / n)`` (Gneiting, Balabdaoui & Raftery 2007);
* per input feature, the two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov statistic and p-value between the reference (training) inputs
  and the new inputs (``scipy.stats.ks_2samp``; Massey 1951), Bonferroni-corrected over the features;
* the fraction of new inputs outside the training box ``bounds``;
* a Mann-Kendall trend test of the residuals against their order of arrival (Mann 1945; Kendall 1975), computed as
  Kendall's tau between the time index and the residual (``scipy.stats.kendalltau``).

The decision is a screening heuristic, not a statistical guarantee; every threshold is a field of
:class:`DriftThresholds`. A *flag* is raised by each of: a significant bias, an nRMSE above ``nrmse_review``, an
interval coverage more than ``coverage_z`` binomial standard errors below ``level``, a KS p-value below
``ks_alpha / d`` on any feature, an out-of-range fraction above ``oob_review`` and a significant residual trend.
The decision is ``"retrain"`` when a hard limit is crossed (nRMSE above ``nrmse_retrain`` or out-of-range fraction
above ``oob_retrain``) or when ``n_flags_retrain`` or more flags are raised, ``"review"`` with at least one flag, and
``"ok"`` otherwise.

References
----------
Massey, F. J. (1951). The Kolmogorov-Smirnov test for goodness of fit. *JASA* 46(253), 68-78.

Mann, H. B. (1945). Nonparametric tests against trend. *Econometrica* 13(3), 245-259.

Kendall, M. G. (1975). *Rank Correlation Methods*, 4th ed. Griffin.

Gneiting, T., Balabdaoui, F. & Raftery, A. E. (2007). Probabilistic forecasts, calibration and sharpness.
*J. R. Stat. Soc. B* 69(2), 243-268.

classes.name: DriftThresholds
classes.doc:
Thresholds of the ``ok`` / ``review`` / ``retrain`` decision of :func:`assess_drift`.

nrmse_review, nrmse_retrain : nRMSE (RMSE / std of the truth) that raises a flag / forces retraining.
bias_z : a flag when ``|mean(r)| > bias_z * std(r) / sqrt(n)``.
coverage_z : a flag when coverage ``< level - coverage_z * sqrt(level (1 - level) / n)``.
ks_alpha : family-wise level of the per-feature KS tests (Bonferroni: each feature at ``ks_alpha / d``).
oob_review, oob_retrain : out-of-range fraction that raises a flag / forces retraining.
trend_alpha : level of the Mann-Kendall trend test.
n_flags_retrain : number of simultaneous flags that turns ``review`` into ``retrain``.

classes.name: DriftReport
classes.doc: Result of :func:`assess_drift`. Per-output arrays have shape ``(m,)``; per-feature arrays ``(d,)``.

methods.name: summary
methods.doc: One line per quantity, then the decision and its reasons.

functions.name: assess_drift
functions.sig: (y_true, y_pred, sigma = None, X_ref = None, X_new = None, bounds = None, level: float = 0.95, thresholds: DriftThresholds | None = None) -> DriftReport
functions.doc:
Check a batch of surrogate predictions for accuracy loss, miscalibration, input shift and residual trend.

Parameters
----------
y_true, y_pred : arrays (n,) or (n, m), in order of arrival (the trend test uses this order).
sigma : optional predictive standard deviation, same shape as ``y_pred``; enables the coverage check.
X_ref : optional reference (training) inputs (n_ref, d); with ``X_new`` enables the per-feature KS tests.
X_new : optional inputs (n_new, d) of the new batch.
bounds : optional training box, a tuple ``(lo, hi)`` of arrays (d,) or an array (d, 2); with ``X_new`` gives the
    out-of-range fraction. If omitted and ``X_ref`` is given, the min/max of ``X_ref`` is used.
level : central coverage of the Gaussian interval ``y_pred +- z sigma``, ``z = Phi^-1((1 + level) / 2)``.
thresholds : :class:`DriftThresholds` (defaults when omitted).

Returns
-------
DriftReport

children.doc:
Deep Ensemble uncertainty quantification.

References
----------
Lakshminarayanan, B., Pritzel, A. & Blundell, C. (2017). *Simple and Scalable
Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles*. NeurIPS.

classes.name: EnsembleConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for Deep Ensemble UQ.

Attributes
----------
n_members:
    Number of ensemble members to create when using the factory
    constructor :meth:`EnsembleUQ.from_config`.  Has no effect when
    ``EnsembleUQ`` is instantiated directly with a list of models.
diversity_reg:
    Coefficient for an optional diversity regularisation term that can be
    incorporated into a custom loss function.  ``EnsembleUQ`` stores this
    value in :attr:`metadata` but does **not** apply it automatically
    during inference.  Pass it to your training loss to encourage ensemble
    diversity.
seed:
    Base random seed used when :meth:`EnsembleUQ.from_config` creates
    ensemble members.  Member *i* is initialised with ``seed + i`` so
    that each member starts from a different random state.

classes.doc:
Deep Ensemble wrapper for predictive uncertainty quantification.

Aggregates predictions from multiple independently-trained models to
estimate both mean and variance of the predictive distribution.

Parameters
----------
models:
    List of independently trained ``nn.Module`` instances.  Each model
    must accept the same input shape and return the same output shape.
config:
    :class:`EnsembleConfig` controlling ensemble-level hyperparameters.

Examples
--------
>>> ensemble = EnsembleUQ(trained_models, EnsembleConfig(n_members=5))
>>> result = ensemble.predict_with_uncertainty(x, device=torch.device("cuda"))
>>> print(result.std.mean())  # average epistemic uncertainty

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.margin
children.doc:
Does a design that passes at its nominal dimensions still pass with its manufacturing tolerances? Monte Carlo
margin study against an upper limit, with checks on the study itself.

``margin_study(fn, nominal, tolerances, limit)`` draws ``n`` designs within the tolerances
(:func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate`, uniform by default: with no process-capability data
there is no basis for a narrower normal), evaluates the model on each and reports the distribution (mean, standard
deviation, min, max, the nearest-rank 95th percentile, the fraction under the limit with its Wilson interval) and a
verdict on the p95: ``FRAGILE`` (p95 above the limit), ``MARGINAL`` (p95 within ``marginal_fraction`` of the limit)
or ``ROBUST``.

Six checks of the result, each PASS / WARNING / FAIL with its number:

1. every sample is finite;
2. p95 stability: an independent batch of the same size gives a p95 within half the p95 margin (at least
   ``min_drift``) of this one;
3. p95 with fewer samples: an independent batch of ``n_small`` gives a p95 within the same band;
4. the hottest sample drawn against the limit;
5. corner stack-up (:func:`corner_stackup`): every tolerance at an end of its band at once, a deterministic method
   independent of the sampling (exact worst case for a model monotone in each input);
6. p95 against the limit (the verdict).

The checks are also given as a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` (FAIL of 4-6 is critical; WARNING is a
non-critical contradiction), so the decision is APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT by the library's rules.

functions.doc: Evaluate ``fn`` at the 2^d corners of the tolerance box ``nominal +- tolerances``.

Monte Carlo margin study of ``fn`` (``(m, d)`` inputs -> ``(m,)``) against the upper ``limit``.

``seed`` draws the main batch, ``check_seed`` the two independent batches of checks 2 and 3 (``None``: fresh).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.mc_dropout
children.doc:
Monte Carlo Dropout for epistemic uncertainty quantification.

References
----------
Gal, Y. & Ghahramani, Z. (2016). *Dropout as a Bayesian Approximation:
Representing Model Uncertainty in Deep Learning*. ICML.

classes.name: MCDropoutConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for Monte Carlo Dropout.

Attributes
----------
n_samples:
    Number of stochastic forward passes used to estimate the posterior
    predictive distribution.  Higher values yield lower variance estimates
    at the cost of more compute.
dropout_p:
    Dropout probability applied to the input of every ``nn.Linear`` layer
    but the first (the hidden activations) during stochastic inference.
seed:
    Optional integer RNG seed for reproducible sampling.  When ``None``
    the global PyTorch RNG state is used.

classes.name: MCDropoutWrapper
classes.sig: (model: nn.Module, config: MCDropoutConfig) -> None
classes.doc:
Wraps any ``nn.Module`` and adds Monte Carlo Dropout at inference time.

A thin ``nn.Dropout`` pre-forward hook is registered on every ``nn.Linear``
layer but the first, so dropout acts on the hidden activations (Gal &
Ghahramani 2016, dropout before each weight layer). It is never applied to
the network's output: dropping an output unit zeroes the prediction itself
and turns the "uncertainty" into ``|mean| sqrt(p / (1 - p))``. The input
coordinates are not dropped either. The wrapper owns the dropout modules;
the wrapped model's parameters are **never** modified.

Parameters
----------
model:
    Any trained ``nn.Module``.  Its weights are frozen from the wrapper's
    perspective (no gradient bookkeeping is changed here).
config:
    :class:`MCDropoutConfig` instance controlling dropout probability and
    number of samples.

Examples
--------
>>> cfg = MCDropoutConfig(n_samples=200, dropout_p=0.15)
>>> wrapper = MCDropoutWrapper(trained_model, cfg)
>>> result = wrapper.predict_with_uncertainty(x, device=torch.device("cuda"))
>>> lower, upper = result.confidence_interval(alpha=0.05)

methods.name: enable_dropout
methods.doc: Enable stochastic dropout on all hooked Linear layers.

methods.name: disable_dropout
methods.doc: Disable dropout — model behaves deterministically.

methods.name: forward
methods.doc: Standard deterministic forward pass (dropout disabled).

methods.name: predict_with_uncertainty
methods.sig: (x: Tensor, n_samples: Optional[int] = None, device: Optional[torch.device] = None) -> UQResult
methods.doc: Run *n_samples* stochastic forward passes and aggregate statistics.

methods.name: remove_hooks
methods.doc: Remove all registered forward hooks from the wrapped model.

classes.name: MCDropout
classes.sig: (model: Callable[[Tensor], Tensor], config: Optional[MCDropoutConfig] = None) -> None
classes.doc:
Convenience class that applies MC Dropout to any callable model.

Unlike :class:`MCDropoutWrapper`, this class accepts **any callable**
(not just ``nn.Module``), making it suitable for wrapped models, partial
functions, or ONNX runtimes that expose a ``__call__`` interface.

Parameters
----------
model:
    Any callable mapping a ``Tensor`` to a ``Tensor``.
config:
    :class:`MCDropoutConfig` instance.  When ``None``, default config is
    used.

Notes
-----
Because this class cannot inject hooks into an arbitrary callable, it
relies on the model having dropout layers that respect ``model.train()``
and ``model.eval()`` (i.e. the model must be an ``nn.Module``).  For
non-module callables, the stochastic variation comes solely from any
randomness already present in the callable.

Examples
--------
>>> mc = MCDropout(model, MCDropoutConfig(n_samples=50))
>>> result = mc.predict_with_uncertainty(x)

methods.name: predict_with_uncertainty
methods.doc: Run stochastic forward passes and return uncertainty estimates.
