children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.pce
children.doc:
Polynomial chaos expansion by least squares: output mean, variance and Sobol indices from one regression.

Every input is written as ``x_i = F_i^-1((xi_i + 1) / 2)`` with ``xi_i`` uniform on [-1, 1] (the inverse-CDF map of
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.distributions`), and the output is fitted on the orthonormal Legendre
polynomials of the ``xi`` of total degree ``<= degree``. With orthonormal terms the mean is the constant
coefficient, the variance the sum of the other squared coefficients, and the Sobol indices are sums of squared
coefficients (Sudret 2008, Reliab. Eng. Syst. Saf. 93:964). The fit is only as good as its leave-one-out error
(``loo_q2``, computed exactly from the hat matrix); a low Q2 means more samples or a higher degree, or a model that
is not smooth enough for this expansion. It is cheap for a few inputs and a low degree: the number of terms is
``C(d + degree, degree)``.

classes.name: PCEResult
classes.doc: Fitted expansion. Output arrays are per output (``m``).

functions.name: multi_indices
functions.sig: (d: int, degree: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: All multi-indices of ``d`` variables with total degree ``<= degree`` (constant first).

functions.name: legendre_design
functions.sig: (xi: np.ndarray, alphas: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Design matrix of orthonormal Legendre products (w.r.t. the uniform density on [-1, 1]^d).

functions.name: n_terms
functions.sig: (d: int, degree: int) -> int

functions.name: polynomial_chaos
functions.sig: (fn, space, degree: int = 3, n: int | None = None, seed: int = 0, max_terms: int = 500) -> PCEResult
functions.doc:
Fit a total-degree Legendre chaos to ``fn`` on ``n`` Latin-hypercube samples of ``space``.

``n`` defaults to twice the number of terms. Raises ``ValueError`` when the expansion would exceed
``max_terms`` terms (it is meant for a few inputs; use Sobol sampling for many).

children.summary: Polynomial chaos expansion by least squares: output mean, variance and Sobol indices from one regression.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.posterior_metrics
children.doc:
Posterior-matching metrics for generative / probabilistic inverse solvers (PosteriorBench).

A solver whose posterior *mean* is right can still have the wrong posterior: too narrow (the
classic MC-dropout failure), too wide, or with the wrong spatial texture. PosteriorBench
(neuraloperator/PosteriorBench, MIT; Wang et al., "PosteriorBench: From Point Estimates to
Posterior Matching in Evaluating Generative Inverse Solvers", NeurIPS 2026, arXiv:2609.20794)
compares predicted and reference posterior *ensembles* of 2D fields with:

- relative L2 of the mean and of the pointwise standard deviation;
- MMD with a multi-scale Gaussian kernel (bandwidths 0.2..5 x the median cross distance);
- sliced Wasserstein distance with Gaussian-random-field projection directions (smooth
  directions, drawn in the DCT domain) instead of isotropic white-noise directions;
- geometric mean of the relative error of the radially averaged power spectrum.

The implementation follows ``posteriorbench/evaluation/metrics.py`` (MIT, Copyright the
PosteriorBench authors); all quantities accept weighted ensembles (e.g. importance-sampled
reference posteriors). Its datasets are on the Hugging Face Hub (``pinneapple_catalog``:
``posteriorbench``).

functions.name: normalize_weights
functions.sig: (weights: Optional[np.ndarray], n: int) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: weighted_mmd
functions.sig: (pred, ref, pred_weights = None, ref_weights = None) -> float

functions.name: weighted_wasserstein_1d
functions.sig: (x, y, wx = None, wy = None) -> float

functions.name: grf_direction
functions.sig: (h: int, w: int, rng: np.random.Generator, alpha: float = 2.0, tau: float = 3.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Unit-norm smooth random direction: GRF with spectrum ~ (pi^2 |k|^2 + tau^2)^(-alpha/2).

functions.name: sliced_wasserstein
functions.sig: (pred, ref, pred_weights = None, ref_weights = None, n_projections: int = 128, seed: int = 0, alpha: float = 2.0, tau: float = 3.0) -> float

functions.name: radial_power_spectrum
functions.sig: (samples, weights = None) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: spectral_relative_geomean
functions.sig: (pred_spectrum, ref_spectrum, eps: float = 1e-10) -> float

functions.name: evaluate_posterior
functions.sig: (pred, ref, pred_weights = None, ref_weights = None, *, n_projections: int = 128, seed: int = 0, swd_mean: Optional[float] = None, swd_std: Optional[float] = None) -> Dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Compare a predicted posterior ensemble (N,H,W) with a reference one (M,H,W). Lower is better.

functions.name: crps_gaussian
functions.sig: (mu, sigma, y) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Closed form for a Gaussian predictive N(mu, sigma^2) (Gneiting et al.,
Mon. Weather Rev. 133 (2005) 1098-1118, Eq. 5). Elementwise.

functions.name: crps_ensemble
functions.sig: (samples, y, *, fair: bool = False) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Ensemble CRPS, ``E|X - y| - 0.5 E|X - X'|`` with members on axis 0
(Gneiting & Raftery, JASA 102 (2007) 359-378, Eq. 21). ``fair=True``
uses the M(M-1) normalisation of the spread term (Ferro, QJRMS 2014),
unbiased for the CRPS of the distribution the members are drawn from.
Computed in O(M log M) per point through the sorted-member identity.

children.summary: Posterior-matching metrics for generative / probabilistic inverse solvers (PosteriorBench).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.quantile
children.doc:
Quantile (distribution-free) uncertainty estimation.

Provides pinball-loss training for quantile regression models and a general
QuantileHead that wraps any point-prediction model.

Unlike conformal prediction, quantile regression *learns* conditional quantiles
from data rather than relying on post-hoc calibration.  Use
:class:`~pinneapple_uq.conformal.ConformalPredictor` when distribution-free
coverage guarantees are required.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import QuantileHead, QuantileLoss, QuantileConfig

    cfg  = QuantileConfig(quantiles=(0.1, 0.5, 0.9))
    head = QuantileHead(base_model, cfg)
    loss = QuantileLoss(cfg.quantiles)

    for x_batch, y_batch in loader:
        y_pred = head(x_batch)          # (B, H, Q)
        metrics = loss(head, y_pred, {"y": y_batch})
        metrics["total"].backward()
        ...

classes.name: QuantileConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for quantile prediction.

Parameters
----------
quantiles : sequence of floats in ``(0, 1)``.
    Default ``(0.1, 0.5, 0.9)`` gives 80 % prediction interval + median.

classes.name: QuantileHead
classes.sig: (base: nn.Module, cfg: QuantileConfig, hidden_dim: int = 64, rearrange: bool = True) -> None
classes.doc:
Wrap a point-prediction model and project outputs to multiple quantiles.

Assumes ``base(x)`` returns ``(B, H)`` or ``(B, H, 1)``.
Output shape: ``(B, H, Q)`` where *Q* = ``len(cfg.quantiles)``.

Parameters
----------
base : nn.Module — backbone forecaster (any architecture).
cfg : QuantileConfig — quantile levels.
hidden_dim : int — width of the projection head.
rearrange : bool — sort the ``Q`` outputs at every point so that a higher level is never predicted below a
    lower one (Chernozhukov, Fernandez-Val and Galichon 2010; the sorted estimate is never farther from the
    true quantile function). Default ``True``; ``False`` returns the raw outputs, which can cross,
    especially early in training and away from the data. :func:`crossing_rate` measures it.

Notes
-----
The head sees only the point prediction ``base(x)``, not ``x``, so the width of the interval depends on ``x``
only through that prediction.

methods.name: forward
methods.doc: Return quantile predictions, shape ``(B, H, Q)``.

classes.name: QuantileLoss
classes.sig: (quantiles: Sequence[float]) -> None
classes.doc:
Multi-quantile pinball loss compatible with the Pinneapple Trainer.

Parameters
----------
quantiles : sequence of floats.

functions.name: pinball_loss_torch
functions.sig: (y_pred: torch.Tensor, y_true: torch.Tensor, q: float) -> torch.Tensor
functions.doc:
Pinball (quantile) loss for a single quantile level *q*.

Parameters
----------
y_pred : Tensor — predicted quantile, shape ``(B, H)`` or ``(N,)``.
y_true : Tensor — targets, same shape as *y_pred*.
q : float — quantile level in ``(0, 1)``.

Returns
-------
Tensor — scalar mean pinball loss.

functions.name: crossing_rate
functions.sig: (y_pred: torch.Tensor, quantiles: Sequence[float]) -> float
functions.doc:
Fraction of predictions whose quantiles are out of order.

Parameters
----------
y_pred : Tensor — ``(..., Q)``, one column per level in *quantiles*.
quantiles : the ``Q`` levels, in the order of the last axis (any order).

Returns
-------
float in ``[0, 1]``: the share of points where a higher level is predicted below a lower one.

children.summary: Quantile (distribution-free) uncertainty estimation.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.reachability
children.doc:
RESEARCH ONLY -- set-based encounter feasibility for relative motion (collision risk, rendezvous).

Inspired by the set-based view of PRISM (A. Enayati, "PRISM: Predictive Reachability-Intercept
Set Model for Relative Motion and Intercept Kinematics", Zenodo 22979350, CC BY 4.0): instead of
propagating two point states and checking a miss distance, each body is a *region* of possible
positions that grows with state uncertainty, velocity uncertainty, information latency and
bounded acceleration; two bodies can meet at time t only if their regions overlap.

Scope of this module (deliberately): the generic, dual-use kinematics for civilian questions --
"could these two objects come into contact within T?" (collision screening for satellites,
drones, vehicles) and "can a chaser reach a target region within T?" (rendezvous / docking
feasibility). It contains no targeting, no guidance law and no engagement planning, and none
will be added: those would turn it into weapon-system tooling. It is marked research only:
a ResearchOnlyWarning is emitted on use and PINNEAPPLE_COMMERCIAL_MODE=1 refuses it.

Model: a body with nominal position p0, velocity v0, position uncertainty radius r_p, velocity
uncertainty radius r_v, control latency tau and acceleration bound a_max (free space, no
gravity -- use relative coordinates, e.g. Clohessy-Wiltshire, when that matters) can be anywhere
in the ball
    B(t) = { p0 + v0 t + e :  |e| <= r_p + r_v t + 0.5 a_max max(t - tau, 0)^2 },
which is exact for the double integrator with |a| <= a_max applied after tau (the reachable set
of a bounded-acceleration point mass is a ball of radius a_max t^2 / 2 around the ballistic path).

functions.name: encounter_feasibility
functions.sig: (a: BodyState, b: BodyState, horizon: float, *, contact_distance: float = 0.0, n: int = 2001, refine: bool = True) -> Dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Margin(t) = |c_a - c_b| - R_a - R_b - contact_distance on [0, horizon].

``possible`` is True when the margin reaches 0: the two regions can overlap, i.e. contact
cannot be ruled out (collision screening) / the encounter is reachable (rendezvous).

functions.name: time_to_reach_region
functions.sig: (chaser: BodyState, target_center: Sequence[float], target_radius: float = 0.0, horizon: float = 1000000.0) -> Optional[float]
functions.doc: Earliest time at which a (static) target region is inside the chaser's reachable ball.

children.summary: RESEARCH ONLY -- set-based encounter feasibility for relative motion (collision risk, rendezvous).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.resampling
children.doc:
Resampling confidence intervals for dependent data: moving-block and group bootstrap, skill scores, jackknife.

Forecast errors are rarely independent: consecutive time steps are autocorrelated and the cases of one event (a
storm, an experiment, a sequence) move together. Resampling single cases then gives confidence intervals that are
too narrow. The functions here resample whole blocks or whole groups instead. NumPy only.

* :func:`block_bootstrap` -- moving-block bootstrap (Kunsch 1989) for a statistic of a time series.
* :func:`group_bootstrap` -- cluster bootstrap that resamples whole groups (Davison & Hinkley 1997, sec. 3.8).
* :func:`skill_score` -- ``1 - E|e_model| / E|e_ref|`` with a paired bootstrap interval (blocks, groups or iid).
* :func:`jackknife` -- delete-one-block jackknife standard error (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, ch. 11).

Every bootstrap returns ``(estimate, lo, hi)``: the statistic on the full sample and the equal-tailed percentile
interval at ``level`` (Efron & Tibshirani 1993, ch. 13). Non-finite entries are dropped before resampling.

References
----------
Kunsch, H. R. (1989). The jackknife and the bootstrap for general stationary observations. *Annals of Statistics*
17(3), 1217-1241.

Efron, B. & Tibshirani, R. J. (1993). *An Introduction to the Bootstrap*. Chapman & Hall.

Davison, A. C. & Hinkley, D. V. (1997). *Bootstrap Methods and their Application*. Cambridge University Press.

functions.name: block_bootstrap
functions.sig: (x, stat: Callable = np.mean, block: int = 20, n: int = 2000, seed: int = 0, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc:
Moving-block bootstrap of ``stat(x)`` for a serially dependent sample (Kunsch 1989).

Each replicate concatenates ``ceil(N / block)`` overlapping blocks of ``block`` consecutive observations, with
block starts drawn uniformly from ``{0, ..., N - block}``, and cuts the result to ``N``. ``block=1`` is the
ordinary iid bootstrap. Choose ``block`` longer than the correlation time of ``x``.

Parameters
----------
x : array (N,) or (N, ...); resampling is along axis 0, rows with a non-finite entry are dropped.
stat : function of an array like ``x`` returning a scalar (default: mean).
block : block length in samples.
n : number of bootstrap replicates.
seed : seed of ``numpy.random.default_rng``.
level : coverage of the equal-tailed percentile interval.

Returns
-------
(estimate, lo, hi) : ``stat(x)`` and the percentile interval.

functions.name: group_bootstrap
functions.sig: (x, groups, stat: Callable = np.mean, n: int = 2000, seed: int = 0, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc:
Cluster bootstrap of ``stat(x)``: resample whole groups with replacement.

Cases inside one group (a storm, an event, a week, an experiment) are strongly dependent while groups are taken
as independent, so each replicate draws ``G`` group labels with replacement out of the ``G`` groups and
concatenates all their cases (Davison & Hinkley 1997, sec. 3.8). With one case per group this is the iid
bootstrap.

Parameters
----------
x : array (N,) or (N, ...); rows with a non-finite entry are dropped (with their group label).
groups : (N,) group label of every row (any sortable type). Groups are ordered as ``numpy.unique`` sorts them.
stat, n, seed, level : as in :func:`block_bootstrap`.

Returns
-------
(estimate, lo, hi)

functions.name: skill_score
functions.sig: (err_model, err_ref, *, block: int | None = None, groups = None, n: int = 2000, seed: int = 0, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc:
Skill score ``1 - E|e_model| / E|e_ref|`` with a paired bootstrap interval.

Positive means the model beats the reference (persistence, climatology, ...), 0 means no skill, 1 a perfect
model: the generic skill score ``(A - A_ref) / (A_perfect - A_ref)`` with ``A`` the mean absolute error and
``A_perfect = 0`` (Wilks 2011, *Statistical Methods in the Atmospheric Sciences*, 3rd ed., ch. 8).
Both error series are resampled with the same indices so their correlation is kept:

* ``groups`` given: whole groups are resampled (:func:`group_bootstrap`);
* else ``block`` given: moving blocks of that length (:func:`block_bootstrap`, Kunsch 1989);
* else: iid cases (Efron & Tibshirani 1993).

Parameters
----------
err_model, err_ref : (N,) errors of the model and of the reference on the same cases (absolute values are
    taken). Cases where either is non-finite are dropped.
block : moving-block length in cases (mutually exclusive with ``groups``).
groups : (N,) group label per case.
n, seed, level : as in :func:`block_bootstrap`.

Returns
-------
(skill, lo, hi)

functions.name: jackknife
functions.sig: (samples, fn: Callable, n_blocks: int = 20)
functions.doc:
Delete-one-block jackknife estimate and standard error of ``fn(samples)``.

``samples`` (axis 0) is cut into ``n_blocks`` contiguous blocks (``numpy.array_split``); ``theta_i`` is ``fn``
on the samples without block ``i``, and

    stderr = sqrt((n_blocks - 1) / n_blocks * sum_i (theta_i - mean(theta))**2)

(Efron & Tibshirani 1993, eq. 11.5). Blocking makes the error honest for autocorrelated Monte Carlo chains when
blocks are longer than the autocorrelation time; ``n_blocks = len(samples)`` is the classic delete-one jackknife.
``fn`` may return an array (e.g. a correlator per time separation): the error is element-wise.

Returns
-------
(estimate, stderr) : ``fn(samples)`` on the full sample (not bias-corrected) and its jackknife standard error.

children.summary: Resampling confidence intervals for dependent data: moving-block and group bootstrap, skill scores, jackknife.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.residual_bound
children.doc:
Residual-to-error calibration (#699): turn the PDE residual of a prediction, which needs no true answer, into an
error bound an engineer can use ("the error is below X with 90 % confidence").

Two routes, both reported:

**Theory (linear elliptic problems).** For a discrete problem ``A u = f`` with ``A`` symmetric positive definite and
``A >= c L`` for a reference operator ``L`` (both SPD), the error of any candidate ``u`` against the discrete solution
``u_h`` obeys

    ||u_h - u||_A  <=  ||r||_{L^-1} / sqrt(c),     r = f - A u,

because ``A^-1 <= L^-1 / c``. For Darcy and steady heat conduction, ``-div(k grad u) = f``, in the cell-centred
finite volumes of ``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` (:func:`darcy_problem`), ``L`` is the same operator with ``k = 1``
and ``c = min k`` (every face coefficient is a harmonic mean, never below ``min k``). The bound is guaranteed and
needs no data; it can be loose when the coefficient contrast is large.

**Calibration (any problem).** :class:`ResidualErrorCalibrator` learns the map residual -> error on a calibration set
with split conformal prediction (the finite-sample quantile of ``uncertainty.conformal``): the score is
``error / g(residual)`` with ``g`` the identity (``mode="ratio"``) or a power law fitted on a separate set
(``mode="power"``), and the bound of a new query is ``q * g(residual)``. Coverage is guaranteed for queries
exchangeable with the calibration set; under an input shift it is measured and reported, not assumed
(:meth:`ResidualErrorCalibrator.evaluate`).

The residual is evaluated with the discretisation of the reference solver, so the reference solution has a residual
of round-off size, not a truncation-error floor (a finite-difference residual of a finite-volume solution would not
be zero).

classes.name: LinearSPDProblem
classes.doc:
``A u = f`` with ``A`` SPD and ``A - c L`` positive semi-definite. ``weight`` is the quadrature weight of the
inner products (the cell area ``h^2`` on a uniform grid), so norms approximate their continuous counterparts.

methods.name: residual
methods.doc: ``f - A u`` (same shape as ``u``).

classes.name: ResidualLoss
classes.sig: (problems: list[LinearSPDProblem])
classes.doc:
A differentiable physics loss for training: ``mean_i ||f_i - A_i u_i||^2 / ||f_i||^2`` over a fixed set of
problems (e.g. :func:`darcy_problem` of each training input), in PyTorch with sparse matrices. Call
``loss(u, idx)`` with predictions ``u`` (``(B, ...)``, any shape with ``n`` values per sample) for the problems
``idx`` (a list or tensor of indices into the set).

classes.name: ResidualErrorCalibrator
classes.sig: (alpha: float = 0.1, mode: str = 'ratio')
classes.doc:
Split-conformal map from a residual measure to an error bound.

``fit`` (``mode="power"`` only) fits ``log err = b0 + b1 log res`` on its own set; ``calibrate`` computes the
conformal quantile of ``err / g(res)``; ``bound(res)`` is ``q * g(res)``.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (res: np.ndarray, err: np.ndarray, label: str = 'held-out') -> CoverageReport
methods.doc:
Observed coverage on queries with known error. ``holds`` when it is at least the target minus two standard
deviations (binomial, over the test and the calibration sizes); below that the report says the guarantee is
broken (e.g. by an input shift).

methods.name: to_check
methods.doc:
A trust-report check "error bound without ground truth" for one query (supports when the bound is below
``limit``; without a limit the bound is reported and the check is not run).

functions.name: darcy_problem
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, f: float | np.ndarray = 1.0) -> LinearSPDProblem
functions.doc:
``-div(a grad u) = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, in the discretisation of
``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d`` (``a``, ``f`` at the ``n x n`` cell centres).

functions.name: heat_conduction_problem
functions.sig: (k: np.ndarray, q: float | np.ndarray) -> LinearSPDProblem
functions.doc:
Steady conduction ``-div(k grad T) = q`` with ``T = 0`` on the boundary of the unit square: the same operator
as Darcy, with conductivity ``k`` and heat source ``q``.

functions.name: energy_error_bound
functions.sig: (problem: LinearSPDProblem, u: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Guaranteed bound on ``||u_h - u||_A`` from the residual alone, absolute and relative to ``||u||_A``.

functions.name: coverage_study
functions.sig: (res: np.ndarray, err: np.ndarray, *, alpha: float = 0.1, n_cal: int | None = None, n_splits: int = 200, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Coverage of the ``mode="ratio"`` bound over ``n_splits`` random calibration / test splits of one pool of
exchangeable queries (``n_cal`` calibration queries, default half). One split's coverage fluctuates by about
``sqrt(alpha (1 - alpha) / n)``; the mean over splits is what the conformal guarantee is about.

children.summary: Residual-to-error calibration (#699): turn the PDE residual of a prediction, which needs no true answer, into an error bound an engineer can use ("the error is below X with 90 % confidence").

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.study
children.doc:
One uncertainty study of one model output: is the prediction reliable here, and which cases need the solver?

:func:`uncertainty_study` composes the pieces of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty`:

1. split-conformal intervals calibrated on ``(X_cal, y_cal)`` with their coverage **measured** on ``(X_test, y_test)``
   (never used to calibrate), plus the coverage of the raw ensemble interval when the model has a spread;
2. an applicability gate fitted on reference inputs (the training inputs when known) and the declared validity range;
3. screening of ``cases`` (scenarios, a batch of designs): prediction, interval, gate, route, and optionally the
   high-fidelity answer for the routed cases (or all), which shows whether the rule sent the right cases;
4. propagation of uncertain inputs around a nominal operating point (MC / LHS / Sobol, and polynomial chaos when
   cheap), with the probability of meeting the limits with and without the model's own error, and the share of the
   propagated samples that leave the region where the model was checked.

Every number in the returned dict comes from these runs; nothing is assumed.

functions.name: uncertainty_study
functions.sig: (model, output: str, X_cal, y_cal, X_test, y_test, *, alpha: float = 0.1, scale: str = 'absolute', X_ref = None, bounds: Mapping[str, tuple] | None = None, cases = None, case_names: Sequence[str] | None = None, tolerance: float | None = None, tolerance_pct: float | None = None, limits: tuple[float | None, float | None] | None = None, high_fidelity: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = No...
functions.doc:

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance
children.doc:
Monte-Carlo propagation of input (manufacturing, operating) tolerances through any model.

Each input ``i`` is drawn independently around its nominal value ``x0_i``:

* ``"normal"``: ``x_i ~ N(x0_i, t_i^2)`` -- the tolerance ``t_i`` is the standard deviation;
* ``"uniform"``: ``x_i ~ U(x0_i - t_i, x0_i + t_i)`` -- the tolerance is the half-width, variance ``t_i^2 / 3``
  (``(b - a)^2 / 12`` with ``b - a = 2 t_i``).

The model is evaluated once on the ``(n, d)`` sample matrix and the output statistics are the sample mean, standard
deviation and percentiles (JCGM 101:2008, "Propagation of distributions using a Monte Carlo method"). The
probability of meeting the specification limits ``lo <= y <= hi`` (jointly over the outputs and per output) comes
with the Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion (Wilson 1927; Brown, Cai & DasGupta 2001), which stays
inside [0, 1] and keeps its coverage when the proportion is close to 0 or 1 -- the usual case for a yield.

References
----------
JCGM 101:2008. *Evaluation of measurement data -- Supplement 1 to the GUM -- Propagation of distributions using a
Monte Carlo method*. BIPM.

Wilson, E. B. (1927). Probable inference, the law of succession, and statistical inference. *JASA* 22(158),
209-212.

Brown, L. D., Cai, T. T. & DasGupta, A. (2001). Interval estimation for a binomial proportion. *Statistical
Science* 16(2), 101-133.

classes.name: ToleranceResult
classes.doc:
Result of :func:`propagate`. Output arrays have shape ``(m,)`` (``m = 1`` for a scalar model).

``p_within`` is the probability that all outputs meet their limits jointly, ``p_within_ci`` its Wilson interval,
and ``p_within_each`` the per-output probabilities; they are ``None`` without ``limits``.

functions.name: wilson_interval
functions.sig: (k: int, n: int, level: float = 0.95) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc:
Wilson score interval for a binomial proportion ``k / n`` (Wilson 1927; Brown, Cai & DasGupta 2001, eq. 4):

(p + z^2 / 2n -+ z sqrt(p (1 - p) / n + z^2 / 4n^2)) / (1 + z^2 / n),   z = Phi^-1((1 + level) / 2).

``method`` is ``"mc"`` (plain Monte Carlo), ``"lhs"`` (Latin hypercube: same estimator, lower variance of the

children.doc:
pinneapple_uq — Uncertainty Quantification for physics-informed neural networks.

This module provides a unified, PyTorch-native toolkit for estimating and
evaluating predictive uncertainty in PINNs and related surrogate models.

Uncertainty types
-----------------
``AleatoricHead`` / ``aleatoric_nll_loss``
    **Aleatoric (data) uncertainty** — irreducible noise in the data.
    The model learns both mean μ(x) and log-variance log σ²(x).
    Optimized via heteroscedastic Gaussian NLL.

``MCDropout`` / ``EnsembleUQ``
    **Epistemic (model) uncertainty** — reducible uncertainty from limited data
    or model capacity.  MC Dropout runs *n* stochastic forward passes;
    ensembles aggregate multiple independently-trained models.

``decompose_uncertainty``
    **Decomposition** — splits total variance into aleatoric + epistemic
    components from *n* stochastic passes of an AleatoricHead model.

``ConformalPredictor``
    **Conformal prediction** — distribution-free coverage guarantees via a
    held-out calibration set.

Quantile regression
-------------------
``QuantileHead`` / ``QuantileLoss``
    Learn conditional quantiles via pinball loss; also accessible from
    ``pinneapple_timeseries.uncertainty``.

Calibration utilities
---------------------
``CalibrationMetrics``
    Static methods for ECE, coverage, sharpness, and Gaussian NLL.

Resampling
----------
``block_bootstrap`` / ``group_bootstrap`` / ``skill_score`` / ``jackknife``
    Confidence intervals for autocorrelated or grouped errors (NumPy only).

Monitoring and tolerances
-------------------------
``assess_drift`` / ``DriftReport``
    Accuracy, interval coverage, per-feature KS input shift, out-of-range fraction and residual trend of a
    deployed surrogate, with an ok / review / retrain decision (NumPy + SciPy).
``propagate`` / ``ToleranceResult``
    Monte-Carlo propagation of input tolerances through any model, with the probability of meeting limits.
``propagate_space`` / ``polynomial_chaos``
    Propagation of inputs with any distribution (``distributions``: uniform, normal, truncated normal, lognormal,
    triangular) by Monte Carlo, Latin hypercube or Sobol sampling; least-squares polynomial chaos with its
    leave-one-out error and the Sobol indices it implies.

Studies on any model's predictions (NumPy)
------------------------------------------
``conformal_study``
    Split-conformal intervals calibrated on one split and their coverage measured on another (Wilson interval,
    per-group coverage, reliability across levels); absolute or normalised scores.
``ApplicabilityDomain`` / ``route_cases``
    Range and k-NN data-density gates on the inputs, and the rule that sends a case to the high-fidelity solver.
``uncertainty_study``
    All of the above for one model output: held-out coverage, gate, screened cases (with optional high-fidelity
    checks), propagation around an operating point.

Unified interface
-----------------
``uq_predict(model, x, method=...) -> UQResult``
    Single entry-point for all methods.  Supported *method* values:
    ``"mc_dropout"``, ``"ensemble"``, ``"aleatoric"``, ``"decompose"``.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import uq_predict, AleatoricHead, decompose_uncertainty
>>> # Aleatoric-only
>>> head = AleatoricHead(base_model, out_dim=1, in_dim=2)
>>> result = uq_predict(head, x_test, method="aleatoric")
>>> print(result.aleatoric_std)
>>>
>>> # Full decomposition (aleatoric + epistemic via MC Dropout)
>>> from pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty import MCDropoutWrapper, MCDropoutConfig
>>> mcd = MCDropoutWrapper(head, MCDropoutConfig(n_samples=50))
>>> result = decompose_uncertainty(mcd, x_test)
>>> print(result.aleatoric_std, result.epistemic_std)

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena
pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.blue
children.doc:
Blue team: calibrated thresholds with a stated false-alarm rate, one combined test, and hardening.

**Defence.** A set of checks with a threshold each; a case is rejected when any check exceeds its threshold. Round
0 of the arena is the hand-set tolerances of the checks (``Defence.from_checks``).

**Calibration** (``calibrate``). The checks are combined into one statistic so that false alarms do not grow with
the number of checks. With the clean calibration cases split in two halves A and B:

1. each check's scale ``s_j`` is the split-conformal quantile of its values on A
   (``pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.conformal.conformal_quantile``), at least 1 % of the check's own tolerance;
2. the combined statistic of a case is ``T = max_j value_j / s_j``;
3. its threshold ``q`` is the split-conformal quantile of ``T`` on B at level ``alpha_cal``.

``T`` is a fixed function of a case once A is used, so for a new clean case exchangeable with B,
``P(T > q) <= alpha_cal`` (Vovk, Gammerman & Shafer 2005; Angelopoulos & Bates 2022, arXiv:2107.07511) for the
whole family of checks at once: the family-wise false-alarm rate. The guarantee needs
``ceil((n_B + 1)(1 - alpha_cal)) <= n_B``; ``Defence.alpha_guaranteed`` says whether that holds. ``alpha_cal`` is
``safety * alpha`` (default ``safety = 0.5``) so that the rate measured on a finite held-out set stays below the stated
``alpha``. The combined test is the same as per-check thresholds ``q s_j``, which the reports list.

**Hardening** (``harden``). Stored false alarms are correct cases: ``q`` is raised just above their statistic (this
only lowers the false-alarm rate). Then, while a stored escape passes, the check of the library that catches the most
remaining escapes (after recalibration) is added; the log says which checks were added and what each one caught.

A cases file holds the problem (name and options), the hardened defence (check names and thresholds) and every
escape and false alarm the red team found, each as a few numbers: the seed and variation of the correct case, and
the generator with its parameters. Replaying regenerates each case, runs the stored defence and requires every
escape to be rejected and every false alarm to pass. A file is JSON::

    {"format": "pinneapple-arena-cases/1", "problem": "darcy_2d", "options": {...},
     "defence": {"checks": [...], "thresholds": {...}, ...},
     "cases": [{"kind": "escape", "seed": 123, "variation": {}, "generator": "coefficient_field",
                "params": {...}, "true_error": 0.14, ...}, ...]}

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.generators
children.doc:
Red-team generators: parametrised families of wrong-but-plausible outputs that the evasion search explores.

A generator maps a correct case and a parameter vector to ``(faulty_case, correct_field)``. Parameters are named,
with bounds; the search works on the unit box and ``Generator.params`` maps back. Families:

* ``mutant``: the mutation operators of the fault library combined (bias, scale, smoothing, noise), the model-side
  operators of mutation testing for deep learning (DeepCrime, Humbatova et al. 2021; MuFF, arXiv:2501.09846).
* ``smooth_modes``: a smooth distortion that keeps the boundary or initial condition exactly (Darcy: sine modes
  vanishing on the boundary; Burgers: periodic modes growing from zero at t = 0).
* physics-consistent attacks, outputs that solve a nearby problem exactly, so the PDE residual stays small:
  Darcy ``coefficient_field`` (a smooth change of log a) and ``source_field`` (a smooth change of f); Burgers
  ``viscosity`` (another nu), ``hard_ic_evolution`` (the exact initial condition at t = 0, then the evolution of a
  smoothed and rescaled one, what a hard-constrained PINN with spectral bias returns) and ``time_warp``
  (u(x, s t)).
* ``fault:<name>``: one fault of the fault library at a given magnitude (escapes found by the mutation score are
  stored with these).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.loop
children.doc:
The arena loop: rounds of red team then blue team, and the report.

``run_arena(problem, checks=None, budget=...)``:

* **Round 0 defence**: ``checks`` with their own tolerances (default: ``default_checks(problem)``, what users run
  today).
* **Red** (each round): the mutation score of the defence on the fault library (and the mutants that matter but
  pass), evasion searches with every generator on ``n_bases`` correct cases, and the false-alarm search over correct
  cases. Escapes (true relative error >= ``min_error`` and accepted) and false alarms (correct and rejected) are
  stored as regression cases.
* **Blue** (each round): split-conformal calibration of the combined test on clean calibration cases, hardened with
  checks from ``check_library(problem)`` until every stored escape is rejected; stored false alarms pass.
* **Evaluation** (each round): false-alarm rate on a held-out clean set, stored escapes rejected, stored false
  alarms accepted, mutation score after the round, and per check the detection rate, false-alarm rate, ROC AUC over
  fault magnitude and minimal detectable magnitude (from the fault-injection matrix).

Everything is seeded; ``ArenaReport.save_cases`` writes the regression cases replayed by
``pinneapple check --arena-cases``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.red
children.doc:
Red team: search for escapes (wrong but passing) and false alarms (right but rejected) against a defence.

* ``evasion_search``: for one generator and one correct case, maximise the true error of the generated output
  (against the reference solver) while every check stays under its threshold. Objective (minimised on the unit box):
  ``-min(error, 2) + 10 * sum_j max(0, margin_j + 0.02)``, ``margin_j = value_j / threshold_j - 1``; the best
  point that the defence accepts is the escape, if its error is at least ``min_error`` (10 % by default).
* ``false_alarm_search``: over correct cases (the problem's ``variation_space``: coefficient contrast, feature size,
  amplitude, viscosity, solver resolution, for several random fields), maximise the largest margin of the defence:
  the most suspicious-looking correct case, a false alarm when its margin is positive.
* ``mutation_score``: the share of the fault library's mutants that matter (true error >= ``min_error``) which the
  defence rejects, from a fault-injection detection matrix; the mutants that pass are escapes too.

Every search is seeded; a finding carries what it needs to be regenerated (case seed and variation, generator and
parameters).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena.search
children.doc:
Black-box minimisers on the unit box for the red team: differential evolution (SciPy), CMA-ES and a
finite-difference L-BFGS-B (a gradient method for objectives that are smooth in the fault parameters).

CMA-ES is written from N. Hansen, "The CMA Evolution Strategy: A Tutorial" (arXiv:1604.00772, 2016): weighted
recombination, cumulative step-size adaptation, rank-one and rank-mu covariance updates with the default constants
of the tutorial's Table 1. Box constraints are handled by evaluating the projection of each sample onto the box.

Every minimiser takes an evaluation budget, a seed, and returns the best point and value and the number of
evaluations used; all are deterministic for a given seed.

Red team / blue team for validation (#707): adversarial generators of wrong-but-plausible cases against the
checks, and a loop that hardens them.

Built on the fault library of :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection` (#697)::

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation import arena
    rep = arena.run_arena("darcy_2d", budget="small", alpha=0.05)     # or arena("darcy_2d", ...) / pp.validate.arena
    print(rep.to_markdown())          # escapes, false alarms, mutation score, ROC/AUC, minimal detectable magnitude
    rep.save_cases("darcy_cases.json")    # replayed in CI by `pinneapple check --arena-cases darcy_cases.json`

Modules: :mod:`.search` (differential evolution, CMA-ES, L-BFGS-B on the unit box), :mod:`.generators` (mutation
operators and physics-consistent attacks), :mod:`.red` (evasion and false-alarm search, mutation score),
:mod:`.blue` (split-conformal combined test, hardening), :mod:`.cases` (regression cases, replay), :mod:`.loop`
(rounds and report). The module itself is callable: ``arena(problem, checks, budget=...)`` is ``run_arena``.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map
children.doc:
Where is a field wrong? Pointwise error of a prediction against a reference on the same points, the regions where
it concentrates, and a short text that compares them with the global number.

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation.error_map import error_map
    em = error_map(points, pred, ref, regions={"clamp": clamp_nodes, "tip": tip_nodes})
    em.error                # |pred - ref| per point (vectors: norm of the difference)
    em.hotspots             # clusters of the largest errors: centre, extent, max, share of the squared error
    em.regions              # per named region: share of the squared error against its share of the points
    em.summary()            # "Relative L2 error 3.9 % ... 41 % of the squared error is in clamp (10 % of the points)"

Every number comes from the arrays given: nothing is estimated or interpolated here (map the reference onto the
prediction's points first when the meshes differ). ``weights`` (cell volumes, nodal areas) make the shares integrals
instead of point counts.

methods.doc:
Short sentences: the global number (and reported ones to compare with, label -> relative error, e.g. the
study mean), where the error concentrates among the named regions, and the largest hotspot.

``link`` (default 1.5 times the median point spacing: neighbours along the mesh lines, not across them). The ``n`` clusters with the largest maximum error, each with
its centre (error-weighted), bounding box, number of points, max and mean error, the location of its max and its
share of the total squared error (weighted by ``weights`` if given).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection
pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection.checks
children.doc:
The checks under test, as ``physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck`` objects scoring a :class:`~.problems.Case`.

A check is ``fn(field, case) -> value`` with a tolerance; it flags a case when ``value > tolerance`` (or the value is
not finite). The values are continuous, so the same check can be thresholded by hand (the defaults here), calibrated
(:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena`) or attacked (an optimiser sees how close a case is to being flagged).

Building blocks reused, not reimplemented: the finite-difference provider and relative residual of
:mod:`pinneapple_check.numerics` (``GridD``, ``rel_rms``), the conservative Darcy operator of the verified solver
(``operator_benchmarks.darcy_operator``) and its Burgers integrator (``burgers_1d``), the spectral shells of
``validation.field_metrics``, the Darcy consistency and the duplicate and leakage detectors of the dataset audit
(``pinneapple_data.audit``), and the bounds and training-envelope checks of ``pinneapple_physics.physics_audit.monitor``.

Two check sets per problem:

* ``default_checks(problem)``: what a user would run today (a finite-difference PDE residual, boundary and bounds
  checks, the training envelope), with hand-set tolerances. This is round 0 of the arena.
* ``check_library(problem)``: every check available, including stronger ones (the conservative residual on the
  solver's own stencil, a one-step re-integration, conservation, spectral content, invariants). The blue team of
  the arena picks from it.

Dataset checks (``dataset_checks``) score a whole :class:`~.problems.Dataset`: near-duplicate inputs, train/test
leakage, and the worst per-sample value of each case check.

functions.name: score
functions.sig: (check, case: Case) -> float
functions.doc: The value of ``check`` on ``case`` (``inf`` when it cannot be computed or the field is not finite).

functions.name: flags
functions.sig: (check, case: Case, tolerance: float | None = None) -> bool
functions.doc: True when ``check`` rejects ``case`` (``tolerance`` overrides the check's own).

functions.name: check_library
functions.sig: (problem: BenchmarkProblem) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Every check available for ``problem`` (name -> ``ValidityCheck`` with a hand-set tolerance).

functions.name: default_checks
functions.sig: (problem: BenchmarkProblem) -> list
functions.doc: The checks a user runs today (round 0 of the arena).

functions.name: dataset_checks
functions.sig: (problem: BenchmarkProblem, case_checks: list | None = None) -> list
functions.doc:
Checks of a whole dataset: near-duplicate inputs and test inputs that copy training inputs (the detectors of
``pinneapple_data.audit``), and the worst per-sample value of every case check (default: the whole
``check_library`` but the training envelope, which the data defines).

children.summary: The checks under test, as physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck objects scoring a ~.problems.Case.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection.faults
children.doc:
The fault library: controlled defects of a model's output or of a dataset, each with a magnitude.

A model fault turns a correct :class:`~.problems.Case` into what a defective model would return for the same
question, and gives the correct field it should be compared with (a fault that changes the inputs, such as
out-of-range use, changes the correct answer too). A data fault turns a correct :class:`~.problems.Dataset` into
what a defective datapipe would hand to training.

Model faults (#697): ``bias``, ``scale``, ``noise`` (high frequency), ``smoothing`` (spectral bias),
``wrong_boundary``, ``source_sign_flip``, ``out_of_range`` (a model used outside its input range), ``stale_model``
(trained on an older physics configuration, as in the rover zoo v1.0 case).

Data faults: ``coefficient_drift`` (a discretisation coefficient off by a constant factor, modelled on the Darcy2D
datapipe report NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2036), ``duplicates`` and ``low_diversity`` (NVIDIA/physicsnemo#2035),
``leakage`` (test samples copied from training), ``unit_mixup`` (outputs in mm instead of m), ``swapped_channels``.

Each fault has a ladder of magnitudes and a ``documented`` magnitude: the one the detection matrix promises to catch
with at least one check (the acceptance test of #697).

methods.name: documented_for
methods.doc: The documented magnitude on ``problem`` (a fault can be harder to see on one problem than another).

functions.doc:
ROC AUC of a score separating ``faulty`` (positives) from ``clean``: P(faulty > clean) + P(tie) / 2
(Mann-Whitney). 0.5 = no better than chance, 1 = perfect separation.

functions.doc: The random stream of one fault injection (so a single trial can be replayed).

functions.name: run_fault_injection
functions.sig: (problem: str | BenchmarkProblem = 'darcy_2d', *, checks: Sequence | None = None, data_checks: Sequence | None = None, model_faults: Sequence[Fault] | None = None, data_faults: Sequence[Fault] | None = None, n_cases: int = 50, n_datasets: int = 20, dataset_size: tuple[int, int] = (16, 8), seed: int = 0, min_rate: float = 0.9, include_data: bool = True, **problem_options) -> FaultInjectionReport
functions.doc:
Build the detection matrix of ``checks`` (default: the problem's ``check_library``) against the fault
library on ``problem`` (``"darcy_2d"``, ``"burgers_1d"`` or a :class:`BenchmarkProblem`).

Clean cases are drawn with ``sample_varied`` (correct but unusual); every model fault is injected into each of
them at every magnitude (seeded). Data faults are injected into ``n_datasets`` datasets of ``dataset_size``
(train, test) correct samples and scored with ``data_checks`` (default: ``dataset_checks``).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection.problems
children.doc:
Benchmark problems with a verified reference solver, as sources of correct cases for the fault-injection suite.

A :class:`Case` is one input/output pair of an operator-learning problem: the inputs the model is given, the field it
returned on a fixed grid, and the parameters of the equation. The two problems wrap the verified solvers of
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.operator_benchmarks` (checked in ``tests/test_operator_benchmarks.py``):

* :class:`DarcyProblem`: ``-div(a grad u) = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, ``a`` a thresholded
  Gaussian random field (Li et al. 2021); the field is ``u`` at the ``n x n`` cell centres.
* :class:`BurgersProblem`: ``u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx`` on the periodic interval [0, 1); the field is the space-time
  solution ``u(t_k, x_j)`` at ``n_t`` snapshots from 0 to ``t_end`` (what a space-time PINN or an autoregressive
  operator returns).

Every case is reproducible from its ``seed`` and its ``variation`` (the knobs of the false-alarm search: coefficient
contrast, feature size, amplitude, viscosity, solver resolution), so a stored regression case is a few numbers.

classes.name: Case
classes.doc:
One input/output pair. ``field``: the output on the problem's grid; ``inputs``: what the model was given;
``params``: the equation's parameters for this case; ``seed`` and ``variation`` regenerate the correct case.

classes.name: Dataset
classes.doc: A training and a test split of cases (what a datapipe hands to training).

classes.name: BenchmarkProblem
classes.sig: (**options)
classes.doc:
A problem with a verified reference solver. Subclasses define ``name``, ``defaults`` (options),
``variation_space`` (the ranges of the false-alarm search, all inside the training envelope) and
``_solve(seed, variation)``.

methods.name: case
methods.doc: The correct case of ``seed`` (the input drawn from the training law, perturbed by ``variation``).

methods.name: sample
methods.doc: ``n`` correct cases with seeds derived from ``seed``.

methods.name: sample_varied
methods.doc:
``n`` correct cases whose ``variation`` is drawn uniformly from ``variation_space`` (unusual but
correct: the clean population a threshold must not flag).

methods.name: resolve
methods.doc:
The reference field for ``case`` with some of its inputs or parameters changed (a model that solves a
nearby problem exactly: the physics-consistent faults).

methods.name: predict_reference
methods.sig: (inputs: Mapping[str, np.ndarray], params: Mapping[str, float]) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: The reference solver as a model ``predict(inputs, params) -> field`` (the ``audit_model`` interface).

methods.name: features
methods.doc: Scalar descriptors of the input (for the training envelope).

methods.name: input_case
methods.doc: The inputs of ``case(seed, **variation)`` without solving (``field`` is empty).

methods.name: envelope
methods.doc:
The training envelope (``physics_audit.Envelope``) over the input features of ``n_train`` inputs drawn
from the training law (``variation_space`` uniformly, seed ``envelope_seed``).

methods.name: true_error
methods.doc: Relative L2 error of ``case.field`` against the correct field.

classes.name: DarcyProblem
classes.doc:
``-div(a grad u) = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary.

Options: ``n`` (cells per side), ``high``/``low`` (the two permeabilities), ``alpha``/``tau`` (law of the
underlying Gaussian random field), ``f`` (uniform source). Variation (all within the training envelope):
``contrast`` (multiplies ``high / low`` around their geometric mean, 0.8 .. 1.25), ``tau`` (feature size),
``level`` (threshold of the random field: the fraction of high-permeability cells), ``refine`` (the reference
solved on a 1x, 2x or 3x finer grid and averaged onto the ``n x n`` cells: a different but consistent
discretisation).

methods.name: resolve
methods.sig: (case: Case, *, a: np.ndarray | None = None, f: float | np.ndarray | None = None, axis_weights: Sequence[float] = (1.0, 1.0)) -> np.ndarray

classes.name: BurgersProblem
classes.doc:
``u_t + (u^2/2)_x = nu u_xx`` on the periodic interval [0, 1), ``u(x, 0) = u0(x)``.

Options: ``n`` (points), ``n_t`` (snapshots from 0 to ``t_end``, both included), ``nu``, ``dt`` (solver time
step), ``alpha``/``tau``/``sigma`` (law of the initial condition, a periodic Gaussian random field). Variation
(within the training envelope): ``amplitude`` (multiplies ``u0``, 0.7 .. 1.3), ``tau`` (feature size),
``nu_factor`` (viscosity of the case, 0.8 .. 1.25 times ``nu``: the model takes ``nu`` as an input),
``refine`` (reference solved on a 1x, 2x or 3x finer grid with a smaller time step and sampled back).

methods.name: resolve
methods.sig: (case: Case, *, u0: np.ndarray | None = None, nu: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray

functions.sig: (problem: str | BenchmarkProblem, **options) -> BenchmarkProblem
functions.doc: A problem by name (``"darcy_2d"``, ``"burgers_1d"``; ``"darcy"``/``"burgers"`` work too) or as given.

children.summary: Benchmark problems with a verified reference solver, as sources of correct cases for the fault-injection suite.

children.doc:
Fault injection: measure how often each validation check catches known model and data defects (#697).

A "pass" from a check carries no stated power until the check has been run against defects of known size. This
package injects a library of controlled faults into correct cases of problems with a verified reference solver and
records every check's response::

    from pinneapple_analysis.validation.fault_injection import run_fault_injection
    rep = run_fault_injection("darcy_2d", n_cases=50)
    print(rep.to_markdown())            # detection matrix, false alarms, minimal detectable magnitudes
    assert rep.passed                   # every fault caught at its documented magnitude, <= 1 % false alarms

Modules: :mod:`.problems` (Darcy 2-D and Burgers 1-D cases from ``operator_benchmarks``), :mod:`.checks` (the
checks under test, as ``physics_audit.monitor.ValidityCheck``), :mod:`.faults` (the fault library), :mod:`.matrix`
(the detection matrix and its report). The adversarial arena (:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.arena`) is
built on these.
children.summary: Fault injection: measure how often each validation check catches known model and data defects (#697).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.field_metrics
children.doc:
PDEBench-style error metrics for gridded fields (NumPy, no torch).

Given a prediction and a reference on the same regular grid, report the
error the way neural-operator / surrogate benchmarks do, so a PINNeAPPle
model can be compared with published PDEBench numbers:

``rmse``      root-mean-square error over space, averaged over the rest
``nrmse``     ``rmse / rms(target)`` per sample/channel/time, then averaged
``max_error`` worst absolute pointwise error
``crmse``     error of the spatial *mean* (conserved-quantity error)
``brmse``     RMSE restricted to the boundary faces of the box
``frmse``     RMSE split into low / mid / high radial-wavenumber bands
``vrmse``     RMSE / std(target) -- The Well's headline metric (variance-scaled)
``pearson``   spatial Pearson correlation between prediction and target

Definitions follow PDEBench (Takamoto et al., NeurIPS 2022 Datasets &
Benchmarks; code ``pdebench/models/metrics.py``, MIT), adapted:

- **Full spectrum.** PDEBench's 2-D/3-D Fourier metric accumulates only the
  ``i, j < n/2`` quadrant of the FFT (negative frequencies are skipped), so
  half (2-D) or three quarters (3-D) of the spectral error is ignored. Here
  every FFT coefficient is binned by its integer radial wavenumber
  ``floor(|m|)``, with ``m`` the signed mode index, so nothing is dropped and
  Parseval holds: the shell energies sum to ``rmse^2`` (tested).
- **Normalisation.** ``frmse`` is reported per shell in the same units as
  ``rmse`` (``sqrt(shell_energy)``), then averaged within each band, instead
  of PDEBench's ``/n * L`` scaling, so the numbers are comparable across
  resolutions.
- **Boundary RMSE** averages over every boundary node once per face, as in
  PDEBench, for any dimension.

``vrmse`` and ``pearson`` follow The Well (Ohana et al., NeurIPS 2024 Datasets &
Benchmarks; ``the_well/benchmark/metrics/spatial.py``, BSD-2-Clause), so
numbers can be compared with its leaderboard: VRMSE = sqrt(MSE / Var(target)),
computed per sample/channel/time and then averaged. Unlike nRMSE it does not
reward predicting the mean of a field with a large offset.

Layout: arrays are ``(..., *space)`` -- any leading axes (batch, time,
channel) followed by ``ndim`` spatial axes.

functions.name: spectral_error_shells
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray, ndim: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Mean-square error per integer radial wavenumber shell.

Returns ``(..., n_shells)`` with ``sum(axis=-1) == mean((pred-target)**2)``
over the spatial axes (Parseval), shells ``0 .. floor(max |m|)``.

functions.name: field_error_metrics
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, target: np.ndarray, *, ndim: int, bands: Sequence[int] = (4, 12), eps: float = 1e-12) -> FieldErrorReport
functions.doc:
Compute :class:`FieldErrorReport` for ``pred`` vs ``target``.

``bands = (i_low, i_high)``: shells ``[0, i_low)`` are "low",
``[i_low, i_high)`` "mid", ``[i_high, ...)`` "high" (PDEBench defaults 4, 12).
Every metric is computed per leading index and then averaged.

children.summary: PDEBench-style error metrics for gridded fields (NumPy, no torch).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.gallery
children.doc:
The ending every example in ``examples/validation/`` shares (#705): the validation report of a good model, the
trust card, the outputs ``pinneapple check`` reads in CI, and one real failure the checks catch on a broken variant.

:func:`conclude` compares the two reports, requires the expected check to fail on the broken model and not on the
good one, writes ``report.json`` / ``trust_card.json`` / ``report.sarif`` / ``failure.json`` and returns a
:class:`GalleryResult`. The gallery test runs every example at smoke size and checks these results.

functions.name: conclude
functions.sig: (name: str, good, bad, *, expect: str, family, physics, out_dir: str | Path | None = None) -> GalleryResult
functions.doc:
``good`` / ``bad``: :class:`ValidationReport` of the model and of its broken variant. ``expect``: the id (or
id prefix) of the check that must catch the failure. Raises ``AssertionError`` when it does not.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.metamorphic
children.doc:
Metamorphic tests for surrogates: relations between inputs and outputs that physics guarantees whatever the true
answer is, so a model can be tested where no reference solution exists (NumPy only; any callable model).

A relation transforms a sampled input, runs the model on both, and measures how far the outputs are from what the
relation requires, relative to the output scale. The worst sample is kept as the counterexample.

Relations
---------
``Symmetry``
    ``f(T x) = S(x, f(x))``: reflect or rotate the input field or geometry, and the output transforms accordingly
    (``reflect_field``, ``rotate_field`` build ``T``/``S`` for gridded fields).
``Similarity``
    Dimensionless groups unchanged, so the dimensionless output is unchanged: ``g(T x, f(T x)) = g(x, f(x))`` (same
    Reynolds number at another size or speed, same Biot or Fourier number, Darcy with ``a`` and ``f`` scaled
    together).
``Invariance``
    A change that must not move the output at all (``f(T x) = f(x)``), e.g. the thermal resistance of a linear
    conduction-convection model under a change of power.
``Monotonicity``
    More of an input gives no less (or no more) of an output: more heat input, no lower peak temperature; more air
    speed, no higher thermal resistance; larger permeability, no larger pressure drop.
``Superposition``
    Linear problems (Darcy with a fixed coefficient, linear elasticity, heat conduction):
    ``f(a + b) = f(a) + f(b)`` (with ``f(0)`` subtracted for affine maps) and optionally ``f(c a) = c f(a)``.
``ResolutionConsistency``
    For operators: a conserved or integral quantity of the output is the same when the input is given at another
    resolution.

Search
------
:func:`check_relations` draws inputs from a sampler (random search, vectorised) and, with ``search="hypothesis"``
when the ``hypothesis`` package is installed, also asks hypothesis for a violating sample (property-based search over
the sampler's seed or the input box, with shrinking). The worst violation found is returned as evidence.

Inputs can be anything the model takes: a batch array ``(n, ...)`` (fields) or a dict of ``(n,)`` columns (tabular
models such as the zoo predictors, whose outputs are dicts). ``output=`` selects an output column when the model
returns a dict.

classes.name: Relation
classes.doc: Base class. ``violations(model, x)`` returns ``(per-sample relative violation, evidence per sample)``.

methods.name: violations
methods.sig: (model: Callable, x: Batch) -> tuple[np.ndarray, dict[str, Any]]

classes.name: Symmetry
classes.doc:
``f(T x) = S(x, f(x))``: ``transform_in(x)``; ``transform_out(x, y)`` acts on the output in the model's own
form (array or dict) and defaults to the identity.
fields: transform_out: Callable[[Batch, Any], Any] | None = None

classes.name: Similarity
classes.doc: ``g(T x, f(T x)) = g(x, f(x))`` with ``dimensionless(x, y) -> array`` (default: the output itself).
fields: dimensionless: Callable[[Batch, Any], Any] | None = None

classes.name: Monotonicity
classes.doc:
``output`` does not decrease (``direction=+1``) or increase (``-1``) when ``input`` grows.

For dict inputs, ``input`` names a column and the step is ``step`` times the width of the sampler's box (the
increased point is clipped into the box). For other inputs pass ``increase(x) -> x'`` instead. The violation is
the size of the move in the wrong direction relative to the spread (standard deviation) of the output over the
samples, so an offset such as an ambient temperature does not hide it (0 when the relation holds).
fields: bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None

classes.name: Superposition
classes.doc:
``f(a + b) - f0 = (f(a) - f0) + (f(b) - f0)`` with ``f0 = f(0)`` when ``affine`` (else 0); with
``homogeneity`` also ``f(c a) - f0 = c (f(a) - f0)``. ``combine(a, b, ca, cb)`` forms ``ca a + cb b`` (default:
arrays, or the ``linear_inputs`` columns of a dict, other columns taken from ``a``).
fields: combine: Callable[[Batch, Batch, float, float], Batch] | None = None

classes.name: ResolutionConsistency
classes.doc:
``q(f(x)) = q(f(restrict(x)))``: ``restrict`` maps the input batch to another resolution, ``quantity`` maps an
output batch to ``(n, k)`` integral quantities (default: the mean over all non-batch axes).

functions.name: box_sampler
functions.sig: (bounds: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]], fixed: Mapping[str, float] | None = None, log: Sequence[str] = ()) -> Sampler
functions.doc: Uniform (or log-uniform for names in ``log``) samples in a box of named inputs, as a dict of columns.

functions.name: field_sampler
functions.sig: (make: Callable[[np.random.Generator], np.ndarray]) -> Sampler
functions.doc: Batch of fields from a one-sample generator ``make(rng) -> array``.

functions.name: reflect_field
functions.sig: (axis: int) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Reflect a batch of fields ``(n, *space)`` along spatial ``axis`` (0-based, after the batch axis).

functions.name: rotate_field
functions.sig: (k: int = 1, axes: tuple[int, int] = (0, 1)) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Rotate a batch of fields ``(n, *space)`` by ``k`` quarter turns in the plane of two spatial axes.

functions.name: check_relations
functions.sig: (model: Callable, relations: Sequence[Relation], sampler: Sampler, *, n: int = 64, seed: int = 0, search: str = 'random', max_examples: int = 50) -> MetamorphicReport
functions.doc:
Run every relation on ``n`` samples (``search="random"``) and, with ``search="hypothesis"``, add a
property-based search for a violating sample (falls back to random search, noted, when hypothesis is missing).

functions.name: relations_from_spec
functions.sig: (spec: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]]) -> list[Relation]
