children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.physics_learning
children.doc:
Physics learning verification: has a model learned the physics, or only a low loss?

A low physics loss (the residual on the model's own collocation points) and a low held-out error (on the training
distribution) do not show that a model responds to causes as the physics does. This verifier tests the *learned
relations* themselves, independently of the training loss:

``intervention:*``
    Change one cause (power, source location, a conductivity, the cooling, a contact resistance the model was
    never given) and compare the model's response with the reference solver's response to the same change, at
    informative points and on the peak temperature: magnitude and sign. The expected responses are solved, not
    hand-written rules.
``residual``, ``interface_flux``, ``boundary:*``, ``energy_balance``
    The governing equation inside each layer, continuity of heat flux across each interface, the boundary
    conditions, and the global heat balance -- on the model's own field, at points chosen by the verifier.
``symmetry``, ``scaling``
    The mirror image of the source gives the mirror field; twice the power gives twice the temperature rise
    (linear conduction).
``neighbour_consistency``
    Inside a layer the field is harmonic, so its value equals the mean over a small circle around the point
    (mean-value property): a stencil-free consistency test between a point and its neighbours.
``sufficiency``
    For each informative point, does the model's *input* set contain every cause that changes the physics there?
    The reference sensitivity of the temperature at the point to each physical parameter (over a plausible
    variation) is compared with the parameters the model takes; points where an omitted cause matters are listed
    -- no training could make the model right there.

Informative points (:func:`select_points`) are chosen from the physics instead of sweeping the domain: the largest
reference responses to the interventions, the interfaces, the source, the boundaries, spread out by a farthest-point
rule. :func:`baselines` computes what the usual metrics would say (the PINN-style physics loss at random collocation
points, the held-out error on the training distribution), so a report can show what each catches.

Knowledge built into an architecture is told from learned knowledge by re-running the structural checks on the
model with *untrained* weights (``Model.reinit``): a property that holds for random weights is guaranteed by the
architecture; one that holds only after training is learned (and here demonstrated); otherwise not demonstrated.

The case (geometry, parameters, reference) is :class:`.physics_learning_cases.Section`; the result is a
:class:`VerificationReport` with a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`.

methods.name: failed
methods.doc:
Failed checks within the model's scope (interventions on causes it does not take are reported, and
listed by ``out_of_scope``, but are not defects of the model).

functions.name: select_points
functions.sig: (case: Section, theta: dict, k: int = 48, seed: int = 0, interventions = INTERVENTIONS, pool: int = 3000) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[str]]
functions.doc:
``k`` informative points: scored by the reference's own response to every intervention, plus quotas near
each interface, the source and the boundaries; spread by farthest-point sampling within each group.

functions.name: random_points
functions.sig: (case: Section, k: int, seed: int = 0) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: fv_residual
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section, th: dict, rows: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Finite-volume residual of the model's own values on the given cells: ``K T_model - f`` on those rows only
(the model is evaluated at the cell centres of each row's stencil), in W/m, relative to the larger of the mean
heat per column and the cell's own source. Zero for the reference; truncation-sized for a smooth exact field;
large where the model breaks the equation, an interface condition or a boundary condition.

functions.name: structural_checks
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section, theta: dict, X: np.ndarray, probes: bool = True) -> list[Finding]
functions.doc:
Checks on the model's own field that need no reference values: the discrete residual of the governing
equation inside the layers, across the interfaces and on each boundary (on the cells of the informative points
and of a sparse set of probes, never the whole grid), the global heat balance, mean-value consistency between a
point and its neighbours, symmetry and scaling.

functions.name: intervention_checks
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section, theta: dict, X: np.ndarray, interventions = INTERVENTIONS) -> list[Finding]
functions.doc: Response of the model to each intervention against the reference response, at ``X`` and on the peak.

functions.name: sufficiency
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section, theta: dict, X: np.ndarray) -> tuple[Finding, list[dict]]
functions.doc:
For each point, the physical parameters outside the model's inputs whose plausible variation changes the
reference temperature there by more than ``TOL['sufficiency']`` x the local temperature rise.

functions.name: verify
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section | None = None, theta: dict | None = None, *, k: int = 48, seed: int = 0, points: np.ndarray | None = None, probes: bool = True) -> VerificationReport
functions.doc:
All checks of the module docstring on ``model`` at ``theta`` (default: the nominal point). ``points``:
use these instead of :func:`select_points`; ``probes=False``: no interface and boundary probe cells (the
random-point ablation).

functions.name: baselines
functions.sig: (model: Model, case: Section | None = None, *, n_theta: int = 12, n_points: int = 400, seed: int = 1) -> dict
functions.doc:
What the usual metrics say, on the training distribution (:func:`.physics_learning_cases.
training_distribution`): the relative L2 error at random points (held-out error), and a physics loss -- the
mean squared discrete residual (as :func:`fv_residual`) at random cells, which is what a PINN's loss averages.

functions.name: detection_study
functions.sig: (severities = (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0), budgets = (4, 8, 16, 48), *, seed: int = 0, extra_models: list[Model] | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Detection of the verifier against the usual metrics: every defective model of
:func:`.physics_learning_cases.defective_models` at each severity, the controls of
:func:`.physics_learning_cases.good_models` (false alarms), the verifier with informative points against the
same checks on random points at equal budgets, and the baselines with :data:`BASELINE_LIMITS`.

children.summary: Physics learning verification: has a model learned the physics, or only a low loss?

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.physics_learning_cases
children.doc:
Verification case for :mod:`.physics_learning`: a cross-section of a die, TIM and lid heated at the junction.

Steady conduction in ``(x, z)`` per unit depth (W/m, temperature rise above ambient):

* die (silicon, 100 um, ``k_die``), TIM (30 um, ``k_tim``), lid (copper, 500 um, ``k_lid``), ``L = 2 mm`` wide;
* a Gaussian line source of ``P`` W/m at the bottom of the die, centred at ``x_s`` (fraction of ``L``), width
  ``sigma`` (fraction of ``L``);
* Robin cooling ``h`` on the top of the lid, adiabatic sides and bottom;
* an optional contact resistance ``R_c`` (m^2 K / W) on the die/TIM interface.

The reference is the cell-centred finite-volume scheme of :mod:`pinneapple_condense.fv` on a fine grid (milliseconds
per solve), so every expected response of the verifier comes from solving the physics, not from a rule.

``theta`` is a dict over :data:`PARAMS`; :data:`TRAIN_BOX` is the domain the models under test were built for.
:func:`defective_models` builds the deliberately defective models of the report (low loss and low mean error, wrong
in one physical respect each) and :func:`good_models` the controls.

classes.name: Section
classes.doc: Grid and reference solver of the cross-section.

methods.name: interfaces
methods.doc: z of the die/TIM and TIM/lid interfaces (m).

methods.name: source
methods.doc: Line-source density (W/m^2 into the bottom face, per unit depth).

methods.name: solve
methods.doc: Reference temperature rise on the cell centres, shape ``(nx, nz_total)``.

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
Reference at arbitrary points ``X`` (N, 2) in metres: a cubic spline through the cell centres of each
layer, so the field is smooth inside a layer and keeps its kink at the interfaces (derivatives of the
reference are meaningful for the checks).

methods.name: outflow
methods.doc: Reference heat leaving through the top (W/m).

classes.name: Model
classes.doc:
A model under test: ``fn(X, theta) -> T`` with ``X`` (N, 2) metres; ``inputs``: the parameters it takes
(others are fixed at :data:`DEFAULT` inside it); ``reinit``: a copy with untrained weights (for networks), used
to tell properties built into the architecture from learned ones.

functions.name: good_models
functions.sig: (sec: Section, amplitudes = (0.003,), modes = (1,)) -> list[Model]
functions.doc:
Controls: the reference itself, and the reference with smooth errors ``a cos(2 pi j x / L)`` that respect the
boundary conditions and the mirror symmetry (good but imperfect models).

functions.name: defective_models
functions.sig: (sec: Section, severity: float = 1.0) -> list[Model]
functions.doc:
Each is accurate on the training distribution by the usual metrics and wrong in one physical respect.
``severity`` scales each defect (1: the size described in the report; the out-of-box and spurious-correlation
models have no size).

functions.name: training_distribution
functions.sig: (n: int, rng: np.random.Generator, *, correlated: bool = True) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Parameter samples like the ones the models under test were trained on: ``k_tim`` near its nominal value,
and (``correlated``) the cooling tied to the power, ``h = 1e2 P`` -- as in a data set taken from one product
line. The usual held-out metrics are computed on this distribution.

functions.name: surrogate_model
functions.sig: (sec: Section, n_train: int = 48, *, correlated: bool = True, seed: int = 0) -> Model
functions.doc:
A POD + Gaussian-process surrogate of the whole field over ``(P, x_s, k_tim, h)`` trained on reference
solutions. ``correlated``: on :func:`training_distribution` (cooling tied to power, ``k_tim`` near nominal, as
data from one product line would be); otherwise on independent uniform samples of :data:`TRAIN_BOX`.

functions.name: pinn_model
functions.sig: (sec: Section, *, hard_sides: bool = False, adam_steps: int = 3000, lbfgs_steps: int = 500, n_collocation: int = 3000, seed: int = 0, theta: dict | None = None)
functions.doc:
A physics-informed network for the nominal case, trained with :func:`.pinn.train_pinn`: one sub-network
output per layer, the conduction equation inside each layer, continuity of temperature and heat flux on both
interfaces, the source flux on the bottom, Robin cooling on the top and adiabatic sides as soft constraints.
``hard_sides``: the lateral coordinate enters through ``cos(pi x / L)``, so the sides are adiabatic for any
weights (a property of the architecture). Returns ``(Model, info)``; the model takes no parameters.

children.summary: Verification case for .physics_learning: a cross-section of a die, TIM and lid heated at the junction.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.pinn
children.doc:
PINN validation (#703): the residual at points never used in training, detectors for the known failure modes, the
exact-solution gate and a training-time monitor.

A PINN's training loss is measured on its own collocation points and mixes the residual with boundary and initial
terms, so a low loss says little about the solution. :func:`validate_pinn` evaluates a trained network on fresh points
and names what went wrong:

``pinn.residual``
    The PDE residual on a dense uniform grid, on fresh random points and on adaptive points (the neighbourhood of the
    largest residuals of a large random sample): RMS and maximum, normalised by the problem's residual scale; the map
    on the grid is in the evidence.
``pinn.trivial``
    Near-trivial solution: the spread and the gradient energy of the field against the exact solution's (or the
    problem's expected scale). A network that stopped near its initial, nearly constant state fails here.
``pinn.causality``
    Propagation failure in time (compare Wang, Sankaran & Perdikaris 2022, "Respecting causality is all you need"):
    the residual concentrated at late times, or -- with an exact solution -- an error that grows in time while the
    residual stays small (a solution of the PDE that did not come from the initial condition).
``pinn.boundary`` / ``pinn.initial``
    Boundary and initial conditions on fresh points, against the solution scale. When they fail while the residual
    passes, the condition was traded off against the residual (a boundary weight too small).
``pinn.spectrum``
    Frequency content against the exact solution (``validation.spectral``), or of the operator ``L[u]`` against the
    forcing ``f`` when there is no exact solution: a PINN's spectral bias is missing high-band energy.
``pinn.exact``
    Relative L2 and maximum error against the exact solution, where one exists (manufactured solutions, Cole-Hopf for
    Burgers, Kovasznay).

Built-in problems: :func:`burgers_1d` (Cole-Hopf by quadrature), :func:`poisson_2d` (manufactured) and
:func:`kovasznay` (steady Navier-Stokes). Any other problem is a :class:`PINNProblem` with a residual written with
:func:`d` (autograd derivatives). :class:`PINNMonitor` runs the same checks every N epochs and stops a training run
on a failure mode.

classes.name: PINNProblem
classes.doc:
What :func:`validate_pinn` needs to know about a problem.

``residual(u, X)``: the PDE residual(s), ``(N, k)``, from the network output ``u`` ``(N, m)`` at ``X`` (``(N, dim)``,
requires grad; use :func:`d`). ``boundary(n, rng)`` / ``initial(n, rng)``: fresh points and target values
``(n, m)`` (NaN where an output is unconstrained). ``exact(X)``: ``(N, m)`` numpy. ``lhs`` / ``forcing``: the
operator and right-hand side, ``L[u] = f``, for the spectrum check without an exact solution. ``scale``: the
magnitude of the solution; ``residual_scale``: of the terms of the PDE (the residual is reported relative to it).
fields: boundary: Callable[[int, np.random.Generator], tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]] | None = None
initial: Callable[[int, np.random.Generator], tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]] | None = None
lhs: Callable[[Any, Any], Any] | None = None

methods.name: failure_modes
methods.doc: The failing checks, most specific diagnosis first (the residual and the exact error are symptoms).

classes.name: PINNMonitor
classes.sig: (problem: PINNProblem | str, *, every: int = 100, warmup: int = 0, patience: int = 2, stop_on: Sequence[str] = ('pinn.trivial', 'pinn.causality', 'pinn.boundary', 'pinn.initial'), n_points: int = 1024, grid: Sequence[int] | None = (32, 32), **kw)
classes.doc:
The checks of :func:`validate_pinn` every ``every`` epochs during training.

Call ``monitor(model, epoch)`` from the training loop; it returns the report when it ran (else None) and sets
``stop`` once a failure mode in ``stop_on`` (check ids, e.g. ``"pinn.boundary"``) has failed ``patience`` times
in a row after ``warmup`` epochs (early on, every network is near-trivial). ``history`` keeps (epoch, failing
ids). Small ``n_points`` and ``grid`` keep it cheap.

functions.name: d
functions.sig: (u, X, i: int, order: int = 1)
functions.doc: ``d^order u / d X_i^order`` by autograd (``u``: ``(N,)`` or ``(N, 1)``, ``X``: ``(N, dim)`` with grad).

functions.name: validate_pinn
functions.sig: (model, problem: PINNProblem | str, *, n_points: int = 4096, grid: Sequence[int] | None = None, train_points: np.ndarray | None = None, tolerances: dict[str, float] | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> PINNReport
functions.doc:
Validate a trained PINN ``model`` (a torch module or callable ``X -> u``) on ``problem``.

``train_points``: the collocation points used in training, if known, to report the residual there next to the
fresh-point residual (a ratio well above 1 is overfitting the collocation set). ``tolerances`` override
:data:`TOLERANCES`.

functions.name: mlp
functions.sig: (n_in: int, n_out: int, width: int = 32, depth: int = 4, activation: str = 'tanh')
functions.doc:
A multilayer perceptron, the usual PINN network: ``depth`` hidden layers of ``width``, activation ``"tanh"``
or ``"gaussian"`` (``exp(-z^2)``).

functions.name: train_pinn
functions.sig: (problem: PINNProblem | str, model = None, *, n_collocation: int = 2000, n_condition: int = 400, adam_steps: int = 1500, lbfgs_steps: int = 1000, lr: float = 0.002, weights: dict[str, float] | None = None, monitor: PINNMonitor | None = None, seed: int = 0, data: tuple | None = None, callback: Callable[[int, float], None] | None = None)
functions.doc:
Train a PINN on ``problem`` with soft constraints: Adam, then L-BFGS; loss = mean squared residual (relative to
the residual scale) + ``weights["boundary"]`` x boundary + ``weights["initial"]`` x initial misfit (default 10
each; 0 drops the term). ``monitor`` is called every Adam step and ends training when it sets ``stop``.

``problem.constraints`` (residual conditions such as Neumann) add ``weights["constraint"]`` (default 10) x their
mean square; ``data=(X, Y)`` adds ``weights["data"]`` (default 10) x the misfit to observations (NaN in ``Y``:
unobserved), which with trainable coefficients inside ``problem.residual`` makes an inverse PINN. ``callback(step,
loss)`` is called every Adam step.

Returns ``(model, info)`` with ``info = {"train_points", "steps", "stopped", "loss", "history"}``. A plain
reference trainer for testing the checks, not a tuned one.

functions.name: cole_hopf
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, t: np.ndarray, nu: float, n: int = 2001) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Exact solution of ``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx``, ``u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x)``, by the Cole-Hopf transform (the
heat-kernel integral, trapezoidal rule over 10 standard deviations, exponent shifted for range).

functions.name: burgers_1d
functions.sig: (nu: float = 0.05 / math.pi) -> PINNProblem
functions.doc:
``u_t + u u_x = nu u_xx`` on ``x in [-1, 1], t in [0, 1]``, ``u(x, 0) = -sin(pi x)``, ``u(+-1, t) = 0``
(Raissi et al. 2019 with a larger viscosity by default). Inputs ``(x, t)``; exact by Cole-Hopf.

functions.name: poisson_2d
functions.sig: (kx: int = 1, ky: int = 2, exact: bool = True) -> PINNProblem
functions.doc:
``-lap u = f`` on the unit square, ``u = 0`` on the boundary, manufactured ``u = sin(kx pi x) sin(ky pi y)``.
``exact=False`` hides the exact solution (the spectrum check then compares ``-lap u`` with ``f``).

functions.name: kovasznay
functions.sig: (re: float = 40.0) -> PINNProblem
functions.doc:
Steady incompressible Navier-Stokes, Kovasznay (1948) flow on ``[-0.5, 1] x [-0.5, 1.5]``; outputs
``(u, v, p)``, velocity prescribed on the boundary (the same flow as the dataset ``kovasznay_ns``); the pressure
is compared up to a constant.

functions.name: problem_from_spec
functions.sig: (spec, model, *, ctx: dict | None = None) -> PINNProblem
functions.doc:
A :class:`PINNProblem` from a PDE ``ProblemSpec`` (``ProblemBuilder(...).build()`` or a preset factory): the
box of ``spec.domain_bounds`` and the residual the solver trains on
(:func:`pinneapple_physics.pinn_solver.compiler.pointwise_residual`), evaluated with ``model``. ``ctx`` gives what
the residual needs beyond the spec (``{"source_fn": f}`` for a Poisson source); without it a source is zero.
No exact solution is attached, so the checks that need one report "not applicable".

functions.name: resolve_problem
functions.sig: (problem, model, *, ctx: dict | None = None) -> PINNProblem
functions.doc: A preset name, a :class:`PINNProblem` (anything with ``.mesh``) or a PDE ``ProblemSpec`` -> a PINNProblem.

children.summary: PINN validation (#703): the residual at points never used in training, detectors for the known failure modes, the exact-solution gate and a training-time monitor.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.report_artifact
children.doc:
The validation report as an artifact (#706): a versioned JSON schema, provenance hashes, the difference between two
reports (what a new model version lost), a section for a Hugging Face model card, a badge, and signatures.

``REPORT_SCHEMA``
    JSON schema of ``validation-report/v1`` (the output of ``pp.validate(...).to_dict()``); :func:`check_report`
    validates a report against it and against the check-ID vocabulary of :mod:`.schema`.

    relative tolerance, and changes in the validity envelope. :attr:`ReportDiff.regressed` is what a release gate
    blocks on (``scripts/zoo/validation_reports.py check``, run by the zoo publishing workflow).

    shields.io endpoint badge.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.rollout
children.doc:
Rollout validation of autoregressive surrogates (#701): invariant drift, energy spectrum over the horizon,
divergence time ("trust horizon") and long-run statistics without a reference trajectory.

An autoregressive model can look accurate for a few steps and then drift, lose energy, blur or blow up. Given a
rollout ``pred`` of shape ``(T, ...)`` (time first, then any leading axes, then ``ndim`` spatial axes) and,
optionally, the reference trajectory ``ref`` from the same initial state:

``invariant_series`` / ``invariant_drift``
    Conserved or slowly varying quantities (mass, energy, enstrophy, momentum, or any callable) along the rollout:
    their drift rate (least-squares slope relative to the initial value) and, with a reference, the largest relative
    deviation from the reference's own series (decaying turbulence loses energy; the model must lose it at the same
    rate).
``spectral_drift``
    The high-wavenumber energy ratio (``validation.spectral``) at every horizon, against the reference at that time
    or against the training statistics (a reference spectrum). Spectral blurring is a falling ratio.
``divergence_time``
    The first horizon where the pointwise error, the spectral bias or an invariant deviation crosses its tolerance;
    the trust horizon is the earliest of them.
``long_run_statistics``
    For chaotic systems, where pointwise error is meaningless after a few Lyapunov times: the histogram of the field
    (Wasserstein-1 distance), the temporal autocorrelation (decorrelation time) and the time-averaged spectrum,
    compared with a long reference run, relative to the distance between two halves of the reference itself (the
    sampling noise floor).
``validate_rollout``
    All of the above as ``rollout.*`` checks for ``pp.validate`` and the trust card.

functions.name: rollout
functions.sig: (step: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray], u0: np.ndarray, n_steps: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``(n_steps + 1, ...)`` states of an autoregressive model ``step(u) -> u_next`` from ``u0``; stops early
(and returns what it has) when the state stops being finite.

functions.name: invariant_series
functions.sig: (traj: np.ndarray, ndim: int, invariants: Sequence[str] | Mapping[str, Callable] = ('mass', 'energy')) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``{name: (T,) series}`` (leading axes averaged).

functions.name: invariant_drift
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ndim: int, ref: np.ndarray | None = None, *, dt: float = 1.0, invariants: Sequence[str] | Mapping[str, Callable] = ('mass', 'energy'), window: int = 1) -> dict[str, dict]
functions.doc:
Per invariant: ``rate`` (slope / scale, per unit time), ``max_drift`` (largest |I(t) - I(0)| / scale) and,
with ``ref``, ``max_deviation`` (largest |I_pred(t) - I_ref(t)| / scale, both averaged over ``window`` frames).
The scale is the invariant's largest magnitude (for ``mass``: the mean of ``|u|``).

functions.name: spectral_drift
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ndim: int, ref: np.ndarray | None = None, *, ref_spectrum: np.ndarray | None = None, periodic: bool = True, window: int = 1, floor: float = 1e-06) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
High-wavenumber energy bias ``E_pred / E_ref - 1`` at every horizon, the band being the top third of the
shells the reference resolves (energy above ``floor`` times its peak: amplitudes below 0.1 % of the peak are
round-off for a float32 model, not content); against ``ref[t]`` (same initial state) or a fixed reference spectrum (e.g. the
mean spectrum of the training data). Energies are averaged over ``window`` frames first, so the fluctuations of a
chaotic state do not count as bias. Returns ``hf_bias`` (``(T,)``) and the ``band``.

functions.name: divergence_time
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, *, dt: float = 1.0, err_tol: float = 0.2, spec_tol: float = 0.25, inv_tol: float = 0.05, periodic: bool = True, invariants: Sequence[str] | Mapping[str, Callable] = ('mass', 'energy'), window: int = 10) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
First horizon (in time units, ``dt`` per frame) where each criterion crosses its tolerance, and the trust
horizon (the earliest). ``None`` = never crossed within the rollout. A non-finite state crosses everything.
The spectral and invariant criteria use ``window``-frame running means (statistics, not instantaneous values).

functions.name: long_run_statistics
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, *, dt: float = 1.0, burn_in: int = 0, periodic: bool = True) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Compare invariant measures of a long model run with a long reference run (no common initial state needed).

``w1`` (Wasserstein-1 of the value histograms), ``tau`` (decorrelation times) and ``spectrum`` (largest |log
ratio| of the time-averaged energy in the low, mid and high thirds of the resolved shells), each also for the two
halves of ``ref`` -- the distance sampling alone produces. A model is consistent when its distances are within a
small multiple of that floor (default 2).

functions.name: validate_rollout
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ndim: int, ref: np.ndarray | None = None, *, dt: float = 1.0, conserved: Sequence[str] = (), invariants: Sequence[str] | Mapping[str, Callable] = ('mass', 'energy'), long_ref: np.ndarray | None = None, burn_in: int = 0, periodic: bool = True, window: int = 10, chaotic: bool = False, tolerances: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> RolloutReport
functions.doc:
``rollout.*`` checks of a model rollout (status pass / fail / not-applicable with evidence).

``ref``: the reference trajectory from the same initial state; ``conserved``: invariants that must stay constant
(checked without a reference; built-in names or keys of ``invariants``, a mapping ``name -> f(traj, ndim)``);
``ndim = 0``: the state is a vector (particles, a ROM's coefficients), with no spatial spectrum; ``long_ref``: a long reference run for the statistics of a chaotic system (the
model's run ``pred`` must be long too); ``chaotic``: after the pointwise error crosses its tolerance the two
trajectories are decorrelated, so a later spectral or invariant crossing compares two different states of the
attractor and is reported, not failed (``rollout.statistics`` judges that regime). Tolerances: ``error``, ``spectrum``, ``invariants`` (divergence time),
``drift`` (conserved invariants, relative), ``floor`` (statistics: allowed multiple of the noise floor).

children.summary: Rollout validation of autoregressive surrogates (#701): invariant drift, energy spectrum over the horizon, divergence time ("trust horizon") and long-run statistics without a reference trajectory.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.schema
children.doc:
The vocabulary of a validation report, in one place: statuses, credibility factors and levels, and the stable check
IDs used by ``pp.validate`` (``pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate``), the trust card and ``pinneapple check``.

Other modules map their own results onto these IDs; new checks add an entry here (the report refuses unknown IDs).

Statuses
    ``pass``, ``warn``, ``fail``, ``not-applicable``. A check that cannot apply (no reference, no PDE stated, a
    tabular model asked for a spectrum) is reported as ``not-applicable`` with the reason, never silently skipped.

Credibility factors
    Modelled on NASA-STD-7009A (credibility assessment) and ASME V&V 40 (credibility factors): the evidence for a
    model is grouped by what it supports. The levels are this library's own reading of those standards, not a
    certification under them.

Credibility levels (per factor)
    0 no evidence (every check not applicable), 1 evidence contradicts the model (a critical check failed), 2 passes
    with warnings (a non-critical check failed or warned) or only qualitative evidence, 3 passes quantitative checks,
    4 passes against an independent reference or a guaranteed bound.

functions.name: spec_of
functions.sig: (check_id: str) -> CheckSpec
functions.doc:
The spec of ``check_id``; sub-checks inherit from their family (``metamorphic.symmetry.reflect-x`` ->
``metamorphic``, ``data.physics.solve`` -> ``data.physics``).

children.summary: The vocabulary of a validation report, in one place: statuses, credibility factors and levels, and the stable check IDs used by pp.validate (pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate), the trust card ...

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.spectral
children.doc:
Spectral fidelity of a predicted field: energy spectra, high-wavenumber bias, phase error, coherence, structure
functions and gradient-based errors (NumPy only, no torch).

Relative L2 error rewards smooth predictions: a blurred field can have a small L2 error and still miss the small
scales that carry heat transfer, mixing or loads. The metrics here measure what L2 hides.

``energy_spectrum``
    Radially binned spectrum ``E(k)`` of a field on a regular grid, integer shells ``k = rint(|m|)`` (``m`` the signed
    mode index), shell-summed so that ``sum_k E(k) = mean(u^2)`` (Parseval). Leading axes (samples, time, channels)
    are averaged. Non-periodic fields are mean-removed and multiplied by a Hann window normalised to unit mean square,
    so the windowed spectrum keeps the field's energy on average.
``spectral_comparison``
    Prediction against reference per shell and per band: energy ratio, phase error and coherence. The **high-wavenumber
    bias** is ``E_pred / E_ref - 1`` summed over the high band: about ``-1`` for a field with its small scales smoothed
    away, ``0`` for the reference against itself, positive for added noise. Bands are fractions of the *resolved*
    range: the shells where the reference has energy above ``floor * max(E_ref)``, so a dealiased reference (exact
    zeros above ``n / 3``) does not divide by zero.
``structure_functions``
    ``S_p(r) = <|u(x + r) - u(x)|^p>`` along each grid axis (averaged over the axes), the signed third-order function
    and the flatness ``S_4 / S_2^2`` (3 for a Gaussian field; larger at small ``r`` for an intermittent field).
``gradient_metrics``
    Errors in ``|grad u|``, in the full gradient, and for a velocity field in vorticity and strain-rate magnitude, plus
    the error of a wall flux ``-k du/dn`` on declared faces.
``spectral_fidelity``
    All of the above in one :class:`SpectralFidelityReport` with a pass/fail on the high-wavenumber bias, used by
    ``pinneapple check`` (PC704), by ``pp.benchmark`` field problems and by ``pp.validate``.

Layout: arrays are ``(..., *space)``: any leading axes followed by ``ndim`` spatial axes (as in
:mod:`pinneapple_analysis.validation.field_metrics`).

functions.name: energy_spectrum
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, ndim: int | None = None, *, periodic: bool = True, window: str | None = 'hann', kmax: int | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``(k, E)``: shell-summed spectrum of ``u`` (``(..., *space)``), ``k = 0 .. kmax`` in mode-index units
(multiply by ``2 pi / L`` for a physical wavenumber), ``sum(E) == mean(u**2)`` for a periodic field.

``kmax`` defaults to the Nyquist shell of the smallest axis: shells beyond it are only partly filled (the corners
of the box) and would bias a radial average.

functions.name: fit_power_law
functions.sig: (k: np.ndarray, E: np.ndarray, kmin: float, kmax: float) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: Least-squares fit ``E = C k^slope`` on ``kmin <= k <= kmax`` (log-log); returns ``(slope, C)``.

functions.name: spectral_comparison
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, *, periodic: bool = True, window: str | None = 'hann', bands: Sequence[float] = (1 / 3, 2 / 3), floor: float = 1e-10) -> SpectralComparison
functions.doc:
Compare the spectra of ``pred`` and ``ref`` (same shape).

``bands`` are fractions of the highest resolved shell: low ``[1, f1)``, mid ``[f1, f2)``, high ``[f2, top]``.

functions.name: high_wavenumber_bias
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, **kw) -> float
functions.doc: ``E_pred / E_ref - 1`` over the high band (see :func:`spectral_comparison`).

functions.name: structure_functions
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, ndim: int, *, orders: Sequence[int] = (2, 3), lags: Sequence[int] | None = None, periodic: bool = True) -> StructureFunctions
functions.doc:
Structure functions along each spatial axis, averaged over the axes and all leading axes.

``lags`` (grid steps) default to ``1, 2, 4, ...`` up to a quarter of the smallest axis. Order 4 is always
computed for the flatness.

functions.name: gradient_metrics
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, spacing: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, *, periodic: bool = False, vector_axis: int | None = None, walls: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = (), conductivity: float = 1.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Relative RMS errors of gradient-based quantities.

``vector_axis``: the axis of ``pred`` holding velocity components (``ndim`` of them, in the order of the spatial
axes); adds vorticity (2-D: scalar, 3-D: magnitude) and strain-rate magnitude ``sqrt(2 S:S)``. Without it the
field is a scalar and ``walls`` (``(spatial axis 0..ndim-1, side 0 or -1)``) give the error of the mean wall flux
``-conductivity du/dn`` (``n`` the outward normal).

functions.name: spectral_fidelity
functions.sig: (pred: np.ndarray, ref: np.ndarray, ndim: int, *, periodic: bool = True, window: str | None = 'hann', bands: Sequence[float] = (1 / 3, 2 / 3), tol: float = 0.25, spacing: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, vector_axis: int | None = None, walls: Sequence[tuple[int, int]] = (), conductivity: float = 1.0) -> SpectralFidelityReport
functions.doc:
Spectral fidelity of ``pred`` against ``ref``: passes when ``|hf_bias| <= tol`` (high-band energy within
``tol`` of the reference), and reports the S2 ratio at the smallest lag and the gradient errors alongside.

children.summary: Spectral fidelity of a predicted field: energy spectra, high-wavenumber bias, phase error, coherence, structure functions and gradient-based errors (NumPy only, no torch).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.validation.validate
children.doc:
``pp.validate``: one call, one validation report for a Physics AI model (#696).

``validate(model, problem, data=None, reference=None, level="standard", query=None)`` picks the checks that apply to
the model and the problem from the existing modules, runs them, and returns a :class:`ValidationReport`: per-check
evidence and a pass / warn / fail status, a credibility level per factor (``schema.FACTORS``) and a deploy decision.
A check that cannot apply is reported as not applicable with the reason.

Models: a zoo model (``pp.zoo.load(...)`` or its name), a ``torch.nn.Module`` (PyTorch, PhysicsNeMo), an ONNX file
(``.onnx``, run with onnxruntime) or any callable. Problems: a zoo model's own card (``problem=None``), ``"darcy_2d"``
(or ``{"pde": "darcy", "f": 1.0}``: field operators ``a -> u`` on the cell-centred grid of
``operator_benchmarks.darcy_2d``), or a small spec ``{"valid_range": {...}, "relations": [...]}`` for a tabular
callable.

What runs (``level``):

=================  ==============================================================================================
``quick``          applicability (validity range, training envelope), solution verification (guaranteed residual
                   bound, flux balance), reference error, the zoo gate, the method's catalog status
``standard``       + spectral fidelity, metamorphic relations, the data audit, the calibrated error bound
``thorough``       + robustness to input perturbations; fault injection (#697) and rollout checks (#701) when they
                   apply
=================  ==============================================================================================

The modules it composes: ``uncertainty.residual_bound`` (#699), ``validation.spectral`` (#702),
``validation.metamorphic`` and ``pinneapple_hub.zoo.relations`` (#698), ``pinneapple_data.audit`` (#700),
``pinneapple_hub.zoo.validate`` (the zoo gate), ``physics_audit.assumptions.Envelope`` (applicability) and
``pinneapple_catalog`` (method status).

methods.name: decision
methods.doc: ``fail`` when a critical check fails, ``warn`` when a non-critical one fails or any warns, else ``pass``.

methods.name: verdict
methods.doc: The deploy verdict in one line, e.g. ``fail: out of validity range``.

methods.name: credibility
methods.doc: Credibility level per factor (``schema.LEVELS``) with the checks behind it.

methods.name: to_trust_report
methods.doc: The same evidence as a :class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport` (the trust card's decision).

methods.name: to_check_report
methods.doc:
A ``pinneapple check`` report (SARIF, JUnit, GitHub annotations through ``pinneapple_check.report``):
one outcome per check that has a rule; warnings keep their rule's severity but pass.

methods.name: render
methods.doc: ``json``, ``html``, ``text``, or a ``pinneapple check`` format (``sarif``, ``junit``, ``github``).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification
pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_critique
children.doc:
Adversarial review of a proposed Physics-AI architecture/pipeline
design -- "assume the role of a Principal Engineer trying to prove this
architecture is wrong" as a structured, checked-menu LLM tool, not free-
form commentary.

Why a fixed checklist instead of an open-ended "critique this" prompt:
the whole point of an adversarial review is to catch failure modes the
architecture's OWN author didn't think to ask about -- an open-ended
prompt tends to just restate whatever the author already emphasized. This
module forces the LLM to produce a verdict for EVERY category in
``FAILURE_MODE_CHECKLIST`` (data leakage, shortcut learning, dimensional
inconsistency, identifiability, extrapolation failure, unstable training,
bad benchmark design, misleading metrics, malformed physics constraints,
excessive simulator/solver dependency, deployment risk) -- the same
"checked menu, reject anything outside it, reject an incomplete response"
anti-hallucination pattern already used throughout this codebase
(``pinneapple_llm.cad_draft``/``geometry_draft``, and this package's own
``geometry_intelligence._llm_assign_semantics``).

This is explicitly a STRUCTURED PROMPT for a general-purpose LLM, not a
new trained classifier -- it does not (and cannot) guarantee the LLM's
critique is correct; it guarantees the critique's SHAPE is complete and
checkable (every category addressed, every verdict/severity value drawn
from a fixed vocabulary, an invented category name or verdict outside
that vocabulary is rejected rather than silently accepted) -- the same
honesty tradeoff every other LLM-facing tool in this codebase makes.

functions.name: run_adversarial_review
functions.sig: (architecture_description: str, spec: Any = None, *, provider: str = 'ollama', model: Optional[str] = None, api_key: Optional[str] = None, conversation_store: Any = None) -> AdversarialReviewReport
functions.doc:
Run a structured adversarial review of *architecture_description*
(free-text: the proposed model/pipeline design, e.g. "FNO surrogate
trained on 200 OpenFOAM runs, fine-tuned with a physics residual
loss, deployed for real-time inference") against the fixed
:data:`FAILURE_MODE_CHECKLIST`. See the module docstring for exactly
what this checked-menu design does and does not guarantee.

Parameters
----------
architecture_description : the design to critique, in plain text.
spec : optional ``ProblemSpec`` -- if given, its ``pde.kind``/coords/
    domain_bounds are included as context so the review is grounded
    in the actual physics, not just the architecture description
    alone.
provider / model / api_key / conversation_store : forwarded to
    ``pinneapple_llm.call_llm`` unchanged.

Raises
------
ValueError
    The LLM response is not valid JSON, is missing a category, names
    a category/verdict/severity outside the fixed vocabulary, or
    assigns a non-null severity to a non-"concern" verdict -- a
    hallucinated or malformed response is rejected, never silently
    accepted (the same discipline as every other checked-menu tool
    in this codebase).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation
children.doc:
Which PINNeAPPle neural architecture to reach for FIRST, given a
problem's real characteristics -- data availability, whether an existing
solver can generate more, whether the model needs to generalize across
parameters/geometry, and whether the target is a forward or inverse
problem. The sibling of ``solver_orchestration`` (which recommends among
PINNeAPPle's own classical numerical solvers) and ``tool_recommendation``
(external software) for the neural-architecture axis specifically.

This is deliberately a RECOMMENDATION-BEFORE-YOU-TRAIN tool, not a
replacement for empirical comparison. ``pinneapple_arena``'s
``physics_aware_rank()`` (train several real architectures, rank by
accuracy while flagging PDE-residual outliers) is the AFTER-you've-tried-
things tool this module's recommendation is meant to narrow down to a
short list for, not compete with -- this module has never trained
anything and makes no accuracy claim; it only says which architectures'
own well-known, documented design intent (not this module's opinion)
covers the stated problem characteristics.

Decision structure (the "PDE type x data availability x parameter-space
generalization -> architecture" pattern): the two axes that matter most
are (1) how much labeled/simulated data is available, and if none, is
there at least an existing solver to fall back on, and (2) whether the
trained model needs to generalize across a family of parameters/
geometries (an operator-learning problem) or only needs to solve ONE
fixed instance well (a function-fitting problem):

    little/no data, no solver available  -> PINN (pure physics-residual
        training -- vanilla_pinn/modified_mlp; xpinn if the domain is
        large/geometrically complex enough to benefit from domain
        decomposition)
    little/no data, solver available     -> hybrid_ml (use the solver to
        generate the missing data on demand, or as an online physics
        check during training -- not a different architecture per se,
        a data-generation strategy layered on top of whichever
        architecture the OTHER axis below recommends)
    lots of data, no generalization need -> PINN/XPINN still applies
        (a single, fixed-domain fit) -- more data mainly helps as extra
        supervision alongside the residual, not a reason by itself to
        reach for an operator-learning architecture
    lots of data, generalization need    -> a neural OPERATOR: FNO (fixed
        structured grid, periodic/near-periodic domains -- literally what
        FNO was demonstrated on, Li et al. 2020), DeepONet (irregular/
        scattered geometry, a branch/trunk split naturally handles varying
        sensor locations), MeshGraphNet (arbitrary unstructured mesh
        topology that itself varies across the family), PINO (wants BOTH
        the operator-learning generalization AND a physics-residual loss,
        not supervision alone)

**Whether to learn a model at all** (#1176). With ``solve_seconds`` (the solver's measured cost per solve) and
``n_evaluations`` (how many evaluations the study needs: a DOE, an optimisation, a Monte Carlo), the first answer
can be ``none``: call the solver directly. It is when the direct cost ``solve_seconds * n_evaluations`` is within
``direct_budget_s``, or when the study needs no more evaluations than a surrogate needs training samples (it would
not save a single solve). The reason states the numbers.

**What the chosen model must pass** before it is used: ``ArchitectureRecommendation.checks`` lists, for the first
family, the held-out error at ``accuracy_target``, no extrapolation outside the sampled ranges, and what its kind
adds (a physics residual for physics-informed models, resolution invariance for operators, calibrated
uncertainty for a Gaussian process, the solver's own checks for ``none``).

``output_kind`` (``scalar`` | ``grid_field`` | ``mesh_field`` | ``time_series``) and ``n_inputs`` describe what the
model maps: a few smooth scalars over a handful of inputs go to the KPI regressor (a Gaussian process), a field on
one grid to a grid operator, a field on varying meshes to a graph network.

``is_inverse_problem=True`` adds ``inverse_pinn``/an ``inverse_params``-
capable base architecture as a caveat/addition regardless of the other
axes, since PINNeAPPle's inverse-problem machinery
(``pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems``, see ``uncertainty_inverse.py``)
specifically expects that convention.

functions.name: recommend_architecture
functions.sig: (*, n_high_fidelity_simulations: int = 0, has_lots_of_data: Optional[bool] = None, has_analytical_solver: bool = False, needs_parameter_generalization: bool = False, geometry_varies: bool = False, is_inverse_problem: bool = False, catalog: Optional[Dict[str, ArchitectureCandidate]] = None, target_kind: Optional[str] = None, fixed_topology: Optional[bool] = None, has_physics_postprocessor: bool ...
functions.doc:
Recommend which PINNeAPPle neural architecture family to reach for
first, from the problem's own real characteristics -- see the module
docstring for the full decision structure and honesty scope (this
never claims accuracy; only documented-design-intent match).

Parameters
----------
n_high_fidelity_simulations : how many real simulation results are
    already available (or realistically obtainable) -- used to infer
    ``has_lots_of_data`` if not given explicitly.
has_lots_of_data : override the ``n_high_fidelity_simulations``-based
    threshold heuristic with a direct answer, when the caller has a
    better-informed judgment for their specific problem.
has_analytical_solver : whether an existing solver (classical or
    otherwise) could generate more training data on demand -- only
    matters when data is scarce; changes the recommendation to
    "hybrid_ml" (a data-generation STRATEGY, not a different base
    architecture) rather than a pure physics-only PINN.
needs_parameter_generalization : the trained model must generalize
    across a FAMILY of parameter values/initial-boundary conditions,
    not just solve one fixed instance.
geometry_varies : the family also varies in GEOMETRY (not just
    parameters) -- pushes the recommendation toward MeshGraphNet
    over FNO/DeepONet when combined with ``needs_parameter_generalization``.
is_inverse_problem : the unknown is a physical parameter to calibrate
    against observations, not the field itself -- adds
    ``inverse_pinn`` as a caveat/addition regardless of the other axes.
catalog : override ``ARCHITECTURE_CATALOG``. The decision tree's
    branches resolve to fixed category keys (``"pinn"``, ``"fno"``,
    ``"mesh_graph_net"``, ``"xpinn"``, ``"deeponet"``, ``"pino"``,
    ``"inverse_pinn"``), so a replacement catalog must provide entries
    under those same keys (e.g. to swap in a different
    ``registry_key``/description for one category) -- this overrides
    entry CONTENT, not the category taxonomy itself. A catalog missing
    a key some branch resolves to raises ``KeyError`` rather than
    silently falling back, so an incompatible override is caught
    immediately, not at some later, harder-to-trace call site.
solve_seconds, n_evaluations, direct_budget_s : the solver's measured cost per solve, the evaluations the
    study needs and the direct budget; with the first two, ``none`` (call the solver) can be the answer.
output_kind : ``scalar``, ``grid_field``, ``mesh_field`` or ``time_series`` (sets ``target_kind``,
    ``fixed_topology`` and ``geometry_varies`` when they are not given).
n_inputs : how many inputs vary.
accuracy_target : the relative error the model must reach on held-out solves (its first check's limit).

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification.causal_discrepancy
children.doc:
Two roadmap points from the product README's honest 21-point scope table:

Point 15 -- Causal / intervention engine
-----------------------------------------
"What happens if I increase pressure 20%?" -- ``run_intervention`` re-runs
the ``pipeline.analyze`` pipeline once as a baseline, then
once per requested parameter value with that one parameter overridden in
the drafted preset's kwargs, and reports REAL percentage changes (final
training loss, the guardrail's re-computed PDE residual, and the trained
model's own prediction at a fixed query point for every field the preset
produces) -- never a fabricated number, and never a percentage change
presented as reliable when the guardrail marked that run (or the
baseline itself) NOT TRUSTWORTHY.

``draft_problem`` is only ever invoked once (inside the single baseline
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.pipeline.analyze` call); every
perturbed run below repeats just the execution + verification steps
(``pinneapple_physics.get_preset``/``solve_pde`` and
``pinneapple_llm.PhysicsGuardrail``) with one kwarg overridden.

Cost note / future optimization (not built here): every intervention
value in this module currently retrains a PINN from scratch. A real
deployment would want to cache/reuse the baseline-trained model as a
warm start (or freeze/fine-tune) when the architecture and epoch budget
are unchanged between the baseline and the perturbed run, rather than
paying the full training cost per intervention value. Kept out of scope
for this pass; test epoch counts are kept small (100-200) specifically
to keep this honest (no shortcuts) but still fast to run for real.

Point 10 -- Model discrepancy / physics+ML hybrid model
---------------------------------------------------------
``fit_discrepancy_model`` implements the standard SciML "model-form
discrepancy" technique: Kennedy & O'Hagan, "Bayesian Calibration of
Computer Models", J. R. Stat. Soc. B, 63(3), 2001 -- the reference model
is ``y(x) = eta(x) + delta(x)``, where ``eta`` is the (imperfect) physics
model and ``delta`` is a small, separately-fit statistical correction for
whatever the physics model's structural form is missing. Here ``delta``
is a small MLP fit by ordinary MSE regression against the REAL residual
``reference_y - physics_model(reference_x)`` -- this is data regression,
not PDE-residual training, so it deliberately does not go through
``solve_pde``. Training reuses PINNeAPPle's own generic supervised
``pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer``/``TrainConfig`` (not a hand-rolled
loop) and its real ``pinneapple_data.splits.split_indices`` train/val/test
splitter, so the reported diagnostics (variance explained, RMSE) are
computed on a genuine held-out test split the correction model never saw
during training.

classes.name: DiscrepancyModel
classes.doc:
``y(x) ~= physics_model(x) + delta(x)`` -- Kennedy & O'Hagan (2001)
model-form discrepancy. ``delta`` (``correction_model``) is a small MLP
fit by MSE regression on the real residual ``reference_y -
physics_model(reference_x)``.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: The hybrid prediction: physics_model(x) + discrepancy_only(x).

fields: reference: str = "Kennedy, M. C. & O'Hagan, A. (2001). 'Bayesian Calibration of Computer Models'. J. R. Stat. Soc. B, 63(3), 425-464."

functions.name: run_intervention
functions.sig: (base_description: str, param_name: str, param_values: Sequence[float], *, physical_parameters: Optional[Dict[str, float]] = None, provider: str = 'ollama', model_name: str = 'llama3.2:3b', **analyze_kwargs) -> InterventionReport
functions.doc:
"What happens if I increase pressure 20%?" -- run the real
pipeline once as a baseline, then once per value in ``param_values``
with ``param_name`` overridden in the drafted preset's kwargs
(e.g. ``param_name="nu"`` for a Burgers preset's viscosity), and
report REAL percentage changes vs. the baseline in: final training
loss, the guardrail's re-computed PDE residual (when computable for
this preset's ``pde_kind``), and the trained model's own prediction
at one fixed query point for every field the preset produces.

``analyze_kwargs`` (``epochs``, ``n_collocation``, ``residual_threshold``,
``reference_benchmark``, ``candidate_architectures``, ``flow_geometry``,
...) are forwarded to the one baseline ``analyze()`` call exactly as
given; ``epochs``/``n_collocation``/``residual_threshold`` are then
reused (same values, not re-drafted) for every perturbed re-run so the
comparison is apples-to-apples. If more than one
``candidate_architectures`` was given, only the baseline's WINNING
architecture is retrained per intervention value (retraining the
whole shortlist per value would multiply the already-nontrivial
training cost with little extra signal for a "what if I change one
parameter" question).

functions.name: fit_discrepancy_model
functions.sig: (spec: Any, physics_model: Any, reference_x: Any, reference_y: Any, *, hidden_dim: int = 32, n_layers: int = 2, epochs: int = 400, lr: float = 0.001, batch_size: int = 32, seed: int = 42) -> DiscrepancyModel
functions.doc:
Fit a small MLP discrepancy-correction model on the real residual
between ``reference_y`` and ``physics_model(reference_x)`` (Kennedy &
O'Hagan 2001's model-form discrepancy technique -- see this module's
docstring and ``DiscrepancyModel.reference``).

``spec`` is accepted (mirroring the rest of this codebase's
``ProblemSpec``-centric API, and so a future caller already holding a
``ProblemSpec`` doesn't need to separately track ``in_dim``/``out_dim``
itself) but is not otherwise required -- the correction network's
input/output dimensions are inferred directly from
``reference_x``/``reference_y``'s own shapes, which is what actually
determines what the network needs to consume/produce.

Training is via ``pinneapple_neural.trainer.Trainer``/``TrainConfig``
(PINNeAPPle's own generic supervised trainer) with a plain MSE
``loss_fn`` -- deliberately NOT ``solve_pde``/a PDE-residual loss,
since this fits an ML correction to DATA, not a physics equation.
The train/val/test split is a real, seeded random split via
``pinneapple_data.splits.split_indices`` (re-exported as
``pinneapple_neural.trainer.splits``); diagnostics
(``variance_explained_test``, the two RMSEs) are computed ONLY on the
held-out test split, which never appears in any training batch.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification.convergence
children.doc:
Grid-convergence / mesh-independence study automation.

Public API
----------
    richardson_extrapolate(
        f_coarse, f_medium, f_fine, r, *,
        p_assumed=None, safety_factor=1.25, asymptotic_tolerance=0.10,
    ) -> ConvergenceResult

    mesh_independence_study(
        solve_fn, resolutions, quantity_extractor, *,
        refinement_ratio=None, p_assumed=None, safety_factor=1.25,
        asymptotic_tolerance=0.10,
    ) -> MeshIndependenceStudyResult

This closes the gap flagged in the capability audit: PINNeAPPle has a real
mesh-*quality* module (``mesh_intelligence.py``, geometric aspect
ratio/skewness/y+ estimates from a single mesh) and real numerical solvers
with configurable resolution (``pinneapple_simulation/numerical_solvers/
fdm.py``, ``fem.py``, ``lbm.py``, etc.), but nothing that runs a solver at
several systematically-refined resolutions and asks the orthogonal
question "is the SOLUTION converging as resolution increases, and can we
estimate the discretization error and the resolution-independent 'exact'
answer from that trend?" -- i.e. mesh-*independence*, not mesh-*quality*.

This module is deliberately solver-agnostic: it never imports anything
from ``pinneapple_simulation`` and knows nothing about FDM/FEM/LBM
specifics. ``mesh_independence_study`` takes an arbitrary ``solve_fn(resolution)``
callable and an arbitrary ``quantity_extractor(solution)`` callable, so any
solver that can be re-run at different resolutions (or any external
tool wrapped in a Python function) can be plugged in unchanged.

Formula references
-------------------
Both the apparent (observed) order of accuracy and the Grid Convergence
Index (GCI) implemented here are the standard formulas from:

    Roache, P.J., "Perspective: A Method for Uniform Reporting of Grid
    Refinement Studies," ASME Journal of Fluids Engineering, 116(3),
    405-413, 1994.

(the same formulas were later re-popularized, unchanged in substance, by
Celik, I.B. et al., "Procedure for Estimation and Reporting of Uncertainty
Due to Discretization in CFD Applications," ASME J. Fluids Eng., 130(7),
2008 -- the notation below follows that paper's widely-used f1/f2/f3
(fine/medium/coarse) labeling since it is the more commonly cited form of
the same Roache method).

Let ``r`` be the constant refinement ratio between three systematically
refined grids (``r = h_coarse/h_medium = h_medium/h_fine > 1``, e.g.
``r=2`` for grid doubling), and ``f_coarse``, ``f_medium``, ``f_fine`` the
solution's quantity of interest computed on each grid.

1. **Apparent (observed) order of accuracy** ``p``, solved from the three
   solution values themselves (no a-priori assumption about the scheme's
   nominal order is required)::

       p = ln(|(f_coarse - f_medium) / (f_medium - f_fine)|) / ln(r)

   This is the constant-refinement-ratio special case. When the ratios
   differ (``r21 = h_medium/h_fine`` and ``r32 = h_coarse/h_medium``, pass
   ``r=(r21, r32)``), ``p`` is the fixed point of Celik et al. (2008),
   Eq. (3)::

       p = |ln|eps32/eps21| + q(p)| / ln(r21)
       q(p) = ln((r21^p - s) / (r32^p - s)),  s = sign(eps32/eps21)

   with ``eps32 = f_coarse - f_medium`` and ``eps21 = f_medium - f_fine``;
   ``q`` vanishes identically when ``r21 == r32``. The extrapolation and
   the fine-grid GCI use ``r21``, the coarse-grid GCI uses ``r32``.

2. **Richardson-extrapolated ("exact", grid-independent) value**::

       f_extrapolated = (r^p * f_fine - f_medium) / (r^p - 1)

3. **Grid Convergence Index** (a standardized, physically-interpretable
   discretization-error UNCERTAINTY BAND -- not just a raw error
   estimate -- expressed as a percentage-like number), for both the
   fine-medium pair and the medium-coarse pair::

       GCI_fine   = Fs * |(f_fine - f_medium) / f_fine|     / (r^p - 1)
       GCI_coarse = Fs * |(f_medium - f_coarse) / f_medium| / (r^p - 1)

   with ``Fs`` a recommended safety factor -- **1.25** for studies using
   three or more grids (this module always requires >=3), vs. the more
   conservative **3.0** Roache originally recommended for two-grid
   studies only (not applicable here; see Roache 1994 and Celik et al.
   2008 Table 1).

4. **Asymptotic-range check**: in the true asymptotic convergence regime,
   ``GCI_coarse`` and ``GCI_fine`` are related by the refinement ratio
   raised to the observed order, i.e. ``GCI_coarse / (r^p * GCI_fine)``
   should be close to 1. This module reports that ratio directly
   (``asymptotic_ratio``) and flags ``is_asymptotic`` when it falls within
   ``asymptotic_tolerance`` of 1.0 (default 10%, a commonly-cited round
   engineering threshold -- not a universal constant, exactly like
   ``mesh_intelligence.py``'s own documented-but-configurable thresholds).

Honesty note, matching this repo's established ethic: a grid-convergence
study is only ever as good as the three solves it is built from. This
module never fabricates or smooths a value it wasn't given -- if the
three input values don't imply monotonic convergence (fine-medium and
medium-coarse differences have different signs -- oscillatory
convergence), it computes the formulas exactly as Roache/Celik define
them (using absolute values, as they do) but raises a ``UserWarning`` so
the caller knows the asymptotic assumption behind ``p``/GCI may not hold.

classes.name: ConvergenceResult
classes.doc:
The result of a three-grid Richardson extrapolation / GCI analysis.
See the module docstring's "Formula references" section for the exact
formulas and citation (Roache, 1994).
fields: citation: str = "Roache, P.J., 'Perspective: A Method for Uniform Reporting of Grid Refinement Studies', ASME J. Fluids Eng., 116(3), 405-413, 1994."

classes.name: MeshIndependenceStudyResult
classes.doc:
A full mesh-independence study: the raw per-resolution values (for
plotting a convergence curve) plus the three-finest-grid
:class:`ConvergenceResult`.

functions.name: richardson_extrapolate
functions.sig: (f_coarse: QuantityArray, f_medium: QuantityArray, f_fine: QuantityArray, r: float | Sequence[float], *, p_assumed: float | None = None, safety_factor: float = _DEFAULT_SAFETY_FACTOR, asymptotic_tolerance: float = _DEFAULT_ASYMPTOTIC_TOLERANCE) -> ConvergenceResult
functions.doc:
Richardson-extrapolate a quantity of interest computed at three
systematically-refined resolutions and compute Roache's (1994) Grid
Convergence Index. See the module docstring for the exact formulas.

Parameters
----------
f_coarse, f_medium, f_fine : the quantity of interest evaluated on the
    coarse, medium, and fine grids respectively. Each may be a plain
    Python/numpy scalar or an array (e.g. a full solution field) of
    identical shape -- if arrays, the observed order and GCI are
    computed from the L2 norm of the pairwise differences (see
    :func:`_flat_norm`), while ``extrapolated_value`` is computed
    elementwise and keeps the input's shape.
r : the refinement ratio between successive grids, e.g. ``r=2`` for
    grid doubling (``h_coarse/h_medium == h_medium/h_fine == r``), or a
    pair ``(r21, r32) = (h_medium/h_fine, h_coarse/h_medium)`` when the
    refinement is not constant (Celik et al. 2008). Each must be > 1.
p_assumed : if given, skip solving for the observed order from the
    three solution values and use this value directly for the
    extrapolation and GCI formulas instead (useful when the scheme's
    nominal order is already known/trusted, or to sanity-check a
    theoretical order against the data-derived one separately).
safety_factor : Roache/Celik's ``Fs`` -- 1.25 by default (recommended
    for studies with >=3 grids; see module docstring).
asymptotic_tolerance : relative tolerance (default 0.10 = 10%) used to
    decide ``is_asymptotic`` from ``asymptotic_ratio``.

Raises
------
ValueError
    if ``r <= 1``, or if ``f_medium`` equals ``f_fine`` (or
    ``f_coarse`` equals ``f_medium``) exactly, which would make the
    observed-order formula divide by zero -- rather than silently
    returning ``inf``/``nan``, this is reported as an explicit error
    so the caller knows the three solves did not actually differ
    enough to support a convergence-order estimate.

functions.name: mesh_independence_study
functions.sig: (solve_fn: Callable[[Any], Any], resolutions: Sequence[Any], quantity_extractor: Callable[[Any], QuantityArray], *, refinement_ratio: float | None = None, p_assumed: float | None = None, safety_factor: float = _DEFAULT_SAFETY_FACTOR, asymptotic_tolerance: float = _DEFAULT_ASYMPTOTIC_TOLERANCE) -> MeshIndependenceStudyResult
functions.doc:
Run a mesh-independence / grid-convergence study by calling an
arbitrary solver at increasing resolutions and Richardson-extrapolating
the three finest results.

This is deliberately solver-agnostic: it knows nothing about FDM, FEM,
LBM, or any other discretization scheme. ``solve_fn`` and
``quantity_extractor`` are the only two hooks -- any solver in
``pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers`` (or any external tool
wrapped in a Python callable) can be plugged in without this module
changing.

Parameters
----------
solve_fn : called as ``solve_fn(resolution)`` for each entry of
    ``resolutions``, in order; must return whatever solution object
    ``quantity_extractor`` expects (a full field, a dict, a custom
    result type -- entirely up to the caller's solver).
resolutions : an ASCENDING sequence of resolution values (e.g. grid
    point counts, cell counts, or any resolution knob the caller's
    solver accepts) representing systematically-refined grids, finest
    last. At least 3 values are required.
quantity_extractor : called as ``quantity_extractor(solution)`` on
    each of ``solve_fn``'s return values to pull out the scalar or
    array quantity of interest (e.g. a probe value, a max/L2 norm of
    the field, a drag coefficient -- whatever the study is tracking).
refinement_ratio : the constant ratio between successive resolutions'
    effective grid spacing. If not given, it is inferred from
    ``resolutions`` themselves as
    ``resolutions[i+1] / resolutions[i]`` (appropriate when
    ``resolutions`` are counts -- points/cells per some fixed domain
    length, so spacing h ~ 1/resolution and this ratio already equals
    h_coarser/h_finer); a ``UserWarning`` is raised if the inferred
    ratios are not roughly constant across the sequence (a genuine
    grid-convergence study requires a *systematic*, constant-ratio
    refinement -- Roache's formulas assume it).
p_assumed, safety_factor, asymptotic_tolerance : forwarded to
    :func:`richardson_extrapolate`.

Returns
-------
MeshIndependenceStudyResult
    The raw per-resolution quantities (for plotting a convergence
    curve) plus the :class:`ConvergenceResult` from the three finest
    resolutions.

Raises
------
ValueError
    if fewer than 3 resolutions are given, or ``resolutions`` is not
    strictly ascending.

children.summary: Grid-convergence / mesh-independence study automation.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification.dimensional_analysis
children.doc:
Real, first-principles dimensionless-number calculations + a simple,
honestly-scoped flow-regime classifier.

This is genuinely new (not previously in PINNeAPPle) and is the concrete
implementation of the user's own architectural point 3
("Dimensional analysis / scaling... o sistema deveria automaticamente
calcular e raciocinar sobre Reynolds, Prandtl, Peclet, Mach, Nusselt,
Damkohler, Fourier, Weber, Froude"). Every formula below is a standard,
textbook dimensionless group -- cited in each function's docstring --
computed directly from the physical parameters the caller supplies, not
guessed or LLM-generated. This is the layer that lets the engine
"reason automatically" about which physical regime a problem is in
*before* deciding which PDE closure/solver family is appropriate, e.g.
Stokes flow (Re << 1) needs no turbulence closure at all, while Re >
4000 in a pipe needs one.

Regime classification is DELIBERATELY simple and honestly caveated: real
transition thresholds depend on geometry (external flow past a sphere
transitions at different Re than internal pipe flow), so
``classify_flow_regime`` documents exactly which geometry its thresholds
assume, rather than presenting one universal answer as if it always
applies. This is the same "state precisely what was and wasn't checked"
ethic as the rest of this codebase.

classes.name: DimensionlessNumbers
classes.doc:
Every dimensionless group actually computable from the physical
parameters supplied to :func:`compute_dimensionless_numbers` --
fields are ``None`` when the inputs needed for that particular
number weren't given, rather than silently defaulted, so a caller
can tell "not computed" apart from "computed and happens to be
small".

functions.name: compute_dimensionless_numbers
functions.sig: (*, velocity: Optional[float] = None, length: Optional[float] = None, density: Optional[float] = None, dynamic_viscosity: Optional[float] = None, kinematic_viscosity: Optional[float] = None, thermal_diffusivity: Optional[float] = None, specific_heat: Optional[float] = None, thermal_conductivity: Optional[float] = None, mass_diffusivity: Optional[float] = None, speed_of_sound: Optional[float] = ...
functions.doc:
Compute every dimensionless number the supplied subset of
parameters actually supports. All formulas are standard textbook
definitions (e.g. Incropera & DeWitt, *Fundamentals of Heat and Mass
Transfer*; White, *Viscous Fluid Flow*):

- Reynolds:  Re = rho * U * L / mu = U * L / nu
- Prandtl:   Pr = nu / alpha = cp * mu / k
- Peclet (heat): Pe_h = Re * Pr = U * L / alpha
- Peclet (mass): Pe_m = U * L / D
- Mach:      Ma = U / c
- Froude:    Fr = U / sqrt(g * L)
- Weber:     We = rho * U^2 * L / sigma
- Damkohler (Da_I, first-order reaction vs. residence time): Da = k_rxn * t_res

functions.name: classify_flow_regime
functions.sig: (re: Optional[float], *, geometry: str = 'internal_pipe') -> str
functions.doc:
A simple, HONESTLY GEOMETRY-SPECIFIC flow-regime classification --
real transition Reynolds numbers depend on the flow geometry, so this
function requires the caller to say which one its thresholds should
assume, rather than presenting one universal answer.

geometry="internal_pipe" (fully-developed pipe/duct flow, the most
common textbook case): Re<2300 laminar, 2300<=Re<4000 transitional,
Re>=4000 turbulent (Moody-diagram convention).
geometry="external_bluff_body" (flow past a sphere/cylinder): Re<1
Stokes/creeping flow, 1<=Re<~1e3 laminar-separated wake,
Re>=~1e3-2e5 subcritical turbulent wake (order-of-magnitude, not a
sharp transition -- external-flow transitions are inherently fuzzier
than internal pipe flow).

children.summary: Real, first-principles dimensionless-number calculations + a simple, honestly-scoped flow-regime classifier.

children.name: pinneapple_analysis.verification.evidence_graph
children.doc:
A run-level Evidence Graph -- ties one analysis run's
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.provenance.ProvenanceRecord`
together with its (optional) real
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.physics_confidence_score.PhysicsConfidenceScore`
and any solver-vs-solver
:class:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.solver_orchestration.ComparisonReport`
objects into one small, queryable claim -> evidence graph.

Why this is a distinct module from ``knowledge_graph``
--------------------------------------------------------
``knowledge_graph.py`` builds ONE graph describing PINNeAPPle's general
physics knowledge (phenomena, equations, presets, references) -- it is
the same graph regardless of which run asked a question. This module
builds a DIFFERENT graph per RUN: "why should THIS specific result be
trusted", grounded only in the real checks that specific run actually
produced. It never re-derives new numbers (exactly like
``physics_confidence_score``'s anti-fabrication design) -- it is a
graph *view* over evidence objects a caller already has in hand.

Node kinds
----------
``claim``
    Exactly one root node per graph: "the result of run <run_id> is
    trustworthy". Its ``trustworthy`` attribute is ``True``/``False``/
    ``None`` (unknown -- e.g. no guardrail ran at all), taken directly
    from ``provenance.guardrail_trustworthy`` -- never computed by this
    module.
``run``
    One node carrying the run's identifying facts (problem description,
    architecture, drafted preset) straight from the ``ProvenanceRecord``.
``guardrail_check``
    One node per entry in ``provenance.guardrail_checks`` (each a real
    dict with ``name``/``passed``/``detail``, the shape every
    ``core/pipeline.py``-style caller in this codebase already produces).
``confidence_component``
    One node per :class:`ConfidenceComponent` in an optional supplied
    ``PhysicsConfidenceScore`` -- only present when a caller actually
    computed one; never fabricated here.
``solver_comparison``
    One node per optional supplied ``ComparisonReport``.

Edges always point FROM the claim node (directly or transitively via
``run``) TO the evidence that supports or contradicts it, labeled
``supports`` or ``contradicts`` based on that evidence's own real
pass/fail status -- this module never decides truth, it only routes
already-decided verdicts into a queryable shape.

functions.name: build_evidence_graph
functions.sig: (provenance, confidence = None, comparisons: Optional[List[Any]] = None) -> 'nx.DiGraph'
functions.doc:
Build a small evidence graph for one run.

Parameters
----------
provenance : pinneapple_analysis.verification.provenance.ProvenanceRecord
    The run's real provenance record. Required -- this is the only
    thing every run in this codebase always has.
confidence : Optional[pinneapple_analysis.verification.physics_confidence_score.PhysicsConfidenceScore]
    A real, already-computed confidence score (from
    ``compute_physics_confidence(...)``), if the caller has one.
comparisons : Optional[List[pinneapple_analysis.verification.solver_orchestration.ComparisonReport]]
    Real solver-vs-solver comparisons, if the caller ran any.

Returns
-------
networkx.DiGraph
    Never raises for "nothing but provenance was supplied" -- a
    graph built from provenance alone is still a valid, if smaller,
    evidence graph (mirrors ``PhysicsConfidenceScore``'s own
    ``coverage`` honesty mechanism: less evidence is represented as
    fewer nodes, never as a fabricated one).

functions.name: evidence_summary
functions.sig: (g: 'nx.DiGraph') -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A structured summary of an evidence graph -- counts of evidence
nodes by kind and by supports/contradicts, plus the claim's own
stated trustworthiness. Never re-derives trustworthiness itself.

functions.name: explain_trust
functions.sig: (g: 'nx.DiGraph') -> str
functions.doc:
A plain-text "why should I trust this" rendering of an evidence
graph -- mirrors ``knowledge_graph.explain_preset``'s pattern of
producing an LLM-context-ready string from real graph contents, but
grounded in one run's actual evidence instead of general physics
knowledge. Never invents a reason not present in the graph.
